meta.title: AI safety concern directory — source index

verified.true: The URL or address was fetched during research and the contact route was seen on the page itself.
verified.false: The route is cited by a secondary source but the page could not be read. Treat as a lead to confirm, not an address to rely on.
verified.null: Not independently checked. Applies to homepage and framework links, which were recorded as listed rather than confirmed.

entity_public_input.open: Publishes a route a member of the public can use without affiliation or credentials.
entity_public_input.limited: Has a route, but it is restricted by constituency, membership, account status, programme invitation, or language.
entity_public_input.none: Publishes no public contact route for this purpose. Recorded deliberately — absence is a finding.

value_kind.other: Postal address, phone number or free text

dataset.register: AI Safety Concern Register — 229 institutions and their contact routes.
dataset.seats: Where to Take an AI Concern — committees and bodies with AI jurisdiction.
dataset.organisations: Where to Take an AI Concern — campaigns, civil society, professional and industry bodies.

caveats: Compiled 22 September 2026. Contact routes move; named seat-holders move faster.
129 of the register's 589 routes are unverified and are marked as such.
The UK's DSIT was abolished in July 2026 and the Commons committee reverted to its former name; some register entries written against the older structure are partly stale.
The International Network of AI Safety Institutes was renamed in December 2025, dropping 'safety' from its title.
Non-US, non-EU committee entries rely on bodies reconstituted annually; Indian and Japanese chairs in particular should be re-confirmed.
No email address or URL in this dataset was generated. Where a route could not be found, the record says so rather than guessing.

institutions.name: Anthropic
institutions.remit: Safeguards team enforces the Usage Policy and runs Constitutional Classifiers; Alignment Science and Frontier Red Team run capability/misalignment evaluations feeding the Responsible Scaling Policy, overseen by a Responsible Scaling Officer.

routes.label: Model safety issues and jailbreaks
routes.scope: Safety issues, jailbreaks, harmful model behaviour. Named on both the Responsible Disclosure Policy and the Usage Policy.
routes.note: The single most useful address for a member of the public with a model-behaviour concern. Anthropic asks for 'sufficient details for us to replicate the issue'.

routes.label: Questions about the disclosure policy
routes.scope: Questions about the Responsible Disclosure Policy itself, not for submitting reports.
routes.note: Policy questions only; actual reports go to HackerOne or usersafety@.

routes.label: Responsible Disclosure Policy
routes.scope: Infrastructure vulnerabilities AND model safety. States: 'We welcome reports concerning safety issues, "jailbreaks," and similar concerns so that we can enhance the safety and harmlessness of our models.'
routes.note: Unusual among labs in explicitly putting model safety inside the disclosure policy rather than excluding it.

routes.label: HackerOne submission form
routes.scope: Vulnerability submissions under the Responsible Disclosure Policy.
routes.note: Embedded form, no HackerOne account gatekeeping described on the policy page.

routes.label: Model Safety Bug Bounty Program (application)
routes.scope: Universal jailbreaks that defeat Constitutional Classifiers, especially CBRN. Up to $35,000 per novel universal jailbreak.
routes.note: Application-only and invite-based via HackerOne; participation requires an NDA. Program details: https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12119250-model-safety-bug-bounty-program

routes.label: Usage Policy / Trust & Safety appeals
routes.scope: Appealing enforcement decisions against your own account.
routes.note: Not a safety-reporting channel; for account holders only.

institutions.reality_check: Best-documented pathway of any lab. AI Frontiers' 2026 review of jailbreak disclosure found Anthropic runs two programs — a restricted NDA-bound CBRN bounty and an open cyber jailbreak program where 'anyone can submit without an NDA, findings may be publicly disclosed once timing is coordinated' — and named it as one of the few labs with a genuinely working route. Independent researchers pursuing cross-model universal jailbreaks in 2025-26 reported labs have 'very heterogeneous disclosure pathways (or none at all)' but that some, including Anthropic, remediated. No public evidence of usersafety@ being a black hole, but also little public evidence of reply rates.
institutions.notes: Write to usersafety@anthropic.com with a reproducible transcript. Safe harbour is real but conditional: 'If you, in our sole determination, make a good faith effort to research and disclose vulnerabilities in accordance with this Policy... we will not pursue any legal action because of your research or responsible disclosure' — note 'in our sole determination'. Whistleblowing is internal only: the RSP Noncompliance Reporting and Anti-Retaliation Policy routes through NAVEX to the Responsible Scaling Officer and is written for employees and Board members, with no public-facing channel.

framework.title: Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy, Version 3.4 (effective 8 July 2026)

institutions.name: OpenAI
institutions.remit: Safety Systems, Preparedness and Alignment teams, with a Safety and Security Committee at board level; Preparedness runs capability thresholds and the Model Spec defines intended model behaviour.

routes.label: Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure Policy
routes.scope: States: 'We invite you to report vulnerabilities, bugs, safety and abuse issues, or security flaws you discover in our systems.'
routes.note: Broad invitation on its face, but the operative programs are on Bugcrowd and split security from safety.

routes.label: OpenAI Bug Bounty (Bugcrowd)
routes.note: URL cited on OpenAI's own policy page; Bugcrowd page is JS-rendered and could not be read directly.

routes.label: OpenAI Safety Bug Bounty (Bugcrowd)
routes.scope: Model safety / CBRN jailbreaks. Separate engagement from the main bounty.
routes.note: Linked from OpenAI's coordinated disclosure policy. AI Frontiers reports all prompts, completions, findings and communications under it are NDA-covered — you cannot publish what you find.

routes.label: Report Content
routes.scope: Publicly open form for policy violations and illegal content: violence and self-harm, sexual exploitation, child exploitation, bullying, fraud, privacy, IP.
routes.note: The only genuinely open, no-account-needed public channel. It is a content/abuse route, not an alignment route.

routes.label: Researcher Access Program
routes.scope: Open and active. Up to $1,000 of API credits for 'researchers using our products to study areas related to the responsible deployment of AI and mitigating associated risks'. Reviewed quarterly.
routes.note: Explicitly welcomes 'early stage researchers' and those with 'limited financial and institutional resources'. Low-friction way in.

routes.label: Red Teaming Network
routes.note: CLOSED. Page states 'Applications are now closed' (deadline was 1 December 2023); says it may reopen. Do not count on it.

routes.label: Model behavior feedback form
routes.scope: DEPRECATED. Page now reads: 'We've deprecated this web form in favor of other channels.'
routes.note: Redirects you to in-product thumbs-down, the API dashboard, or support. A named safety channel that was closed.

routes.label: Model Spec feedback form
routes.scope: CLOSED. 'This feedback form is now closed.'
routes.note: The public-comment process on the Model Spec no longer exists; updates are now published to a GitHub page instead.

institutions.reality_check: Mixed and worsening for unpaid routes. Two named public feedback channels — the model behavior feedback form and the Model Spec feedback form — are both now closed or deprecated, so a citizen's only open door is the content-report form. OpenAI's September 2026 model misalignment reporting framework is explicitly internal: 'Any OpenAI employee may flag a misalignment example for investigation' — it creates no external intake. Researchers in the Trusted Access for Cyber / Daybreak program publicly complained in August 2026 (TechCrunch, 19 Aug 2026) that access was revoked with messages saying their identity 'could not be verified', disproportionately affecting researchers outside the US and Europe. The Safety Bug Bounty is reported to be NDA-bound, so findings cannot be published.
institutions.notes: If you have a model-behaviour concern and are not a paid bounty participant, the Report Content form is the only reliable open channel and it is framed around content policy, not alignment. OpenAI's security page says the bug bounty 'provides safe harbor for good-faith testing' but no verbatim safe-harbour clause is published on the policy page itself. No public whistleblower channel for outsiders.

framework.title: Preparedness Framework v2.0 (15 April 2025); Frontier Governance Framework (May 2026); Model Spec (updated continuously)

institutions.name: Google DeepMind
institutions.remit: Responsibility and Safety Council (co-chaired by COO Lila Ibrahim and VP Responsibility Helen King) reviews research and deployments; a separate AGI Safety Council led by co-founder Shane Legg works alongside it on frontier risk.

routes.label: Google AI Vulnerability Reward Program
routes.scope: Security vulnerabilities in AI products. Jailbreaks and in-session harmful content generation are EXPLICITLY OUT OF SCOPE.
routes.note: Page returns HTTP 200 but is fully JS-rendered and could not be read as text. Scope confirmed by a researcher who published Google's verbatim rejection (below).

routes.label: Gemini content reporting (legal troubleshooter)
routes.scope: Content removal under Google policies and applicable law.
routes.note: Cited from Gemini's policy guidelines page. A legal/removal route, not a safety-research route.

routes.label: In-product thumbs-down on Gemini output
routes.scope: The only routine route for flagging a bad model response.
routes.note: AI Frontiers: Google 'relies on in-product thumbs-down reporting with no acknowledgement of receipt, and no means to track that action will be taken.'

institutions.reality_check: Documented black hole for model-safety issues. A researcher who submitted a Gemini guardrail-bypass to the AI VRP on 20 October 2025 published Google's verbatim reply classifying it 'Infeasible / Out of Scope': 'Generating violative content (such as hate speech, violent content, or illegal instructions)...within the user's own session (e.g., jailbreaks, safety bypasses, or alignment bypasses) is not a qualifying report for the AI VRP.' AI Frontiers' 2026 review groups Google DeepMind with Meta and xAI as labs that exclude jailbreaks from their vulnerability programs, leaving only untracked thumbs-down feedback. Neither the Frontier Safety Framework page nor the Responsibility and Safety page publishes any email, form or contact for external safety input — verified by fetching both.
institutions.notes: There is no published address to reach the Frontier Safety Framework team or either safety council. Google's own triage will tell you a jailbreak is not a security bug. If your finding has a genuine security impact (data exfiltration, cross-user harm) the AI VRP is the right door; if it is alignment or harmful-content behaviour, there is effectively no door. Treat this as: not found — general contact only.

framework.title: Frontier Safety Framework, Version 3.1 (17 April 2026)

institutions.name: Meta
institutions.remit: Internal governance function plus a Chief AI Officer and a Director of Alignment and Risk who receive non-compliance reports under the Advanced AI Scaling Framework; preparedness reports are published at model release.

routes.label: Llama policy violation reports
routes.scope: Reporting violations of the Llama Acceptable Use Policy (i.e. someone else misusing the model).
routes.note: Published verbatim in the Llama use policy. Aimed at misuse by third parties, not at model flaws.

routes.label: Risky content / model output feedback
routes.scope: Reporting risky or harmful content produced by Llama models.
routes.note: The closest thing Meta has to a model-behaviour channel. Published in the Llama AUP.

routes.label: Meta security / Whitehat
routes.note: Published in the Llama AUP as the route for 'security concerns'.

routes.label: Meta Bug Bounty — GenAI payout guidelines
routes.scope: GenAI reports assessed by security impact; the page states it illustrates 'how we assess the security impact' of reports.
routes.note: Page is JS-rendered; could not read scope text directly. Security-impact framing implies pure model-safety/jailbreak reports do not qualify.

routes.label: Model issues via GitHub
routes.note: Listed in the Llama AUP as the route for 'model issues'.

institutions.reality_check: Meta publishes more named routes than most, but responsiveness is the documented problem. Cybernews reported researchers complaining on Reddit that 'Meta wasn't even reacting to their reports about allegedly critical bugs', with some 'still waiting for a response months after submitting the report'; Meta received nearly 10,000 reports in 2024 and deemed only around 600 valid. The article notes one researcher who published a 'horrible experience' publicly got a reply within 10 hours and a generous bounty — i.e. public pressure works where the queue does not. AI Frontiers groups Meta with Google and xAI as excluding jailbreaks from vulnerability programs.
institutions.notes: The llama_output_feedback form is the right door for a harmful-output finding; expect no acknowledgement. The Advanced AI Scaling Framework's whistleblower protocol is employees-only — reports route to 'the internal governance function, the Chief AI Officer, and the Director of Alignment and Risk' — with no external equivalent. No public safe-harbour language for AI safety research was found.

framework.title: Advanced AI Scaling Framework, Version 2 (7 April 2026)

institutions.name: Microsoft
institutions.remit: Office of Responsible AI and a Chief Responsible AI Officer maintain the Responsible AI Standard and review revisions to the Frontier Governance Framework; MSRC handles security and an AI-specific severity bug bar.

routes.label: MSRC Researcher Portal
routes.scope: Security vulnerability submissions including AI systems, graded against the AI bug bar.
routes.note: Also reachable as aka.ms/secure-at per the Copilot bounty page.

routes.label: Microsoft Copilot AI Bounty
routes.scope: $250-$30,000. Security vulnerabilities in Copilot surfaces. Explicitly EXCLUDES 'AI prompt injection attacks that do not have a security impact on users other than the attacker', 'model hallucination where the model pretends to run arbitrary code', and 'attacks that aim to leak (part of) the system/meta prompt'. Content issues must be reported separately as 'AI derived harm'.
routes.note: One of the clearest published statements anywhere that jailbreak-style findings are not a bounty item.

routes.label: AI/ML Vulnerability Severity Classification (AI bug bar)
routes.scope: Splits AI issues into security vulnerabilities (CVSS-rated: inference manipulation, membership inference, model theft) and Responsible AI issues (hate speech, misinformation, sexual content, self-harm) classified only 'In Scope' or 'Out of Scope for investigation, without severity ratings'.
routes.note: Notably says Microsoft 'actively welcome[s] submissions related to safety and societal harm' — a rare explicit invitation. CSEAM must go to Report a Concern instead.

routes.label: Report a Concern (Digital Safety)
routes.scope: Harmful content across Microsoft services, including AI-generated.
routes.note: The consumer-facing route MSRC redirects content reports to.

routes.label: Enterprise AI Services abuse report
routes.scope: Reporting abusive, illegal or infringing use of a Microsoft AI Service.
routes.note: Published in the Code of Conduct for Microsoft AI Services.

institutions.reality_check: No large body of public complaints specific to Microsoft's AI safety intake, and the AI bug bar is unusually candid about what it will and will not investigate. The honest read: security-impacting AI bugs get a real, paid, well-run process through MSRC; pure model-behaviour findings get a 'Responsible AI' classification with no severity and no stated timeline, which is closer to a content-moderation queue than a safety review. Microsoft has publicly said it will pay out for high-impact bugs even outside formal bounty scope (The Register, Dec 2025).
institutions.notes: Use the AI bug bar page first to decide which door you are at — it is the single most useful triage document published by any company here. Safe harbour exists as 'Legal Safe Harbor' in the bounty terms at https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/msrc/bounty-guidelines#safeharbor. The Frontier Governance Framework's whistleblower route is internal only, with anonymous reporting and anti-retaliation for employees; there is no external equivalent.

framework.title: Frontier Governance Framework (February 2026; first version February 2025)

institutions.name: xAI (SpaceXAI)
institutions.remit: A safety team (unnamed publicly; the site says it 'is actively hiring researchers and engineers') producing model cards and safety evaluations under the Frontier AI Framework. No named safety office or officer is published.

routes.label: Safety reports
routes.scope: Published on x.ai/safety for 'reporting harmful outputs, jailbreaks, or other safety issues'.
routes.note: On paper this is exactly the address a citizen wants. In practice see reality check.

routes.label: HackerOne bug bounty
routes.note: Linked from x.ai/safety. xAI has a documented habit of redirecting safety emails into this bounty queue.

institutions.reality_check: Worst documented record of the major labs. AI Frontiers (2026) reports a researcher who emailed the safety address in October 2025 with evidence of 'clear, step-by-step guidance on building a massively destructive chemical weapon' and 'did not receive anything other than an automated response'. Separately, GitGuardian documented a disclosure in April/May 2025: no security.txt, an expired HackerOne link on x.com, and when they finally reached safety@x.ai the reply 12 hours later was 'For us to analyze and also for you to receive proper credit, if applicable, would you please submit this to xAI's Bug Bounty Program on HackerOne?' — the leak was quietly fixed with no update to the reporters, 'completely out of bounds of the disclosure process'. GitGuardian's verdict: 'For a company the size of X, replacing an Incident Response Team...with a bug bounty platform should not be an option and should be considered bad practice.' xAI's own framework lists only internal escalation routes and vaguely references 'xAI's appropriate reporting channels' without naming any. There is also a pending lawsuit over the firing of a Grok safety whistleblower.
institutions.notes: safety@x.ai is published and real, but expect an autoresponder and a push to HackerOne. If the finding is serious, document your attempt and consider a coordinated third-party route (CERT/CC, ai-reports.org) in parallel. No published safe-harbour language, no published whistleblower channel.

framework.title: xAI Frontier Artificial Intelligence Framework (effective 30 June 2026)

institutions.name: Amazon / AWS
institutions.remit: Responsible AI function governing Nova frontier models and Bedrock Guardrails; the Frontier Model Safety Framework commits that Amazon 'will not deploy frontier AI models developed by Amazon that exceed specified risk thresholds without appropriate safeguards in place'.

routes.label: AWS security vulnerabilities
routes.scope: Security vulnerabilities in AWS services. AI model safety is not mentioned anywhere in the policy.
routes.note: Infra-only in practice.

routes.label: AWS abuse / trust and safety
routes.scope: Suspected abuse of AWS resources (EC2, S3 etc.).
routes.note: Infrastructure abuse, not model behaviour.

routes.label: AWS Vulnerability Disclosure Program
routes.note: Linked from the AWS vulnerability reporting page.

routes.label: AWS abuse form
routes.scope: Reporting abusive use of AWS resources.

institutions.reality_check: No public accounts found of anyone successfully reaching an Amazon frontier-model safety function from outside. The Frontier Model Safety Framework publishes no contact channel, no external input process and no whistleblower route — verified by fetching the publication page. AWS's security channels are well-run and responsive for infrastructure, but there is no evidence they route AI safety concerns anywhere.
institutions.notes: This is a company with a published frontier safety framework and no published way to talk to the people who wrote it. For a model-behaviour issue with Nova or Bedrock, you are left with general AWS support. Record as: no meaningful public safety channel — general contact only.

framework.title: Amazon's Frontier Model Safety Framework (published 9 Feb 2025, updated 17 Sept 2026)

institutions.name: NVIDIA
institutions.remit: NVIDIA PSIRT handles product security including AI-specific concerns; a Trustworthy AI function publishes model cards and the NeMo Guardrails tooling.

routes.label: NVIDIA PSIRT
routes.scope: Product security vulnerabilities and AI concerns.
routes.note: PGP key at https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/security/pgp-key/

routes.label: Report a Security Vulnerability or NVIDIA AI Concern
routes.scope: Explicitly includes 'AI vulnerability or hack, AI trust concern, malicious prompt engineering, data poisoning possibility'.
routes.note: One of the very few intake forms in this list that names AI trust concerns as a first-class category rather than excluding them.

institutions.reality_check: No public complaints found about NVIDIA PSIRT being unresponsive; PSIRT is an established, publicly active team (it posts as @nvidiapsirt). The AI-concern category on the VDP intake form is genuine and unusual. Note that from 1 October 2026 NVIDIA PSIRT will publish security bulletins only on GitHub (github.com/nvidia/product-security), so that is where to watch for outcomes.
institutions.notes: The intake form's 'NVIDIA Artificial Intelligence (AI) Concern' option is the route to use — it is a real dropdown, not marketing. No explicit safe-harbour language was visible on the report-vulnerability page; check the PSIRT policies page before doing anything aggressive.

framework.title: NVIDIA Frontier AI Risk Assessment (17 February 2025)

institutions.name: Mistral AI
institutions.remit: No publicly named safety or alignment function. Trust Center covers data protection and security compliance; the Usage Policy is enforced through a content-reporting form.

routes.label: Content / usage policy report form
routes.scope: 21 categories of content violation (hate speech, CSAM, violence, NCII, fraud, IP). Intro: 'Mistral AI is committed to maintaining a safe environment for all. This form allows you to report content you believe violates our terms or applicable laws.'
routes.note: Content moderation, not model safety. Requires you to supply a URL or a shared private chat link to the offending content — so it cannot be used to report a general model flaw.

routes.label: HackerOne vulnerability submission
routes.scope: Security vulnerabilities. Published on the contact page, which notes 'General bugs shall be reported via our standard support channels'.
routes.note: No stated AI/model safety scope.

routes.label: Press
routes.note: Listed here only because it is one of the few published addresses.

institutions.reality_check: No public accounts found of anyone reaching a Mistral safety function. No safety@ or disclosure@ address is published anywhere on mistral.ai or legal.mistral.ai — checked the contact page, terms, and usage policy directly. The report form's requirement of a content URL structurally prevents reporting a capability or alignment finding.
institutions.notes: For a European frontier developer this is a thin public surface: not found — general contact only, at https://mistral.ai/contact. If you have a model-safety finding, the HackerOne form is the only route with a human triage attached, but it is framed as security. No safe-harbour language and no whistleblower channel found.

framework.title: No published frontier safety framework or responsible scaling policy found

institutions.name: Cohere
institutions.remit: Chief Scientist holds 'final authority to determine if our products are safe, secure, and ready to be made available to our customers', delegated by the CEO under the Secure AI Frontier Model Framework.

routes.label: Safety and misuse reports
routes.scope: Usage Policy states: 'please notify us immediately at safety@cohere.com'. Covers policy violations, misuse or abuse of Cohere Services, model safety issues, and security research falling outside the disclosure procedure.
routes.note: A real, named, published safety address — rarer than it should be. This is the strongest single route on Cohere's surface.

routes.label: Thumbs-down on output
routes.scope: In-product feedback on a bad model output, offered in the Usage Policy as an alternative to emailing.

routes.label: Responsible Disclosure Policy via Trust Center
routes.scope: Security vulnerability disclosure; the policy document is downloadable from the Trust Center.
routes.note: Document is gated behind the Trust Center; no plain-text email published on the public security page.

institutions.reality_check: No public accounts found either way — no complaints of a black hole, and no published confirmations of response. Cohere is a smaller enterprise-focused developer with a correspondingly low volume of external safety research directed at it. The framework names external partners (NIST, Humane Intelligence) but describes no public intake process.
institutions.notes: Use safety@cohere.com; it is explicitly scoped to model safety in the Usage Policy, which is more than most publish. The framework itself publishes no contact address, so the Usage Policy is the document to cite when you write.

framework.title: The Cohere Secure AI Frontier Model Framework, V1.0 (February 2025)

institutions.name: Allen Institute for AI (Ai2)
institutions.remit: No separately named safety or alignment function. Responsible Use Guidelines govern OLMo, Molmo, Tulu and Ai2 tools; the organisation argues openness is itself the safety mechanism.

routes.label: General support — also the safety channel
routes.scope: The Responsible Use Guidelines name this single address twice: for questions about the guidelines and violation reports, and for 'reporting bugs, security concerns, and inappropriate/unsafe content generated by Ai2 Tools'.
routes.note: One address for everything. Low ceremony, but at least explicitly covers unsafe model output.

routes.label: Research principles
routes.scope: Statement of principles, not a contact channel.

institutions.reality_check: No public accounts found of people reporting model safety issues to Ai2. As a nonprofit research institute that publishes weights, training data and evaluations openly, most criticism and correction happens through papers, GitHub issues and Hugging Face rather than a disclosure channel — which is a genuinely different model of accountability, not an absence of one.
institutions.notes: support@allenai.org is the published route and it explicitly covers unsafe generated content, so use it and say so. The guidelines have not been updated since June 2024, which is old relative to the model releases they cover. No safe-harbour language and no whistleblower channel found.

framework.title: Responsible use guidelines (last updated June 2024)

institutions.name: Stability AI
institutions.remit: 'Stable Safety' — the publicly branded safety function covering open-weight image and audio models, built around six principles including Safety-First Open Source and Banning AI Misuse, plus an annual Integrity Transparency Report.

routes.label: Safety and misuse reports
routes.scope: Reporting misuse of Stability models and safety concerns.
routes.note: Published on the Stable Safety page. A named, dedicated safety address.

routes.label: Appeals request form
routes.scope: Appealing a policy-violation determination believed to be in error.
routes.note: Linked from the safety page.

institutions.reality_check: No public accounts found of response rates to safety@stability.ai. Stability's safety posture has been heavily criticised in the context of open-weight image models and CSAM (the LAION training-data findings), and its transparency reporting is the main published evidence of enforcement. The address is real; its throughput is unknown.
institutions.notes: safety@stability.ai is the route. Note there is no frontier safety framework or scaling policy — the AUP and the six Stable Safety principles are the whole published governance surface. For open-weight models, reporting misuse to the developer has limited effect once weights are distributed; that is a structural limit, not a channel failure.

framework.title: Acceptable Use Policy (Stable Safety principles)

institutions.name: Apple
institutions.remit: No publicly named AI safety or alignment function. Apple Security Engineering and Architecture runs the bounty; Private Cloud Compute is the published mechanism for AI privacy guarantees.

routes.label: Apple Security Bounty
routes.scope: 'If you've discovered a security or privacy vulnerability that affects Apple devices, software, or services, please report it directly to us.' Covers Apple products and public-facing services; rewards up to $2M for exploit chains, over $5M with bonuses. AI/Apple Intelligence is not named in the terms.
routes.note: Security and privacy only. Nothing about model behaviour.

routes.label: Bounty terms and conditions
routes.scope: Section 8 provides a limited exemption from reverse-engineering restrictions where 'The actions were performed during good-faith security research, which was — or was intended to be — responsibly reported to Apple'.
routes.note: This is the safe-harbour language, and it is narrow: it covers reverse engineering, not a general no-legal-action promise, and applies only within the program terms.

institutions.reality_check: Apple's bounty is well-funded and known to pay, but it is a security program. Apple has historically been criticised by researchers for slow triage and for disputes over credit and payout, though the 2025-26 program restructure raised maximums substantially. There is no published channel of any kind for Apple Intelligence model behaviour — no safety@, no model feedback form, no responsible AI contact.
institutions.notes: If your concern is that Apple Intelligence produced something harmful, there is no published route: not found — general contact only, via https://www.apple.com/contact/. The bounty is for security and privacy vulnerabilities only. Apple publishes no frontier safety framework.

framework.title: No frontier safety framework or model spec published

institutions.name: IBM
institutions.remit: AI Ethics Board plus a Responsible Technology function governing watsonx and Granite models; PSIRT handles security and, unusually, explicitly names AI vulnerabilities in scope.

routes.label: IBM PSIRT
routes.scope: 'Potential security and AI vulnerabilities in IBM products and websites.' AI vulnerabilities explicitly in scope. PGP available.
routes.note: One of only a handful of PSIRTs to name AI vulnerabilities in its remit.

routes.label: IBM Safe Harbor Policy
routes.scope: The PSIRT page states vulnerability reporting is 'protected by IBM Safe Harbor Policy', available as a downloadable document.
routes.note: The full text is in a linked PDF rather than inline; read it before testing. Anonymous form submission is also offered.

institutions.reality_check: No public accounts found of AI-specific reports to IBM PSIRT. IBM's AI Ethics Board is well-documented in its governance publications but is an internal review body with no published external intake. The PSIRT route is professional and long-established; whether a pure model-behaviour finding survives triage there is untested in public.
institutions.notes: psirt@us.ibm.com is the route, and you can cite that AI vulnerabilities are in its published scope. There is no channel to the AI Ethics Board. IBM is one of the few here offering both anonymous submission and a written safe harbour policy.

framework.title: Responsible Technology / AI ethics principles (no frontier safety framework published)

institutions.name: Alibaba (Qwen)
institutions.remit: No separately named frontier safety or alignment function published in English. Security is handled by the Alibaba Security Response Center (ASRC); model governance follows PRC regulatory requirements (CAC algorithm and generative AI filings).

routes.label: Alibaba Security Response Center (ASRC)
routes.scope: Vulnerability reporting across Alibaba properties. Page is fully JS-rendered and returned only a 'please enable JS' message when fetched, so scope, AI coverage and registration requirements could not be confirmed.
routes.note: An ASRC Vulnerability Rewards Program exists (https://security.alibaba.com/announcement/announcement?id=151). Chinese SRC platforms typically require account registration and, often, a mainland phone number — a practical barrier for outside researchers.

routes.label: Alibaba Cloud trust center
routes.scope: Compliance documentation, not an incident channel.

institutions.reality_check: No public accounts found of a foreign researcher successfully reporting a Qwen model-safety issue to Alibaba. Qwen weights are widely distributed on Hugging Face and most published safety findings about Qwen (red-teaming reports, jailbreak evaluations) are released as papers or blog posts rather than disclosed to Alibaba, which is itself the signal. CISA's September 2026 advisory on PRC AI developers adds a geopolitical overlay that makes direct engagement harder for some researchers.
institutions.notes: Treat as: no verified English-language model-safety channel. ASRC exists and is real but is an infrastructure security platform with registration friction. If you have a finding about open-weight Qwen models, publishing it and filing on the Hugging Face model repo is likely to have more effect than the SRC.

framework.title: No published frontier safety framework found in English

institutions.name: DeepSeek
institutions.remit: No publicly named safety or alignment function. Safe Use Policy governs the hosted service; the company publishes research papers but no safety framework.

routes.label: Security
routes.scope: Published as a mailto link in the footer of deepseek.com. No published policy defines what is in scope.
routes.note: Verified by reading the raw page source of deepseek.com/en. There is no accompanying disclosure policy, scope statement, SLA or safe harbour — just the address.

routes.label: General service contact
routes.note: Also published in the site footer.

institutions.reality_check: DeepSeek has been the subject of an unusual volume of external security and safety findings — Wiz Research found a publicly exposed ClickHouse database leaking chat history in January 2025, and Cisco's red-teaming reported a 100% attack success rate against R1 on a standard harmful-prompt benchmark. In none of these widely covered cases did the researchers describe a functioning coordinated-disclosure exchange with DeepSeek; Wiz described reaching out and the exposure being closed quickly, but there is no published disclosure process. No bug bounty, no VDP, no safe harbour.
institutions.notes: security@deepseek.com is genuinely published, which puts DeepSeek ahead of several Western labs on the narrow question of having an address. But there is no policy behind it — no scope, no commitment, no safe harbour. Assume anything you send is unprotected and may not be acknowledged.

institutions.reality_check: A live example of the gap: in September 2026 Z.ai disabled features of its ZCode coding assistant after it was found uploading users' repositories — a serious incident surfaced publicly rather than through a disclosure channel. NIST's CAISI published an assessment of GLM-5.2 in July 2026. Zhipu is a signatory to the Frontier AI Safety Commitments made at the AI Seoul Summit, but has not published a corresponding framework or an external reporting route.
institutions.notes: Record as: no meaningful public safety channel. A citizen with a GLM safety concern has no published address. For open-weight GLM releases, the Hugging Face repo discussion tab is the only realistic contact surface.

framework.title: No published frontier safety framework found

institutions.name: Moonshot AI
institutions.remit: No publicly named safety or alignment function. A security team exists and responds via the developer forum; Kimi models are released open-weight and via API.

routes.label: Security reports
routes.scope: Confirmed by a Moonshot staff member relaying their Security Team on the official forum: 'If you discover any potential security issues, please report them to us at: security@moonshot.ai. We kindly ask that you follow responsible disclosure practices and give us reasonable time to investigate and address any finding…'
routes.note: Moonshot confirmed in the same thread that it has NO public bug bounty and NO formal vulnerability disclosure policy.

routes.label: Moonshot / Kimi developer forum
routes.scope: Public forum where staff do respond.
routes.note: Documented as the escalation route that actually works when email does not.

institutions.reality_check: Rare documented case of a channel failing and a workaround succeeding. A security researcher posted on forum.moonshot.ai after emailing security@moonshot.ai and waiting 90 days with no response; a Moonshot staff member (yuikns) then replied on the forum within the thread, relaying the Security Team's confirmation of the address and of the absence of any formal VDP. The lesson is explicit: the email exists, went unanswered for three months, and a public post got a reply.
institutions.notes: Email security@moonshot.ai, but plan to escalate to the public forum if you get nothing — that is the documented path to a human. No safe harbour, no bounty, no whistleblower channel. Nothing covers model safety as distinct from security.

framework.title: No published frontier safety framework found

institutions.name: ByteDance Seed
institutions.remit: A Responsible AI research direction within Seed; TechNode reported in August 2026 that ByteDance formed a new AI Data and Safety department. No named external-facing safety office.

routes.label: No verified safety or disclosure channel found

routes.note: ByteDance operates a security response centre for its consumer products, but no AI-model-safety intake is published for Seed.

institutions.reality_check: ByteDance's AI safety responses in 2026 were driven by legal and commercial pressure rather than researcher reports: it pledged safeguards for Seedance 2.0 only after legal threats from Disney and Paramount over IP, and suspended a photo-to-voice feature over risk concerns. Both were reactive and externally forced. No evidence of a functioning researcher channel.
institutions.notes: Record as: no meaningful public safety channel for the Seed research arm. A concern about Seedance or Doubao output realistically has to go through the consumer product's in-app reporting, or through press and legal pressure — which is what has demonstrably moved them.

routes.note: Could not be fetched and read. Chinese SRC platforms generally require registration and often a mainland identity or phone number.

Baidu's AI governance is driven by CAC filing requirements rather than a voluntary published framework.
institutions.notes: Record as: no verified English-language model-safety channel. BSRC is the only real route and it is security-scoped and Chinese-language.

routes.note: Policy at https://en.security.tencent.com/index.php/policy and payouts at .../payouts.

institutions.reality_check: TSRC is one of the more accessible Chinese security response centres for foreign researchers — it maintains a full English site, a hall of fame and a payouts page, and does not appear to require a mainland identity to register. No public accounts found of AI model-safety reports specifically. Scope for AI is unstated, so a jailbreak report would likely be triaged as out of scope.
institutions.notes: security@tencent.com and the English TSRC form are real and usable. Do not expect model-behaviour findings to be treated as in scope; frame anything you send in security terms if it genuinely has security impact.

framework.title: No published frontier safety framework found in English

institutions.name: NAVER
institutions.remit: Future AI Center, supported by a risk management working group and a board-level risk management committee, operates the AI Safety Framework; frontier systems are reassessed every three months or when capability increases 6x.

routes.label: NAVER Cloud sales/support enquiry
routes.scope: The only contact route published alongside the ASF — a sales enquiry form.
routes.note: Not a safety channel. This is the literal state of NAVER's published external surface for its safety framework.

institutions.reality_check: No public accounts found of anyone contacting NAVER about HyperCLOVA X safety. NAVER was among the earliest non-US companies to publish a frontier safety framework and extended it in 2026 to user-facing services, so the internal governance is real; but the framework document points an interested outsider at a cloud sales form, which is a telling gap between governance and accessibility.
institutions.notes: Record as: framework published, no public safety channel. If you have a concern, the sales/support form is the only published door and you should expect it to be routed commercially.

framework.title: NAVER AI Safety Framework (ASF), published 7 August 2024; ASF 2.0 reported in 2026 extending to user-facing services

institutions.name: Sakana AI
institutions.remit: No publicly named safety or alignment function. Corporate team covers finance, legal, HR and operations; a Defense Policy is published covering defence-related work.

routes.label: No verified safety or disclosure channel found
routes.scope: Not found — general contact only. Fetching the homepage and corporate info page found no email addresses and no mailto links at all; only X and LinkedIn accounts.
routes.note: Terms of service for the Fugu console exist at https://console.sakana.ai/terms-of-service but publish no safety contact.

institutions.reality_check: No public accounts found of anyone attempting to reach Sakana about safety. Sakana's most notable public correction — the 2025 episode where its 'AI CUDA Engineer' claimed speedups that turned out to be a benchmark-gaming artifact — was surfaced on X by independent researchers and acknowledged publicly, not through any disclosure channel. That is the de facto route.
institutions.notes: Record as: no public safety channel. Practically, the X account (@SakanaAILabs) is how findings about Sakana have actually reached the company.

framework.title: No published frontier safety framework found

institutions.name: Safe Superintelligence Inc. (SSI)
institutions.remit: The entire company is framed as a safety-first effort — 'safety and capabilities in tandem' — but no internal safety function, framework, model spec or governance structure has been published.

routes.label: Contact page
routes.scope: The only contact route linked from the homepage. No email address is published anywhere on the site.
routes.note: Verified that the homepage publishes no email addresses; the contact page itself was not readable.

institutions.reality_check: Nothing to report on, which is itself the finding. SSI has shipped no product, published no safety framework, joined no public commitment process with a published framework, and has essentially no public communications surface beyond a single-page site and a jobs link. There is no external safety channel and no evidence anyone has reached one.
institutions.notes: A company whose name is its safety claim publishes no safety framework and no safety contact. Record as: no meaningful public safety channel. For a citizen this is a dead end; the accountability route is press and policy, not correspondence.

framework.title: No published safety framework, scaling policy or model spec

institutions.name: Thinking Machines Lab
institutions.remit: States it will contribute to AI safety by 'maintaining a high safety bar—preventing misuse of our released models while maximizing users' freedom', sharing best practices, and 'accelerating external research on alignment by sharing code, datasets, and model specs'. No named safety team.

routes.label: Security vulnerability reports
routes.scope: Security vulnerabilities in systems, services and infrastructure. PGP key at https://thinkingmachines.ai/.well-known/pgp-key.txt (fingerprint 4FA9 136F 8F68 DDFD 1E78 6EBE CB0B 7A1E 3028 4CB4).
routes.note: Verified by decoding the Cloudflare-obfuscated addresses in the page source. Explicitly no bug bounty: 'we do not operate a bug bounty program and do not offer monetary rewards or compensation of any kind'.

routes.label: Model safety incidents — routed to Legal
routes.scope: The disclosure policy states: 'This policy does not cover model safety. To report an incident related to Inkling, please contact us at [legal@thinkingmachines.ai].'
routes.note: Significant finding: model safety is carved out of the security process and sent to the legal department. Verified by decoding the page source.

institutions.reality_check: Too new for public accounts of responsiveness. The structural signal is clear though: Thinking Machines writes an unusually strong safe-harbour clause for security research and then explicitly excludes model safety from it, routing model-safety incidents to legal@ — which means a model-safety report arrives at a desk whose job is liability, and arrives outside the protections the same page grants to security researchers.
institutions.notes: The safe harbour is one of the best-written in this list, but read its boundary: 'When you conduct security research and vulnerability disclosure in good faith and in compliance with this policy, we consider that research to be authorized, and we will: Not pursue or support any legal action against you for accidental, good-faith violations of this policy, including under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act or the anti-circumvention provisions of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act; Waive any restrictions in our Terms of Service or Acceptable Use Policy...; and If a third party initiates legal action against you..., take reasonable steps to make it known that your actions were authorized.' None of that covers a model-safety finding. Get advice before sending a jailbreak to legal@.

institutions.name: Reflection AI
institutions.remit: No publicly named safety or alignment function and no published safety framework, despite positioning as an open frontier lab.

routes.note: The address itself was redacted by the fetch tool and could not be independently confirmed character-by-character, so it is not reproduced here rather than risk inventing it. Read it directly from the privacy policy page.

institutions.reality_check: No public accounts of safety contact. Reflection raised at frontier-lab scale and positions itself as America's open-weights answer to Chinese labs, but publishes no safety framework, no disclosure policy and no security contact — only a privacy policy with one catch-all address. The fact that 'correction requests regarding AI model outputs' are handled as a privacy-law obligation rather than a safety process is the tell.
institutions.notes: Record as: no meaningful public safety channel. Read the address off the privacy policy yourself; do not trust a transcribed version. Expect it to be handled as a data-subject request.

institutions.remit: No publicly named safety or alignment function. A security team runs the VDP; support handles what Perplexity calls 'safety issues' at the account level.

routes.scope: 'All public facing endpoints of Perplexity. All user-facing clients and API endpoints are in scope.' Explicitly OUT of scope: 'AI-related issues such as hallucinations and model safety are not in scope of the security program.'

routes.label: Support — including what they classify as safety issues
routes.scope: Account, functional and safety issues, per the VDP page.
routes.note: General support queue; not a safety function.

institutions.reality_check: The Comet browser has been a repeated target of serious external security research — Hacktron's one-click UXSS and Brave's prompt-injection findings — and those were handled through the security program, which does function. But model safety is formally excluded from it, and the fallback is a general support inbox. No safe-harbour language is published on the VDP page: it asks researchers to 'avoid actions that could compromise the privacy of our users' but offers no legal protection in return.
institutions.notes: If it is a security bug, Bugcrowd works. If it is a model-behaviour or hallucination harm, Perplexity has told you in writing it is out of scope, and support@ is your only option. Note the absence of safe harbour before doing any testing.

Since Meta's investment and the departure of leadership to Meta, SEAL's independence as a third-party evaluator has been publicly questioned — which matters if you are considering Scale as a neutral route for a finding about another lab.

institutions.name: International Network for Advanced AI Measurement, Evaluation and Science (NAAIMES) — formerly the International Network of AI Safety Institutes
institutions.remit: Intergovernmental network of state AI evaluation bodies. Renamed in December 2025 from 'International Network of AI Safety Institutes' — the word 'safety' was dropped in favour of 'measurement, evaluation and science'. Verified membership as of 2026: Australia, Canada, European Union, France, Japan, Kenya, Republic of Korea, Singapore, United Kingdom, United States. NOTE: India, Italy, Spain, Netherlands, Ireland, Switzerland and China are NOT members. Publishes joint technical outputs (e.g. Feb 2026 consensus areas on automated evaluations). No treaty basis, no legal personality.

routes.label: NIST announcement page (US member, CAISI)
routes.note: VERIFIED fetched. No network contact address or submission channel published.

routes.label: UK AISI blog on network outputs
routes.note: VERIFIED fetched. Confirms the ten members. No network-level contact route.

institutions.reality_check: The network has NO standalone website, NO secretariat email, and NO public-facing channel that I could verify. Coordination runs through whichever member hosts a convening; the US CAISI convened the founding meeting (Nov 2024) and the UK AISI has published network outputs. A member of the public cannot address the network — only individual member institutes. Treat 'the Network' as a publication brand, not a contactable body.
institutions.notes: The rename is real and confirmed by NIST and UK AISI primary sources. Any directory still calling it the 'International Network of AI Safety Institutes' is out of date. Do not confuse the US 'CAISI' (Center for AI Standards and Innovation) with the Canadian 'CAISI' (Canadian AI Safety Institute) — the acronym collision is genuine.

institutions.name: Japan AI Safety Institute (Japan AISI / J-AISI)

institutions.remit: Established 14 Feb 2024 by Cabinet decision (referencing the 2024 Integrated Innovation Strategy). Secretariat hosted at the Information-technology Promotion Agency (IPA), a METI-affiliated incorporated administrative agency. Develops AI safety evaluation methods, standards, red-teaming guides and testing environments; coordinates internationally. Explicitly NON-regulatory — it cannot compel, licence or fine. Japan's AI Promotion Act (Act on Promotion of R&D and Utilization of AI-Related Technologies, in full effect Nov 2025) contains no monetary penalties at all; enforcement is reputational/administrative guidance.

routes.label: Japan AISI general inquiries
routes.note: VERIFIED — published on aisi.go.jp homepage and About page, fetched twice. Best single reachable address of any non-Western AISI.

routes.label: Japan AISI website (About)
routes.note: VERIFIED fetched. English is served via a Google Translate link, not a native English site.

routes.label: IPA parent-agency contact page
routes.note: UNVERIFIED — surfaced in search, not fetched.

institutions.reality_check: A real, monitored mailbox at a real agency, which is more than most peers offer. But Japan AISI runs no public consultation or comment docket: its outputs (evaluation guides, red-teaming methodology, data-quality guidebook) are published finished. Realistically a foreigner can write and may get a courteous reply or none; there is no process that obliges anyone to read it.
institutions.notes: Director Akiko Murakami (non-full-time). Advisors include Arisa Ema and Hiroaki Kitano. Site makes no explicit mention of frontier or catastrophic risk — framing is generic 'AI safety'.

institutions.name: AI Safety Institute (Korea AISI)
institutions.local_name: 인공지능안전연구소
institutions.remit: Launched Nov 2024. Hosted within ETRI (한국전자통신연구원, Electronics and Telecommunications Research Institute) under the Ministry of Science and ICT (과학기술정보통신부, MSIT). routes.note: VERIFIED fetched. NO email address or inquiry form is published on the English homepage.

institutions.reality_check: Poor. Korea AISI has an English site that advertises international collaboration but publishes no contact email, no form, and no submission route — verified by fetching both the English homepage and the dedicated Collaboration page. institutions.name: Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT) — AI Framework Act supervisory authority
institutions.local_name: 과학기술정보통신부; 인공지능 발전과 신뢰 기반 조성 등에 관한 기본법
institutions.remit: Administers the Framework Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and Establishment of Trust ('AI Framework Act'), in force 22 January 2026 — the world's second comprehensive national AI statute. This is a genuine regulator: it designates high-impact AI domains (energy, water, healthcare, medical devices, nuclear, biometric criminal analysis, employment and lending decisions, transport, government functions, student assessment), imposes transparency/labelling, lifecycle risk-management and human-oversight duties, and can levy administrative fines up to KRW 30 million (~USD 21,000). It also sets compute thresholds by Presidential Decree triggering additional safety obligations — the closest thing to a frontier-model trigger outside the EU.

routes.label: Extraterritorial reach / domestic representative duty
routes.note: VERIFIED that the Act binds foreign providers above user/revenue thresholds, who must appoint a Korean domestic representative — this is the practical hook for foreigners. The MSIT complaint/reporting portal URL itself is UNVERIFIED; I did not fetch a working MSIT AI complaint form.

routes.label: Statutory text (English translation, CSET)
routes.note: UNVERIFIED (search result). Third-party translation, not an official channel.

institutions.reality_check: The compute-threshold provision means a foreign frontier lab can fall inside Korean law, which in turn means foreign parties genuinely have standing to raise issues — unusually for Asia. But the compliance route runs through a mandated Korean domestic representative and Korean-language administrative process. I could not verify a public-facing complaint form in English; MSIT's AI supervision channels appear to be Korean-only.
institutions.notes: The fine ceiling (~USD 21k) is trivially small relative to EU AI Act penalties — treat this as a disclosure-and-registration regime with teeth mainly through market access, not through fines.

institutions.name: Canadian Artificial Intelligence Safety Institute (CAISI)
institutions.local_name: Institut canadien de sécurité de l'intelligence artificielle (ICSIA)
institutions.remit: Announced Nov 2024, sits within Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED). Funds and directs AI safety research (investigator-led and government-directed streams, with CIFAR running a research programme and Amii/Mila/Vector involved); advises government on risks from advanced AI systems; produces guidance for developers and the public. Purely research/advisory — Canada has NO in-force AI statute after AIDA (Bill C-27) died on prorogation in January 2025, so CAISI cannot compel or fine anyone.

routes.note: VERIFIED — published directly on the ISED CAISI page and fetched. One of only two clearly published AISI mailboxes worldwide outside the US/UK/EU.

routes.note: UNVERIFIED (search result). Relevant to researchers seeking to work with CAISI rather than to the general public.

institutions.reality_check: Genuinely reachable: a published bilingual government mailbox on a federal domain. Canada's federal correspondence norms mean a foreigner writing in English or French will normally get at least an acknowledgement. But with no AI statute in force there is nothing to complain about in a legally operative sense — CAISI is a funder and adviser.
institutions.notes: Its page references advanced-AI risks including systems that 'may be dangerous or hinder human oversight' and synthetic-content harms, but stops well short of explicit catastrophic/existential framing. Acronym clashes with the US Center for AI Standards and Innovation (also CAISI).

institutions.remit: Designated May 2024. Focus areas: multilingual and multicultural testing, agentic AI testing, societal-impact studies, international partnerships. Research/standards body — the institute itself has no enforcement power, though IMDA as a statutory board has regulatory powers in adjacent media/telecom domains.

institutions.local_name: Institut national pour l'évaluation et la sécurité de l'intelligence artificielle

routes.note: UNVERIFIED (search result).

institutions.reality_check: Worst-in-class for public access among network members. INESIA has no website of its own that I could find, no email, no consultation process, and its own roadmap document publishes zero contact information. Access is only via the four constituent bodies (ANSSI, Inria, LNE, PEReN), each of which has separate French-language channels. A foreigner has no route in.
institutions.notes: Strongest explicit catastrophic-risk language of any body in this list. The roadmap commits INESIA to evaluate how high-impact models 'could generate negative real effects on public health, safety, security, fundamental rights or society itself, propagated at scale', naming information manipulation, offensive cyber, CBRN (NRBC) proliferation and autonomous-agent behaviours. France is the only EU member state in the international network.

institutions.name: Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy (MICDE) — State Department for ICT and the Digital Economy
institutions.remit: Owns the Kenya AI Strategy 2025–2030 and the draft Kenya Artificial Intelligence and Other Emerging Technologies Policy (July 2026). Kenya is the only African member of the international network, though as of Sept 2026 I found NO evidence that a Kenyan AI Safety Institute has actually been stood up — Kenya 'agreed to join' the network with an institute 'in development'. A separate Artificial Intelligence Bill 2026 is before Parliament, which if passed would create statutory powers; until then the ministry is a policy body.

institutions.reality_check: Kenya runs formal 'public participation' — a constitutional requirement under Article 118/201 for legislation and policy, which is genuinely more binding than a discretionary consultation elsewhere. That is a real opportunity. But public participation in Kenya is constitutionally framed around 'the people' and is oriented to Kenyan stakeholders; foreign submissions are not excluded in law but carry no weight. I could not fetch the ministry's site at all (TLS/robots failures), so I cannot confirm the live submission address — flag this as needing manual verification before any directory publishes it.
institutions.notes: English is an official language of Kenya, so no translation barrier. Kenya's network membership is diplomatically significant (sole African seat) but appears institutionally thin.

institutions.name: Australian AI Safety Institute (AAISI)
institutions.remit: Announced 2025 and established November 2025 within the Department of Industry, Science and Resources (DISR), alongside the National AI Plan. Technical AI safety science, evaluation capability, international engagement. Australia abandoned its proposed mandatory guardrails legislation in favour of a non-regulatory, existing-regulator approach, so the institute is advisory/research — it cannot compel or fine.

institutions.reality_check: Australia historically runs excellent, genuinely open consultations through DISR's consultation hub, and past AI consultations (2023 Safe and Responsible AI, 2024 mandatory guardrails) accepted and published submissions from foreign organisations including US labs. That is the realistic route in. The institute itself is new enough (Nov 2025) that I could not verify a direct contact channel — industry.gov.au blocked automated fetching throughout.
institutions.notes: Australia is a full network member. The retreat from mandatory guardrails to a 'gap-filling' approach in 2025 means frontier-risk work here is research-only.

institutions.name: IndiaAI Safety Institute
institutions.remit: Announced 30 January 2025 under the IndiaAI Mission (an Independent Business Division of MeitY, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology), within the Mission's 'Safe & Trusted AI' pillar. Operates on a hub-and-spoke model contracting research to partner institutions via Calls for Partnerships (2025 rounds, deadline extended to 9 July 2025). No statutory basis, no enforcement power. India has no AI Act; the Nov 2025 India AI Governance Guidelines are non-binding and propose an AI Governance Group (AIGG) and a Technology & Policy Expert Committee (TPEC) whose operational status I could NOT verify as of Sept 2026.

institutions.reality_check: India is NOT a member of the international network despite having an institute. Its partnership calls are explicitly restricted to Indian entities — this is the clearest 'domestic only' eligibility statement of any body here. MeitY does run public consultations (it consulted on establishing the institute, and on the Governance Guidelines) and those are technically open, but they are oriented to Indian industry and civil society. A foreigner's realistic route is commenting on a live MeitY draft, not contacting the institute.
institutions.notes: Name appears inconsistently as 'IndiaAI Safety Institute', 'India AI Safety Institute' and 'AI Safety Institute (AISI)' in official IndiaAI communications. Existence is confirmed; operational maturity is uncertain.

institutions.name: Agenzia per l'Italia Digitale (AgID) and Agenzia per la Cybersicurezza Nazionale (ACN) — Italian national AI authorities
institutions.local_name: Agenzia per l'Italia Digitale; Agenzia per la Cybersicurezza Nazionale
institutions.remit: Law No. 132 of 23 September 2025 ('Disposizioni e deleghe al Governo in materia di intelligenza artificiale') made Italy the first EU member state with a national AI statute layered on the EU AI Act. It designates AgID as the notifying authority (promotion, notification of conformity-assessment bodies) and ACN as the market-surveillance authority (inspection and sanction powers under the AI Act). Implementing decrees on governance, training, biometrics and liability were being adopted through 2026. Banca d'Italia, CONSOB, IVASS and Garante Privacy retain sectoral competence. ACN is a genuine enforcement authority; AgID is largely administrative.

institutions.reality_check: Italy is an EU member state, so the operative public route for a foreigner is the EU AI Act's own complaint mechanism to the national market-surveillance authority (ACN) — Article 85 gives ANY person the right to lodge a complaint, with no nationality requirement. That right is real and legally binding. The practical barrier is language: ACN and AgID operate in Italian, and I could not verify an English-language complaint form.
institutions.notes: Italy is NOT a member of the international network. Included because the user asked. Law 132/2025 is significant as the first national AI law inside the EU.

institutions.name: Agencia Española de Supervisión de la Inteligencia Artificial (AESIA)
institutions.local_name: Agencia Española de Supervisión de la Inteligencia Artificial
institutions.remit: Created by Royal Decree 729/2023, headquartered in A Coruña — the first dedicated national AI supervisory agency in the EU. Designated as Spain's market-surveillance authority for most of the EU AI Act, attached to the Ministry for Digital Transformation and the Civil Service. Under the AI Act it can investigate, demand documentation and access to models, order withdrawal of non-compliant systems, and impose administrative fines. Spain's draft national AI law (anteproyecto, 2025) would set the domestic penalty schedule.

institutions.reality_check: Among the best of any body here for an outsider: a published general mailbox on a .gob.es domain plus a real English-language site. And EU AI Act Article 85 gives any person — explicitly not limited to EU residents — the right to complain to a market-surveillance authority. The catch is that a formal complaint (as opposed to an informal email) typically goes through the sede electrónica, which requires Spanish electronic identity credentials. Informal email is the realistic foreign route.
institutions.notes: Spain is NOT a member of the international network. AESIA's public materials emphasise ethical/safe use and AI Act compliance; I found no explicit frontier or catastrophic-risk positioning on the pages fetched.

institutions.name: Department for the Coordination of Algorithmic Oversight (DCA), Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens
institutions.local_name: Directie Coördinatie Algoritmes (DCA), Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens
institutions.remit: Unit inside the Dutch DPA (AP) set up in 2023 to coordinate algorithmic and AI oversight across Dutch regulators, identify and publish high-level algorithmic and AI risks (it issues a recurring AI & Algorithmic Risks Report Netherlands), and prepare AI Act supervision. Under the Dutch AI Act designation settled in 2026, the AP and the RDI (Rijksinspectie Digitale Infrastructuur) take the key supervisory roles — AP for prohibited practices and fundamental-rights-relevant systems, RDI as overall market-surveillance coordinator. AP itself has full GDPR fining power; the DCA as a unit is coordinating/analytical.

routes.note: VERIFIED — published on the AP's English DCA page, which renders it with an anti-spam insertion ('dca@remove-this-text.autoriteitpersoonsgegevens.nl'). The operative address is as given. Page states the DCA 'welcomes feedback from organisations and other parties'.

institutions.reality_check: Strong. A named, published mailbox that explicitly invites feedback from 'organisations and other parties', on a fully English-language regulator site, at a body with real GDPR enforcement muscle. The DCA also publishes recurring risk reports that cite external input. This is one of the few entries where a foreigner writing in English has a plausible chance of being read.
institutions.notes: Netherlands is NOT a member of the international network. The RDI (Rijksinspectie Digitale Infrastructuur) is the co-designated authority; I did not verify RDI contact details and have not listed a URL for it.

institutions.name: AI Office of Ireland (proposed)
institutions.local_name: Oifig IS na hÉireann
institutions.remit: STATUS UNCERTAIN AS OF SEPT 2026 — this body does not yet exist. The Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Bill 2026 was published 17 June 2026 by the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment and would establish 'Oifig IS na hÉireann (AI Office of Ireland)' as an independent statutory body acting as Ireland's central coordinating authority for AI Act implementation. As of this research date the Bill was awaiting passage through the Oireachtas. Ireland had already designated a distributed set of eight/nine existing sectoral regulators as national competent authorities in 2025.

institutions.reality_check: Do not list the AI Office of Ireland as an operating body — it is a creature of a Bill that had not passed when I checked. Ireland matters disproportionately because most major US AI firms have their EU establishment there, so Irish authorities will in practice supervise them. Until the Office exists, the route is the Department and the existing sectoral regulators. No AI-specific public contact route is published.
institutions.notes: Ireland is NOT a member of the international network. Irish Oireachtas committees do accept written submissions on Bills from any party, including foreigners, during pre-legislative scrutiny — that is the realistic input window.

institutions.name: Federal Office of Communications (OFCOM / BAKOM) — Swiss AI regulation lead
institutions.local_name: Bundesamt für Kommunikation (BAKOM) / Office fédéral de la communication (OFCOM)
institutions.remit: Switzerland has NO AI safety institute and no comprehensive AI act. In February 2025 the Federal Council chose a sectoral, minimally-invasive approach: ratify the Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI (signed by Switzerland) and make only targeted sectoral legal amendments, with non-binding measures elsewhere. BAKOM/OFCOM leads the legislative drafting, with the Federal Chancellery (Bundeskanzlei) handling federal-administration AI use. Consultation drafts were expected through 2026. Advisory/legislative-preparation, not a regulator of AI.

institutions.reality_check: Switzerland's Vernehmlassung (consultation) procedure is genuinely open: anyone, including foreign organisations, may submit, and all submissions are published in full. That is a real and unusual channel. But there was no verified live AI consultation at the time of checking, and Switzerland is NOT a network member and has no AI safety institute. Swiss federal sites are in German, French and Italian with partial English.
institutions.notes: Switzerland signed the Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI. Ratification was in progress. No frontier-risk-specific institutional stance identified.

institutions.name: Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC)
institutions.local_name: 国家互联网信息办公室 / 中央网络安全和信息化委员会办公室
institutions.remit: China's principal AI content regulator and by far the most powerful body in this directory. Administers the Algorithmic Recommendation Provisions (2022), Deep Synthesis Provisions (2023), Interim Measures for Generative AI Services (2023) and the Labelling Measures for AI-Generated Synthetic Content (in force 1 Sept 2025). Runs the algorithm and generative-AI filing (备案) regimes. Can order rectification, suspend or terminate services, remove apps from stores, refer for criminal prosecution, and fine. Co-published the AI Safety Governance Framework 2.0 (人工智能安全治理框架2.0) on 15 September 2025 at National Cybersecurity Publicity Week, with the National Internet Emergency Center coordinating and TC260 handling the technical file.

routes.label: CAC official site — generative AI filing announcements
routes.note: VERIFIED accessible. CAC publishes bi-monthly lists of filed generative-AI services (e.g. the Jan 2026 and Jul 2026 announcements), which is the authoritative public record of which models are legally deployable in China.

routes.label: AI Safety Governance Framework 2.0 announcement
routes.note: VERIFIED fetched. Confirms publication date and publishing bodies.

routes.label: Internet Information Service Algorithm Filing System (算法备案)
routes.note: UNVERIFIED — confirmed as the official system via CAC-linked search results, but direct fetch was blocked by robots.txt. Requires a Chinese business licence and real-name credentials. Closed to foreigners in practice.

routes.note: VERIFIED present on the fetched CAC article as '【纠错】'. This is a typo/error-correction form, NOT a substantive complaint channel. Do not present it as one.

institutions.reality_check: CAC does run real public-comment windows on draft measures (征求意见稿), and international companies and law firms have in practice filed comments on drafts such as the Generative AI Interim Measures. Those windows are real. But: they are Chinese-language only, run 30 days or less, are announced without notice, and the filing systems behind them (算法备案, 大模型备案) require a Chinese business entity and real-name verification. There is no route by which an individual foreigner obtains standing. Framework 2.0 is a guidance document with no complaint mechanism attached.
institutions.notes: Framework 2.0 refines risk classification and explores risk grading relative to the 2024 version. The document series does address loss-of-control (失控) risk categories, though the announcement page I fetched does not detail them. CAC is not a member of, and China does not participate in, the international network.

institutions.name: China Internet Illegal and Harmful Information Reporting Centre (12377)
institutions.local_name: 中央网信办违法和不良信息举报中心
institutions.remit: CAC's public reporting channel for illegal and harmful online information. Under the Labelling Measures for AI-Generated Synthetic Content and the Generative AI Interim Measures, unlabelled or non-compliant AI-generated content falls within its scope. Reports feed CAC enforcement, which can compel takedown and service suspension.

institutions.reality_check: Honest assessment: this is a domestic content-policing channel, not an AI safety channel. It is Chinese-language only, is oriented to reporting content the state considers illegal or harmful, and typically expects real-name or Chinese-phone-number registration. A foreigner raising a frontier-safety concern here would be using the wrong instrument entirely, and I could not even verify the site's current form. Include it in a directory only with a clear caveat.

institutions.name: Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT)
institutions.local_name: 中华人民共和国工业和信息化部
institutions.remit: Industrial regulator for AI as a technology sector: compute infrastructure, telecoms, AI standardisation, humanoid robotics, and the 'AI+' industrial programmes. Issued the 'AI+ Information and Communications' Innovation Development Implementation Opinions (2026–2028) in 2026. Runs a standing public-comment section (公开征求意见) on draft standards and guidelines. Has licensing and administrative-penalty powers over telecoms and industrial operators.

Each notice carries its own feedback email and deadline inside the notice text.

institutions.reality_check: MIIT's comment windows are genuine and structurally open — the notices name a contact person and a feedback email. But they are Chinese-language, typically 30 days, aimed at domestic industry and research institutes, and use a downloadable Word feedback form (意见反馈表) with fields for work unit, name, and phone. A foreign individual can technically email a completed form; there is no acknowledgement mechanism and no evidence foreign submissions are considered.
institutions.notes: MIIT's AI work is developmental/industrial rather than safety-focused. It is not a frontier-risk body.

institutions.name: National Information Security Standardization Technical Committee (TC260)
institutions.local_name: 全国网络安全标ardization技术委员会 (全国网络安全标准化技术委员会)
institutions.remit: The standards body that writes China's operative AI safety rules in technical form. Secretariat at the China Electronics Standardization Institute (中国电子技术标准化研究院), under CAC/SAMR guidance. Produced the AI Safety Governance Framework (1.0 Sept 2024, 2.0 Sept 2025), the Ethical Security Guidelines for AI Applications (TC260-005), Practice Guides on labelling AI-generated synthetic content, and in 2026 a draft Practice Guide on general principles for AI application security (TC260-PG-2026NA, 征求意见稿 v1.0, Jan 2026) and a draft development-security guide for agent systems (智能体系统开发安全指南, Sept 2026). Its recommended national standards (GB/T) become de facto mandatory through CAC filing requirements.

routes.note: VERIFIED — published in the TC260 site footer, which I fetched. NO email address is published site-wide; emails appear only inside individual draft-comment notices.

institutions.reality_check: This is the most honest answer to 'can outsiders reach China on AI safety': yes, narrowly, through TC260 draft-standard comment windows — and no, not usefully. The windows are real (typically 30–60 days), the notices name a feedback mailbox, and TC260 has in the past received and visibly incorporated industry comments. But the site is exclusively Chinese with no English page at all (verified), the comment list is JS-rendered and hard to monitor, the feedback template asks for work unit and Chinese contact details, and the entire orientation is toward domestic industry and research institutes. There is no evidence of foreign individual submissions being processed. Anyone building a directory should list TC260 as 'real but effectively domestic-only', and should not promise a working email address — the email changes per notice.
institutions.notes: TC260, not CAC, is where China's AI safety substance is actually drafted. The Framework 2.0 is the single most useful document for understanding China's official risk taxonomy, including its treatment of loss-of-control risk.

institutions.name: China AI Safety and Development Association (CnAISDA)
institutions.local_name: 中国人工智能发展与安全研究网络
institutions.remit: STATUS DELIBERATELY AMBIGUOUS. Unveiled around the Paris AI Action Summit (Feb 2025) and widely described as China's counterpart to the international AISI network. It is a coordinating network, not an institute: it has no independent staff, no research team and no dedicated budget, and federates existing bodies — Tsinghua University (the intellectual centre), Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence (BAAI), CAICT, Shanghai AI Laboratory, the Institute of Automation of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, CCID, and MIIT-linked research groups. Fu Ying described it as 'established with government support'; the precise governmental relationship has never been clarified. Note the Chinese name translates as 'network' (研究网络), not 'association' — the English branding and the Chinese branding do not match.

Its website is English-first, which is itself telling: it is built for foreigners, not for Chinese stakeholders. But I could not extract a single contact address from it. China is NOT a member of the international network; CnAISDA is the parallel structure. Name inconsistency (Association vs Network) is genuine and unresolved.

institutions.remit: Research institute founded in the Beijing AI ecosystem, associated with Yi Zeng (Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences), who is also a member of the UN High-Level Advisory Body on AI and a leading Chinese voice on AI risk.
