A separate Beijing Key Laboratory of AI Safety and Super Alignment also exists at Beijing Normal University — do not conflate them.

institutions.reality_check: This is the one Chinese institution where a foreign AI-safety researcher has a genuinely functioning channel: it publishes in English on arXiv, collaborates openly with Concordia AI, and its researchers respond to academic correspondence. That is a real, working route — but it is a research channel, not a governance or complaint channel. It carries no institutional obligation to respond.
institutions.notes: Its frontier risk framework is the strongest evidence against the claim that China does not engage with catastrophic risk. It explicitly covers loss-of-control and uncontrolled self-replication.

institutions.reality_check: The single most reliable route for a non-Chinese-speaker trying to understand or engage with Chinese AI governance. English-language, responsive, explicitly international in mission. The caveat is the obvious one: it is a private organisation with no authority, cannot transmit complaints to Chinese regulators, and its access depends on remaining uncontroversial with Chinese authorities. Use it for understanding, not for redress.

institutions.name: Autoridade Nacional de Proteção de Dados (ANPD)
institutions.local_name: Autoridade Nacional de Proteção de Dados
institutions.remit: Brazil's data protection authority, an autonomous federal agency. Already regulates AI indirectly through LGPD Article 20 (right to review of automated decisions) and has issued preventive measures against AI training on personal data (notably the 2024 order suspending Meta's use of Brazilian personal data for AI training — real, exercised power). Under PL 2338/2023 as approved by the Senate in December 2024, ANPD would coordinate the proposed Sistema Nacional de Regulação e Governança de IA (SIA). Can investigate, issue preventive suspension orders, and fine (LGPD fines up to 2% of Brazilian turnover, capped at BRL 50 million per infraction).

institutions.reality_check: Mixed. ANPD genuinely runs open consultations and genuinely enforces. But the consultation infrastructure moved during 2025–26 (Participa+Brasil shut down, replaced by Brasil Participativo), so verify any URL before use. Formal complaint filing requires a gov.br account tied to a CPF (Brazilian taxpayer number), which effectively excludes non-residents. Everything is in Portuguese. Informal email to ANPD's ouvidoria is the realistic foreign route, but I could not verify that address.
institutions.notes: Brazil is not a network member and has no AI safety institute.

institutions.name: Brazilian National Congress — PL 2338/2023 (Marco Legal da Inteligência Artificial)
institutions.local_name: Projeto de Lei nº 2.338, de 2023
institutions.remit: STATUS AS OF SEPT 2026: NOT YET LAW. Approved by the Federal Senate in December 2024, then sent to the Chamber of Deputies where a Comissão Especial sobre Inteligência Artificial was constituted. The final vote slipped repeatedly — pushed to December 2025, then to 2026, amid political deadlock and sustained criticism of the text. The Senate-approved version is risk-tiered on an EU-AI-Act model, prohibits certain uses, creates obligations for 'high-risk' and general-purpose systems, and contemplates fines reaching BRL 50 million per infraction. Until enacted it confers no powers on anyone.

routes.label: PL 2338/2023 dossier, Federal Senate
routes.note: UNVERIFIED (search result). The Senate operates an 'e-Cidadania' public opinion tool on bills, open to registered users.

routes.label: Chamber of Deputies Special Committee on AI
routes.note: UNVERIFIED (search result). Committee hearings have taken evidence from industry and civil society.

institutions.reality_check: Do not describe Brazil as having an AI law. It has a Senate-passed bill stuck in the Chamber with repeatedly missed deadlines. The legislative dockets are public and Brazilian committees do hear external witnesses, but this is a Portuguese-language domestic legislative process; foreign input arrives through industry associations, not individuals.
institutions.notes: The bill's treatment of systemic risk from general-purpose models is the closest Latin America comes to frontier-risk regulation.

institutions.name: Artificial Intelligence Office, UAE / Office of the Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence, Digital Economy and Remote Work Applications
institutions.local_name: مكتب الذكاء الاصطناعي
institutions.remit: The world's first dedicated AI ministerial portfolio (Omar Sultan Al Olama, appointed 2017). Sets national AI strategy (UAE National Strategy for AI 2031), runs capability programmes and the AI Charter, and coordinates government AI adoption. Promotional and coordinating rather than regulatory — the UAE has no comprehensive AI statute, and AI-adjacent enforcement sits with sectoral regulators and the data-protection framework. A separate Abu Dhabi AI and Advanced Technology Council (AIATC) handles Abu Dhabi-level investment and strategy; do not conflate the two.

institutions.reality_check: The UAE presents an internationally-facing, English-language front and actively courts foreign AI talent and investment, so it is more approachable in tone than most. But there is no consultation process, no complaint route, and no frontier-risk mandate — the posture is adoption and investment. I could not fetch the site to confirm any contact address; anything published about UAE contact details should be manually re-verified.
institutions.notes: No stated position on frontier or catastrophic risk. The UAE signed the Bletchley Declaration but is not a member of the international network.

institutions.name: Saudi Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority (SDAIA)
institutions.local_name: الهيئة السعودية للبيانات والذكاء الاصطناعي
institutions.remit: The national authority for data and AI, established 2019, reporting to the Prime Minister. Unusually for this list it is BOTH a promoter and a real regulator: it is the competent authority for the Personal Data Protection Law (PDPL), which carries criminal penalties for certain disclosure offences and administrative fines, and it issues AI Ethics Principles (2023, updated 2025), generative-AI guidelines for government and public use, and data-governance regulations. It also runs the National Center for AI (NCAI) and hosts the Global AI Summit. AI-specific rules remain principles-based rather than binding statute.

But SDAIA's site actively blocks automated access, I could verify no contact address, and there is no AI-specific complaint route. PDPL complaints are for data subjects with a Saudi nexus. No frontier-risk mandate whatsoever.
institutions.notes: Saudi Arabia is not a network member. The 2025 update to the AI Ethics Principles is the most recent AI-governance instrument I could confirm.

institutions.name: Ministry of Innovation, Science and Technology — Israel AI policy
institutions.local_name: משרד החדשנות, המדע והטכנולוגיה
institutions.remit: Israel published its 'Policy on Artificial Intelligence Regulation and Ethics' (Dec 2023), jointly with the Ministry of Justice, adopting a deliberately sectoral, soft-law, pro-innovation approach: no AI act, no central AI regulator, guidance to existing sectoral regulators, and a proposed inter-ministerial AI policy coordination centre. The Privacy Protection Authority handles data-related AI issues. As of Sept 2026 I found no evidence that Israel has established an AI safety institute or binding AI legislation.

institutions.reality_check: Weak for outsiders. Israel's approach is explicitly to avoid creating a central AI body, which means there is no address to write to. The policy document was itself produced after a public call for comments (2022), so consultation does happen episodically, but there is no standing channel. gov.il is partially English-language. No frontier-risk institutional stance.
institutions.notes: Israel signed the Bletchley Declaration. Not a network member. I could not verify any 2025–26 institutional change; treat the 2023 policy as the current baseline.

institutions.name: Ministry of Digital Affairs (MODA)
institutions.local_name: 數位發展部
institutions.remit: Taiwan's AI Basic Act (人工智慧基本法) is IN FORCE as of 2026 — a framework statute setting principles (sustainability, human autonomy, privacy, security, transparency, fairness, accountability) and directing agencies rather than imposing direct obligations on developers. MODA is the lead implementing agency, tasked with building risk classification frameworks and evaluation tools; the National Science and Technology Council also has a role. The Act is principles-based with sectoral implementation, so MODA's AI powers are coordinating and standard-setting, not punitive; MODA does hold separate regulatory powers over telecoms and digital services.

That said, the draft-regulation comment platform is Chinese-language, and the published MODA contact email was obfuscated so I cannot supply it. Taiwan's diplomatic status also excludes it from the international network and most multilateral AI processes — a genuine gap.
institutions.notes: Taiwan's AI Basic Act is distinctive for a democratic-governance framing rather than a risk-tier framing. No explicit frontier/catastrophic-risk mandate identified.

institutions.name: Ministry of Communications and Digital Affairs (Komdigi)
institutions.local_name: Kementerian Komunikasi dan Digital
institutions.remit: STATUS IN FLUX AS OF SEPT 2026. Indonesia has no AI act. Komdigi (renamed from Kominfo in late 2024) issued a non-binding AI Ethics Circular (Circular Letter 9/2023) and as of 2026 had submitted two draft Presidential Regulations (Rancangan Peraturan Presiden / Perpres) on AI to the President, with the Deputy Minister publicly explaining that AI would be regulated by Perpres first as a foundation for later primary AI legislation. Komdigi does hold hard powers over electronic system operators under MR 5/2020 — registration requirements, content takedown orders, and the ability to block platforms — which it has used aggressively.

institutions.reality_check: Poor for outsiders. Indonesian AI rulemaking is happening through Presidential Regulations drafted inside the executive, a process with limited public consultation and none in English. Komdigi's real power over foreign platforms (blocking, registration) means foreign companies do engage — but through local counsel and registration compliance, not through any open channel. Bahasa Indonesia only.
institutions.notes: Two draft Perpres on AI were pending as of 2026; I could not confirm whether either had been signed. Treat Indonesian AI regulation as unsettled.

institutions.name: National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) and the Federal Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy
institutions.remit: NITDA is a statutory IT regulator with real powers (registration, standards, sanctions under the NITDA Act) and hosts the National Centre for AI and Robotics (NCAIR). The Federal Ministry owns the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (NAIS), which was itself produced through an unusually open process — a crowdsourced drafting workshop involving Nigerian researchers in the diaspora. A National AI Bill was reported as moving toward approval in 2026, which would create statutory AI powers. The Nigeria Data Protection Commission separately regulates AI's personal-data dimension with fining power.

institutions.reality_check: Nigeria's NAIS drafting explicitly drew on Nigerian researchers abroad, which is genuine openness to non-resident input — though to diaspora, not to foreigners generally. Everything is in English, which removes the main barrier. But I verified no contact address, and the AI Bill's status was unconfirmed. Nigeria's AI governance is developmental in focus with no frontier-risk dimension.
institutions.notes: Nigeria is not a network member. NITDA has genuine enforcement powers, unlike most bodies in this list, but has not to my knowledge exercised them on AI safety grounds.

institutions.name: Department of Communications and Digital Technologies (DCDT)
institutions.remit: Owns South Africa's AI policy process. Published the Draft South Africa National Artificial Intelligence (AI) Policy in Government Gazette No. 54477 on 10 April 2026 for a 60-day public comment period closing 10 June 2026 at 16:00. Policy-making body; enforcement of AI-adjacent harms sits with the Information Regulator (POPIA, which has fining power) and sectoral regulators. South Africa chaired the G20 in 2025 and used it to push African AI capacity issues.

The framing is developmental — capacity, skills, inclusion, infrastructure. This is typical of African AI policy and worth stating plainly in any global directory.

institutions.name: Ministry of ICT and Innovation (MINICT)
institutions.local_name: Minisiteri y'Ikoranabuhanga mu Itumanaho n'Udushya
institutions.remit: Owns Rwanda's National AI Policy, approved by Cabinet in April 2023 — one of the first in Africa, developed with The Future Society and GIZ. Policy/strategy body coordinating AI adoption, skills, data infrastructure and an AI ethics framework; implementation runs through the Rwanda Information Society Authority and the National Cyber Security Authority. Rwanda has hosted the Global AI Summit on Africa and is active in continental AI diplomacy. No AI-specific enforcement powers; data protection sits under Rwanda's 2021 DPP law with the NCSA.

institutions.reality_check: Rwanda is English-language and unusually outward-facing — its AI policy was co-developed with international NGOs, which is direct evidence that foreign input is not merely tolerated but solicited at the institutional level. But that is partnership-based access, not a public channel: I verified no email, no comment process, no complaint route. The policy is developmental, with no frontier-risk content.
institutions.notes: Not a network member. Rwanda's significance is as a convening hub for African AI governance rather than as a regulator.

institutions.name: African Union Commission — Continental Artificial Intelligence Strategy
institutions.remit: The Continental AI Strategy was adopted by African ministers in June 2024 and endorsed by the AU Executive Council in July 2024, alongside the African Digital Compact. It is an Africa-owned, development-first framework covering capacity, infrastructure, datasets, governance and regional cooperation, with an implementation horizon to 2030 and a call for member states to establish national AI strategies and regulatory frameworks. The AU Commission (Department of Infrastructure and Energy / the AU Development Agency AUDA-NEPAD) coordinates; there is no continental AI regulator and no enforcement power. Development was preceded by genuine multistakeholder consultative sessions (2024).

routes.note: UNVERIFIED (search result). AU documents are normally published in all four AU working languages.

routes.label: Multistakeholder consultative sessions announcement
routes.note: UNVERIFIED (search result). Evidence that open consultation sessions were held during drafting; that window has closed.

institutions.reality_check: The AU ran real open multistakeholder consultations during the strategy's development in 2024, and UNESCO supported the process — so there is precedent for external participation. But there is no standing channel, no AI-specific contact address I could verify, and no implementation body with a public interface. The AU's operating reality is member-state diplomacy. For a global directory, the honest entry is: important for context, not contactable on AI matters.
institutions.notes: No frontier or catastrophic-risk content — the strategy is explicitly framed around development, sovereignty, and avoiding extractive AI, and African governments have repeatedly argued that frontier-risk framing crowds out their priorities. That tension is itself a finding worth recording.

institutions.name: Chile — Artificial Intelligence Bill (Boletín 16821-19) and Ministry of Science, Technology, Knowledge and Innovation
institutions.local_name: Ministerio de Ciencia, Tecnología, Conocimiento e Innovación; Proyecto de ley que regula los sistemas de inteligencia artificial
institutions.remit: STATUS AS OF SEPT 2026: STILL A BILL. Chile's comprehensive AI bill, sent by the executive in May 2024 and modelled on the EU AI Act's risk tiers (unacceptable / high / limited / no evident risk), was still in Senate committee proceedings as of February 2026. It would designate an existing or new supervisory authority with sanctioning powers. Chile also has an updated National AI Policy (2024) and leads the Latin American AI Index (ILIA) with Brazil and Uruguay. Until passage, the ministry is a policy body only.

institutions.reality_check: Chile is the most regulatorily advanced Spanish-speaking jurisdiction on AI but still has no law in force. Its previous AI policy consultations were genuinely open and Chile has a good record of participatory policymaking, but I verified no live channel and no URLs. Spanish only. No frontier-risk dimension beyond what it inherits from the EU AI Act template.
institutions.notes: Listed with low confidence. Verify the bill's status directly before publishing — Latin American AI bills have slipped repeatedly.

institutions.local_name: Agencia de Transformación Digital y Telecomunicaciones
institutions.remit: STATUS AS OF SEPT 2026: NO GENERAL AI LAW. The ATDT, created under the Sheinbaum administration, is the federal digital-transformation and telecommunications agency and the likely institutional home for AI coordination. Multiple general AI bills (iniciativas de Ley General de IA) were in legislative process without passage; regulation has instead advanced sector by sector. Mexico's prior AI-relevant oversight body, INAI, was abolished in 2025 as part of the autonomous-bodies reform, with its functions absorbed into the executive — a significant reduction in independent oversight capacity.

institutions.remit: STATUS AS OF SEPT 2026: NO AI LAW AND NO DEDICATED AI BODY I COULD VERIFY. Argentina has a National AI Plan lineage and various bills before Congress, none passed. The concrete 2026 development I could identify is SIGEN Resolution 197/2026 approving a Guide to AI Controls for the Public Sector — an internal-audit instrument for government AI use, not a market regulator. The Agencia de Acceso a la Información Pública handles data-protection aspects. The Milei administration has positioned Argentina as deregulatory and pro-AI-investment.

Treat the legal right as real and the administrative channel as unconfirmed.

Its acronym 'CAISI' collides exactly with the Canadian AI Safety Institute's, and the two are frequently conflated in secondary sources and existing directories.

institutions.name: Independent International Scientific Panel on AI (UN)
institutions.remit: 40-member panel created by UNGA resolution (Aug 2025), members appointed by the General Assembly 12 Feb 2026, co-chairs Yoshua Bengio (Canada) and Maria Ressa (Philippines) elected 3 Mar 2026. Produces one annual evidence-based assessment of AI opportunities/risks/impacts plus thematic briefs; may update the GA up to twice a year. Preliminary Report launched 1 July 2026; first full annual report due at the second Global Dialogue (New York, May 2027).
institutions.threat_model: Deliberately spans the whole range — capability/risk assessment covering misuse, loss-of-control, and systemic/societal impacts — modelled on the IPCC. It is an assessment body, not an advocacy body, so it has no single threat model.

routes.label: Mailing list for Panel updates (only public-facing mechanism found)
routes.scope: Notifications only — not a submission channel
routes.note: Linked from the Panel homepage footer.

routes.label: Generic UN contact form (not Panel-specific)
routes.note: No Panel-specific inbox exists; mail here is very unlikely to reach members.

institutions.reality_check: Effectively closed to outsiders. The FAQ says only that the Panel 'may consult informally with external experts' and may form working groups; there is no call for evidence, no submission portal, and no published contact address. The realistic route in is to reach an individual Panel member through their home institution, or to route through the Global Dialogue's written-inputs process instead.
institutions.notes: Members were selected from 2,600+ applicants across 140+ countries. Bengio simultaneously chairs the International AI Safety Report and runs LawZero, so he is a heavily saturated single point of contact.
institutions.gov_channel: Maximal — reports directly to the UN General Assembly and to the Global Dialogue on AI Governance. But the channel runs one way, from Panel to states.

institutions.name: Global Dialogue on AI Governance (UN)
institutions.remit: Intergovernmental-plus-multistakeholder forum established alongside the Scientific Panel by the Aug 2025 UNGA resolution. Inaugural session held Geneva 6–7 July 2026 (alongside the ITU AI for Good Summit); Co-Chairs' Summary covered four clusters: AI opportunities/implications, bridging AI divides, safe and trustworthy systems, human rights. Joint Secretariat is ITU + ODET + UNESCO. Second session: New York, 3–4 May 2027.
institutions.threat_model: Broad and development-weighted: AI divides and Global South capacity are at least as prominent as safety. Safe/trustworthy AI is one of four clusters, not the organising frame.

routes.label: Written inputs to the AI Dialogue (published submissions archive)
routes.scope: Any stakeholder — governments, civil society, academia, industry
routes.note: Submissions are published via an external portal at https://aiwritteninputs.vercel.app/. The 2026 window has closed; expect a fresh call ahead of the May 2027 New York session.

routes.label: Insights from written submissions (synthesis of what was submitted)
routes.scope: Shows submissions were actually read and synthesised
routes.note: Useful evidence the channel is real, not decorative.

routes.label: Digital Cooperation Fund — route to the Joint Secretariat
routes.note: Travel support for Geneva 2026 has closed.

institutions.reality_check: The single most genuinely open multilateral channel in this whole list. Written submissions are accepted from anyone, are published, and were visibly synthesised for the Geneva session. Low cost, low barrier, and it puts a concern on the permanent record. Weak point: dilution — hundreds of submissions, and no guarantee any one is read by a decision-maker.
institutions.gov_channel: Direct — it is the intergovernmental venue itself, reporting into the UNGA.

institutions.name: International AI Safety Report (Bengio-chaired)
institutions.jurisdiction: International (UK AI Security Institute hosts the Secretariat)
institutions.remit: Mandated by the Bletchley summit; chaired by Yoshua Bengio. 2026 edition published 3 Feb 2026 (arXiv 2602.21012) ahead of the India AI Impact Summit, with an Executive Summary and an Extended Summary for Policymakers. Backed by an Expert Advisory Panel of the 30 Bletchley countries plus the EU, OECD and UN. Synthesises evidence on general-purpose AI capabilities, risks and technical mitigations; it does not make policy recommendations.
institutions.threat_model: Comprehensive by design: malicious use (cyber, bio, manipulation), malfunctions/reliability, systemic risks (labour, concentration, environment), and loss of control are all treated. Notably more balanced across near-term and catastrophic risk than its critics assume.

routes.label: General enquiries
routes.note: Verified by direct fetch of the About page.

routes.label: Secretariat-coordinated review process
routes.scope: Draft review by civil society and industry
routes.note: The About page states the UK Secretariat 'coordinates a review process that gathers feedback from civil society groups and industry leaders'. There is NO published open call for evidence and no public submission form — participation is by invitation into the review round.

institutions.reality_check: Prestigious but not open. There is one inbox and an invitation-only review round. A well-evidenced technical finding emailed to enquiries@ has a plausible path to an author; a general policy opinion does not. The higher-yield route is to get the underlying work cited in the literature the authors survey, since the Report is a synthesis of published evidence.
institutions.gov_channel: Very strong — it is the designated evidence base for the AI summit series and is formally received by ~30 governments plus the EU, OECD and UN.

institutions.name: UNESCO — Recommendation on the Ethics of AI / Global AI Ethics and Governance Observatory
institutions.remit: Adopted Nov 2021, the first global standard-setting instrument on AI ethics: four core values, ten principles, eleven policy action areas. Implementation tools include the Readiness Assessment Methodology (RAM) and Ethical Impact Assessment, a Global Forum on the Ethics of AI, and the Observatory, which maintains a public directory of civil society organisations working on AI ethics. Co-convenor of the UN Global Dialogue Joint Secretariat.
institutions.threat_model: Near-term harms and human-rights framing: discrimination, gender bias, privacy, environmental sustainability, labour, and the digital divide. Explicitly NOT a loss-of-control or frontier-misuse body — do not route a catastrophic-risk concern here expecting traction.

routes.label: Global AI Ethics and Governance Observatory — civil society directory (organisations can be listed)
routes.note: The Observatory hosts profiles of CSOs (e.g. AI Safety Asia) with their contact details.

routes.label: Periodic thematic consultations (e.g. education in the age of AI)
routes.scope: Time-limited open consultations on specific themes
routes.note: Consultations open and close; check the page for a live window.

institutions.reality_check: Bureaucratic and slow, and the bulk of its engagement runs through National Commissions and member-state ministries rather than direct public contact. The Observatory's CSO directory is the one place an outside organisation can actually get itself onto a UN-hosted map at low cost.
institutions.gov_channel: Strong for human-rights and ethics framing; the Recommendation is implemented via national RAM exercises with ministries.

institutions.name: ITU — AI for Good
institutions.remit: ITU's year-round AI platform, co-convened with Switzerland and 50+ UN agencies, organised around Solutions & Knowledge, Skills & Capacity, and Standards & Policy. Hosts the annual Global Summit in Geneva (which co-located with the inaugural Global Dialogue in July 2026), the Innovation Factory startup pitch programme, and the 'Neural Network' community platform (60k+ members).
institutions.threat_model: Overwhelmingly opportunity-framed — SDG applications, capacity building, standards. Safety appears as trustworthiness/standards, not as catastrophic risk. It is the least risk-focused body in the multilateral set.

routes.label: Neural Network community (free to join)
routes.note: Lowest-barrier entry point into the UN AI ecosystem.

routes.label: Engage / partnership enquiries
routes.note: No public email address listed.

institutions.reality_check: Genuinely open to join, genuinely low influence per unit of effort. Good for visibility and contacts; poor for escalating a safety concern.
institutions.gov_channel: Moderate — ITU is a treaty body and runs AI standardisation study groups, but AI for Good itself is a convening platform, not a decision venue. Formal ITU standards work still requires member-state or sector-member status.

institutions.name: OHCHR B-Tech Project (UN Human Rights Office)
institutions.remit: Launched 2019 to apply the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights to the tech sector. Its generative AI workstream has produced a foundational paper on responsible development/deployment of generative AI, a Taxonomy of Generative AI Human Rights Harms, and headline recommendations (2025). Engages states, companies, investors and civil society on human-rights due diligence.
institutions.threat_model: Near-term and structural human-rights harms: discrimination, privacy, freedom of expression, labour, and accountability gaps in corporate AI value chains. Not a loss-of-control body.

routes.label: General OHCHR contact
routes.note: No B-Tech-specific inbox is published.

routes.label: OHCHR Business and Human Rights Helpdesk
routes.scope: Business-and-human-rights queries — the most targeted route
routes.note: Better-aimed than the generic form for a corporate-conduct concern.

routes.label: B-Tech project hub (consultations and papers announced here)

institutions.reality_check: Small team, human-rights framing only. If your concern is a documented corporate harm to identifiable people, this is a serious channel. If it is frontier misalignment, it will not land.
institutions.gov_channel: Real but indirect — feeds Human Rights Council sessions, Special Procedures, and the annual UN Forum on Business and Human Rights. Separately, HRC Special Rapporteurs run their own open calls for input, which is often the faster UN human-rights route.

institutions.name: OECD.AI Policy Observatory (OECD AI Policy Observatory)
institutions.remit: Hub for the OECD AI Principles, national AI policy database, AI Incidents & Hazards Monitor, HAIP transparency reporting, and the GPAI expert community. Underpinned by the Working Party on AI Governance (AIGO) under the Digital Policy Committee.
institutions.threat_model: Governance-neutral and comprehensive: trustworthy AI, incidents, labour market effects, compute and diffusion. Risk taxonomy is broad rather than catastrophe-focused.

routes.label: OECD.AI Network of Experts — nomination only
routes.scope: Members nominated by OECD member states, the European Commission, or one of four recognised stakeholder groups (BIAC business, TUAC labour, CSISAC civil society, ITAC technical)
routes.note: CSISAC is the formal civil-society door into OECD digital policy — that is the concrete route for an individual, not a direct application.

routes.label: Wonk blog — expert commentary
routes.note: UNVERIFIED whether unsolicited pitches are accepted; no submission form was found.

institutions.reality_check: Closed by design. Everything runs through national delegations and the four chartered stakeholder groups. An individual's realistic move is to join a CSISAC-affiliated organisation rather than approach the OECD directly.
institutions.gov_channel: Strong — OECD AI Principles are the reference text for the G7, and OECD work feeds directly into member-state policy.

institutions.name: OECD AI Incidents and Hazards Monitor (AIM)
institutions.remit: Tracks AI incidents and hazards to build an evidence base for policy, currently by automated monitoring of 150,000+ news articles daily via Event Registry, with LLM-based classification against the OECD's common reporting framework for AI incidents.
institutions.threat_model: Realised harms and near-misses across all severities — closest to an aviation-safety model. Empirical rather than theoretical; captures near-term harms far better than speculative catastrophic risk.

routes.label: Open submission process — announced as under development, NOT yet live
routes.scope: Will follow the common reporting framework once launched
routes.note: As of this check the methodology page states the open submission process 'is currently being developed'. There is no public submission form or incident inbox today.

institutions.reality_check: Do not route an incident here yet — there is nowhere to put it. Use the AI Incident Database (incidentdatabase.ai), which accepts public submissions today and which OECD AIM draws on conceptually. Check back when OECD opens submissions.
institutions.gov_channel: Strong — designed explicitly to feed OECD and G7 policy work on incident reporting.

institutions.name: G7 Hiroshima AI Process (HAIP) Reporting Framework
institutions.remit: Voluntary transparency reporting against the G7 Hiroshima Code of Conduct for organisations developing advanced AI. Launched by the OECD Feb 2025; first reports published April 2025; a streamlined version for SMEs launched May 2026. Companies self-report on risk identification, incident handling, security, content authentication and governance; reports are published on a public portal.
institutions.threat_model: Frontier-developer risk management — misuse, security, and safety-framework adequacy. Self-reported, so it measures disclosure, not actual safety.

routes.label: HAIP transparency reporting portal (for organisations that develop AI)
routes.scope: AI-developing organisations of any size, voluntary
routes.note: Not a channel for the general public; it is a self-disclosure form for developers.

institutions.reality_check: Useful as a source of citable company commitments you can hold firms to (as the Midas Project and SaferAI do), rather than as a place to send a concern. There is no public comment or challenge mechanism against a company's self-report — that gap is exactly what the independent trackers fill.
institutions.gov_channel: Direct into the G7 and OECD; reports are cited in G7 ministerial work.

institutions.name: GPAI (Global Partnership on AI)
institutions.jurisdiction: ~44 members, now integrated with the OECD
institutions.remit: Originally an independent multistakeholder partnership (2020); since July 2024 operates as an 'Integrated Partnership on AI with the OECD, under the GPAI brand'. Retains an Expert Community and Centres of Expertise; Council meetings continue (including in New Delhi). Work covers responsible AI, data governance, future of work, and innovation.
institutions.threat_model: Broad responsible-AI agenda; strong on data governance, labour and Global South inclusion. Not frontier-safety focused.

routes.label: GPAI Expert Community — membership via nomination
routes.scope: Experts nominated through member governments and partner institutions
routes.note: Since OECD integration, expert nomination follows the OECD route; no open application was found.

routes.label: GPAI at OECD — overview and contact route

institutions.reality_check: Its independent multistakeholder character has thinned considerably since the OECD merge. Treat it as an OECD programme for access purposes.
institutions.gov_channel: Ministerial-level; GPAI Council statements are government-endorsed.

institutions.name: Council of Europe — Framework Convention on AI (CETS No. 225) and the Committee on AI (CAI)
institutions.remit: First legally binding international treaty on AI, opened for signature 5 Sept 2024. 19 signatories at last check including Albania, Andorra, Armenia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Georgia, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Norway, Moldova, San Marino, Switzerland, Ukraine, the UK, plus non-members Canada, Israel, Japan, the USA and Uruguay, and the European Union. The EU has ratified; the treaty requires five ratifications including three CoE member states to enter into force, so it is NOT yet in force. Obligations cover human rights, democracy and rule of law across the AI lifecycle.
institutions.threat_model: Human rights, democracy and rule of law — so democratic-process harms, discrimination, and rule-of-law erosion. Systemic/structural rather than catastrophic-risk framing.

routes.label: Council of Europe AI unit contact
routes.scope: General enquiries to the AI programme

routes.label: CAI observer status for international NGOs
routes.scope: 68 representatives from civil society, academia and industry participated as observers in the drafting
routes.note: Observer status is granted to organisations, not individuals, and is decided by the committee. UNVERIFIED whether new observer applications are currently open.

institutions.reality_check: Open to organised civil society through observer status, closed to individuals. The CAI historically ran genuinely substantive observer participation during drafting — one of the better multilateral records. Slow: entry into force is still pending.
institutions.gov_channel: Treaty-level — binding on ratifying parties, with implementation reporting through the Conference of the Parties once in force.

institutions.name: HUDERIA (Council of Europe risk and impact assessment methodology)
institutions.remit: Human Rights, Democracy and Rule of Law Impact Assessment for AI systems, developed with the Alan Turing Institute. Two parts: the HUDERIA Methodology, approved by the Committee of Ministers on 26 February 2025, and the HUDERIA Model: COBRA (supporting tools for systematic analysis), approved 25 February 2026. Non-binding guidance that parties may adapt. Supported by HUDERIA Academy tracks including Health and Local Authorities; piloted with businesses in Ukraine.
institutions.threat_model: Human-rights, democratic and rule-of-law harms from deployed AI systems — a structured near-term/structural harms instrument.

routes.label: CoE AI programme contact
routes.note: No HUDERIA-specific email is published.

institutions.reality_check: A usable tool rather than a channel. The practical value for an outsider is to run a HUDERIA/COBRA assessment on a system you are worried about and submit the result to a regulator — it is a recognised format that European authorities will accept.
institutions.gov_channel: Feeds implementation of the Framework Convention by ratifying states and is being piloted with national authorities.

institutions.name: India AI Impact Summit 2026 (AI summit series)
institutions.remit: Successor to the Paris AI Action Summit (Feb 2025), held in New Delhi 19–20 February 2026 — the first global AI summit hosted in the Global South. Structured around three Sutras (People, Planet, Progress) and seven Chakras (Human Capital, Social Empowerment, Safe AI, Resilience & Innovation, Science, Democratising AI Resources, Economic Growth). Adopted the New Delhi Declaration plus investment commitments; the government reported very large public attendance (~600,000 across associated events). The International AI Safety Report 2026 was published ahead of it.
institutions.threat_model: Development-and-diffusion first. 'Safe AI' is one of seven chakras — a demotion relative to Bletchley (2023), continuing the trajectory set at Paris. Emphasis on access, inclusion and economic impact over catastrophic risk.

routes.label: Summit site — events, Global South Showcase, research symposium
routes.scope: Side events, showcases and symposium tracks were open to applications in the run-up
routes.note: The 2026 cycle is closed; civil society participated mainly through side events and the research symposium rather than the main plenary.

routes.label: UN ODET side-events page for the summit

institutions.reality_check: The summit itself is now past. Civil society access in this series has been consistently side-event access, not negotiating-room access, and the safety agenda has thinned at each iteration. UNVERIFIED: no confirmed host or date for the next summit in the series was found at the time of checking — watch for an announcement.
institutions.gov_channel: Head-of-state level; declarations are politically binding signals, not law.

institutions.name: ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 42 — Artificial Intelligence
institutions.jurisdiction: International (ISO/IEC); secretariat held by ANSI (United States)
institutions.remit: The lead international AI standardisation committee, established 2017. Five working groups (WG1 foundational standards, WG2 data, WG3 trustworthiness, WG4 use cases and applications, WG5 computational approaches and system characteristics) plus seven joint working groups with other committees. 59 participating and 25 observing member bodies; 44 published standards and ~49 in development — including ISO/IEC 42001 (AI management systems) and 23894 (risk management).
institutions.threat_model: Trustworthiness as an engineering property: robustness, bias, transparency, risk management, functional safety. Not oriented to catastrophic or loss-of-control risk.

routes.label: Participate via your NATIONAL standards body's mirror committee — the only route for an individual
routes.scope: Anyone in a participating member country
routes.note: Concretely: find your country's ISO member (ANSI in the US, BSI in the UK, DIN in Germany, SCC in Canada, BIS in India, SAC in China, Standards Australia), apply to join its SC 42 mirror committee, and you become eligible to be nominated as a national delegate/expert to SC 42 WGs. Fees and eligibility vary by country — some (e.g. SCC Canada) accept individuals free of charge; others require corporate membership.

routes.label: SC 42 Committee Manager, Heather Benko (ANSI)
routes.note: Named on the ISO committee page.

routes.label: Public enquiry/ballot comment on draft standards — submitted through your national body
routes.scope: Anyone, but comments are channelled and consolidated nationally
routes.note: You cannot comment directly to ISO; your national body aggregates and submits its country position.

institutions.reality_check: Not closed, but gated and slow. A determined individual genuinely can get into the room via a mirror committee, and mirror committees are frequently under-subscribed for civil-society voices — the marginal outsider has unusually high influence there. Expect a 1–3 year horizon and unpaid meeting-heavy work. Drafts are copyrighted and not public, which is the real barrier.
institutions.gov_channel: Very high leverage indirectly — ISO/IEC standards are referenced by regulators worldwide and ISO/IEC 42001 is becoming the de facto compliance artefact.

institutions.name: CEN-CENELEC JTC 21 — Artificial Intelligence
institutions.remit: Established 1 June 2021; 300+ experts from 20+ countries across five working groups. Develops the harmonised European standards that give presumption of conformity with the EU AI Act once cited in the Official Journal — e.g. AI trustworthiness framework, AI risk management, AI quality management system (prEN 18286), conformity assessment, datasets and bias, cybersecurity, robustness, logging. CEN/CENELEC decided in late 2025 to accelerate the work programme after delays.
institutions.threat_model: EU AI Act risk categories: health, safety and fundamental rights of persons affected by high-risk systems, plus GPAI systemic risk. Compliance-engineering framing.

routes.label: Join via your National Standardization Body / National Committee — primary route
routes.note: Contact your NSB (AFNOR, DIN, UNI, NEN, BSI, etc.) and ask to join its JTC 21 mirror committee. This is the concrete individual route.

routes.label: CEN-CENELEC Project Manager Yannis Chourmouziadis — for European/international organisations seeking to join directly
routes.scope: European and international organisations (Annex III-type bodies), not individuals
routes.note: Annex III organisations (ANEC for consumers, ETUC for workers, ECOS for environment, SBS for SMEs) hold standing seats and are the designated civil-society voice.

routes.label: ETUC AI standardisation inclusiveness mailing list
routes.scope: Civil society and worker representatives following JTC 21
routes.note: Practical way to track the work without a committee seat.

routes.label: European Standards & AI LinkedIn group (informal tracking)

institutions.reality_check: The most consequential standards body for anyone in Europe right now, and the most criticised for weak civil-society representation relative to industry. The Annex III organisations are chronically under-resourced and actively want outside expertise — approaching ANEC, ECOS or ETUC is a far more tractable route than approaching CEN-CENELEC directly.
institutions.gov_channel: Direct legal effect — these standards operationalise the EU AI Act.

institutions.name: IEEE Standards Association — 7000 series and CertifAIEd
institutions.remit: IEEE 7000-series standards on ethical system design (IEEE 7000 process standard, 7001 transparency, 7002 data privacy, 7010 wellbeing, etc.), the Ethically Aligned Design framework from the Global Initiative on Ethics of Autonomous and Intelligent Systems, and CertifAIEd, an ethics certification/assessment programme for AI systems with trained assessors.
institutions.threat_model: Applied ethics and value-alignment-by-design at the system level: transparency, bias, privacy, wellbeing, accountability. Near-term and design-stage, not frontier catastrophic risk.

routes.label: IEEE SA individual membership — the distinguishing feature vs ISO/CEN
routes.scope: Any individual, worldwide, for a membership fee
routes.note: IEEE runs an individual-based standards process alongside its entity-based one. You do NOT need a national standards body or an employer to join a working group. This makes IEEE by far the most accessible major standards body for an unaffiliated person.

routes.label: Opportunities to participate (working groups, ballot groups)
IEEE SA contact
routes.scope: General enquiries about joining a working group or balloting

institutions.reality_check: The single most open standards route for an individual. Working groups are frequently small and welcome active contributors; an engaged newcomer can have real drafting influence within months. Trade-off: IEEE 7000-series standards have much less regulatory force than ISO/IEC 42001 or the CEN-CENELEC harmonised standards.
institutions.gov_channel: Moderate — IEEE standards are widely referenced and CertifAIEd has been piloted by public bodies, but IEEE has no regulatory mandate.

institutions.name: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) and AI Resource Center
institutions.remit: AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023) — a voluntary framework structured around Govern, Map, Measure, Manage — plus the Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1), crosswalks to other frameworks, the AI RMF Roadmap, and the AI Resource Center (AIRC) with the Trustworthy & Responsible AI playbooks. The RMF is being revised under the White House AI Action Plan.
institutions.threat_model: Sociotechnical risk across the board: validity, safety, security/resilience, accountability/transparency, explainability, privacy, and bias. The GenAI Profile explicitly covers CBRN information access, confabulation, dangerous/violent content and harmful bias — so it does reach misuse risk, but not loss of control.

routes.label: AI RMF team inbox — reads and logs external comments
routes.scope: Anyone; feedback on the framework, roadmap, crosswalks
routes.note: Published on NIST's own Engage page. NIST has historically published the comments it receives.

routes.label: Formal Requests for Information / public comment dockets
routes.scope: Anyone, during open windows; comments are published
routes.note: Prior RFI responses are archived at https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework/comments-received-rfi-artificial-intelligence-risk-management — evidence that submissions are genuinely published.

routes.label: Mailing list for NIST AI activity announcements (catches new comment windows)

institutions.reality_check: Genuinely responsive by government standards: a real published inbox, real published comment dockets, and a track record of incorporating external crosswalks. A substantive, well-structured comment submitted during an open RFI is one of the highest-yield low-cost actions available anywhere in this list for a US-relevant concern. Note that NIST's AI safety posture shifted substantially with the 2025 AI Action Plan and the CAISI reorganisation — the framing is now innovation-and-security rather than safety.
institutions.gov_channel: Direct — NIST is a US federal agency; the AI RMF is referenced in federal procurement, state legislation and international crosswalks.

institutions.name: Frontier Model Forum
institutions.remit: Industry-supported non-profit founded by Amazon, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI. Publishes technical reports and issue briefs on frontier capability assessments and safety frameworks, with workstreams on AI-Bio, AI-Cyber, AI-Nuclear, AI Security and Safety Frameworks. Runs information-sharing between member labs and with government.
institutions.threat_model: Severe misuse risk at the frontier — CBRN and offensive cyber uplift — plus security of model weights. Explicitly narrow: it is a misuse-and-security body, not an alignment or near-term-harms body.

routes.label: Membership criteria (for frontier developers only)
routes.scope: Organisations that develop and deploy frontier models and have a safety framework
routes.note: Individuals cannot join.

institutions.reality_check: Effectively closed. It is a members' club of the largest labs with a single generic inbox. Sending a concern here is close to sending it to the labs' shared comms function. Its technical publications are worth reading; it is not a route in.
institutions.gov_channel: Strong and quiet — the FMF is a recognised industry interlocutor for the US and UK governments and for the AI Safety/Security Institute network.

institutions.name: MLCommons — AILuminate benchmark (AI Risk & Reliability working group)
institutions.remit: AILuminate is a standardised AI risk assessment benchmark for chat and vision-language models across 12 hazard categories, built with industry, academia and civil society; at last check 59,624 test prompts, 477 test images and 109 models benchmarked, with expanding agentic, multimodal and jailbreak/security suites. Produces public grades per model.
institutions.threat_model: Product-level hazard and reliability: violent crime facilitation, CSAM, hate, self-harm, privacy, IP, defamation, specialised advice. Near-term deployment harms and misuse — NOT loss of control.

routes.label: AI Risk & Reliability working group — open to participants
routes.scope: Researchers and practitioners; working-group participation is the substantive route
routes.note: MLCommons working groups run open calls and mailing lists; this is a genuine build-it-with-us channel.

routes.label: GitHub — code, taxonomy and prompt-set contributions/issues

institutions.reality_check: One of the more genuinely participatory technical bodies. If you can demonstrate a hazard category the benchmark misses, the working group is a place where that can actually change an artefact that companies are graded on. Requires technical credibility and sustained attendance.
institutions.gov_channel: Moderate — AILuminate is cited in policy discussion of evaluation standards and MLCommons engages with NIST and the safety-institute network, but it has no formal mandate.

institutions.name: Partnership on AI (PAI)
institutions.remit: Multistakeholder convener with 100+ partner organisations spanning Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Apple alongside ACLU, ARTICLE 19, Future of Privacy Forum, UNICEF, UNDP and universities. Produces guidance documents and frameworks — notably on safe foundation model deployment, synthetic media, and AI and labour — across four programme areas: AI and Human Connection; AI, Labor and the Economy; Safety-Critical AI; and Public Policy.
institutions.threat_model: Deliberately plural. Its Safety-Critical AI programme touches frontier deployment risk; its labour and human-connection work is squarely near-term/structural. Its distinctive contribution is process norms rather than a risk thesis.

routes.label: Contact form
routes.note: No public email address is listed.

institutions.reality_check: Consensus-bound. With the largest labs as partners, PAI's outputs are negotiated to the level everyone can accept, which limits how sharp a concern it will carry. Organisational partnership is possible; individual input is not really a thing. Middling responsiveness.
institutions.gov_channel: Moderate — PAI guidance is cited in policy processes and it participates in multistakeholder forums, but it is a norm-setter, not an advocate.

institutions.name: AI Incident Database (Responsible AI Collaborative)
institutions.remit: Public, open-source, citable index of realised AI harms and near-harms, modelled on aviation and cybersecurity incident databases. Community-submitted incidents are editorially reviewed and indexed with reports, entities and classifications. Recent entries span AI medical transcription misuse, deepfake tooling, chatbots implicated in violence planning, and law-enforcement technology abuse.
institutions.threat_model: Realised harms of any severity, empirically grounded. Strongest on near-term harms; increasingly captures misuse and agentic failures. Not a theoretical-risk organisation.

routes.label: Submit an incident — open to anyone, no account required
routes.note: THE canonical public route for reporting a concrete AI harm. Submissions are editorially reviewed before publication.

institutions.reality_check: Small, volunteer-heavy, and genuinely reads its submissions — one of the few places in this entire list where an unaffiliated person's report reliably gets human attention and can end up in the permanent public record. If you have a specific realised harm, start here. Editorial review takes time and marginal submissions do get rejected.
institutions.gov_channel: Indirect but real — AIID entries are cited by OECD AIM, academic literature, journalists and regulators. Getting an incident indexed here makes it citable everywhere else.

institutions.name: AI Lab Watch
institutions.remit: Scorecard grading Anthropic, Google DeepMind, OpenAI, Meta, xAI, Microsoft and DeepSeek across seven safety categories: risk assessment, scheming-risk prevention, safety research, misuse prevention, extreme security, risk information sharing, and planning for dangerous capabilities. Created and run solo by Zach Stein-Perlman.
institutions.threat_model: Explicitly catastrophic-risk and loss-of-control framing — scheming, dangerous capabilities, weight security. The sharpest frontier-safety-only scorecard of the trackers.

routes.label: Resources page (still maintained per the site)

institutions.reality_check: DORMANT. The site states the author stopped maintaining it in September 2025, and no contact email is published. Do not route anything here. For a live equivalent use FLI's AI Safety Index, SaferAI's ratings, or the Midas Project's Seoul Tracker and Watchtower.
institutions.gov_channel: None formal.

institutions.name: Future of Life Institute (FLI)
institutions.jurisdiction: US and EU (Brussels presence, EU Transparency Register)
institutions.remit: Advocacy, grantmaking and policy across AI, biotechnology and nuclear weapons. Outputs include the AI Safety Index (latest edition Summer 2026, published July 2026, grading nine companies — Anthropic C+, OpenAI C, Google DeepMind C, Meta D+, Z.ai D-, Alibaba Cloud D-, xAI F, DeepSeek F, Mistral F — reviewed by a seven-member panel of David Krueger, Sharon Li, Tegan Maharaj, Sneha Revanur, Stuart Russell, Robert Trager and Yi Zeng), the 2023 pause letter, EU AI Act advocacy, and substantial grant programmes.
institutions.threat_model: Extreme large-scale and existential risk, with loss of control and uncontrolled capability escalation as the central AI concern. Also carries structural concerns (power concentration, autonomous weapons). Not a near-term-harms organisation, though the Index rates some near-term practices.

routes.label: General enquiries — states a 3-business-day response target
Policy team (including AI Safety Index input)
routes.note: Listed on the Index page as the route for input on the Index.

routes.label: Grant programmes — open calls (PhD/postdoc fellowships, project grants)

institutions.reality_check: Unusually responsive for its size, and the only major org here that publishes an explicit response-time commitment. Well-resourced, so it can act on what it receives. The Index gives it leverage over company behaviour that few others have.
institutions.gov_channel: Strong — EU Transparency Register presence and sustained EU AI Act engagement, plus US state and federal advocacy and UN input.

institutions.name: Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI)
institutions.remit: Originally the founding technical alignment research organisation; since 2024 pivoted almost entirely to communications and policy advocacy for an international halt on frontier AI development. Its site states: 'Our survival depends on some form of globally coordinated and collectively enforced moratorium on the development of ASI, as soon as we can, for as long as necessary.' Outputs are now books, essays and briefings rather than alignment papers.
institutions.threat_model: Pure loss-of-control / misalignment extinction risk, and the strongest version of it — MIRI's public position is that technical alignment has failed to keep pace and that a moratorium is the only remaining lever. Zero emphasis on near-term harms.
institutions.reality_check: Reads its mail but is highly selective about engagement, and is not interested in concerns outside its narrow thesis. If your concern is anything other than existential risk from superintelligence, this is the wrong door. Note: the user's list includes 'Machine Intelligence Research' separately — that is MIRI's own name, not a distinct organisation.
institutions.gov_channel: Moderate and growing — MIRI staff brief policymakers and its arguments circulate widely in Washington and Westminster, but it has no formal advisory seat.

institutions.name: Redwood Research
institutions.remit: Non-profit research organisation that effectively founded the 'AI control' agenda: designing and red-teaming protocols that keep deployments safe even if the model is actively trying to subvert them. Known for control evaluations, monitoring protocols for malign LLM agents, the alignment-faking work with Anthropic, and helping developers build safety cases.
institutions.threat_model: Intentional misalignment and scheming — models that purposefully act against their developers' interests. Distinctively assumes alignment may fail and asks what safety measures survive that assumption. Loss-of-control, not misuse or near-term harms.

routes.label: General enquiries
routes.note: Note the unusual domain — rdwrs.com, not redwoodresearch.org.

routes.label: Research engagement via public writing
routes.note: Redwood staff engage actively and publicly on the Alignment Forum and LessWrong — in practice the highest-bandwidth way to reach them with a technical argument.

institutions.reality_check: Small and technically serious; will engage substantively with a good technical argument, and its researchers are notably responsive in public research forums. Will not engage with policy complaints or non-technical concerns.
institutions.gov_channel: Indirect — AI control has been adopted into frontier-lab safety frameworks and cited in safety-institute work; Redwood advises labs rather than governments.

institutions.name: Apollo Research
institutions.jurisdiction: United Kingdom (London) / US-registered (EIN 93-4310599, EU Transparency Register 837878591690-80)
institutions.remit: Evaluates frontier models for scheming, strategic deception and evaluation-awareness; builds Watcher, a runtime monitoring tool for coding agents; and advises governments on frontier regulation. Ran the in-context scheming evaluations that appear in OpenAI and Anthropic system cards.
institutions.threat_model: Scheming — AI that pursues its own goals while appearing aligned — plus loss of control in automated AI R&D and misaligned models as insider threats. Explicitly a deceptive-alignment organisation.

routes.label: General and research-partnership enquiries
routes.scope: Anyone; the contact page explicitly invites partnership on scheming, loss-of-control and monitoring research

institutions.reality_check: Small, focused, and explicitly soliciting research collaboration on its contact page — one of the more genuinely open technical labs. There is no dedicated route for reporting a concern about a model or a company, only a general inbox.
institutions.gov_channel: Strong for its size — its governance team works with the UK AI Security Institute and EU processes, and it is on the EU Transparency Register.

institutions.name: METR (Model Evaluation & Threat Research)
institutions.remit: Research non-profit that evaluates frontier models for autonomous and dangerous capabilities and publishes the results. Best known for the time-horizon metric (length of task an agent can complete at 50% reliability), pre-deployment evaluations for OpenAI and Anthropic, and work on threats to evaluation integrity — generalised reward hacking and sandbagging. Formerly ARC Evals.
institutions.threat_model: Dangerous autonomous capability and loss of control: autonomous replication, rogue deployment inside a lab, automated AI R&D acceleration, sabotage, and the meta-problem that models may deliberately underperform on evaluations.

routes.label: Careers
routes.note: METR also runs paid contractor/baseliner work for task development, which is an unusual paid entry route for technical outsiders.

institutions.reality_check: Credible and influential well beyond its size, but heavily capacity-constrained and bound by NDAs with the labs it evaluates. A general inbox, no tip line. It will not act as a whistleblowing channel.
institutions.gov_channel: Strong — METR's evaluations are referenced in frontier-lab safety frameworks and by the US and UK safety/security institutes; its time-horizon results are widely cited in policy.

institutions.name: Alignment Research Center (ARC)
institutions.remit: Small theory-focused non-profit. Current agenda is a theoretical foundation for mechanistic explanations of neural network behaviour — heuristic arguments, low-probability estimation, and algorithms that analyse weights directly rather than by sampling, aimed at predicting out-of-distribution behaviour and detecting anomalies. Its evaluations arm spun out to become METR.
institutions.threat_model: Worst-case intent alignment and deceptive alignment — specifically the problem of catching behaviours that never appear during training or testing. The most theoretical agenda in the field.

routes.label: Hiring
routes.note: No contact email is published anywhere on the site.

routes.label: Blog / theory write-ups — engagement happens in public research discussion
routes.note: ARC has historically run prize competitions for progress on its open problems; UNVERIFIED whether one is currently live.

institutions.reality_check: Effectively closed and by far the most inward-facing organisation on this list — no email, no contact form, tiny team, deeply technical agenda. The only way in is a serious mathematical contribution to its stated open problems. Do not route a concern here.
institutions.gov_channel: None. ARC does no policy work.

institutions.name: Resolution (formerly Timaeus; launched as Sequent)
institutions.jurisdiction: United States (Berkeley HQ), with London and Melbourne presence
institutions.remit: Non-profit alignment research organisation formed by merging researchers from Timaeus (which pioneered applying singular learning theory to alignment and developmental interpretability) with the UK AI Security Institute's Alignment Team. Launched under the name Sequent, then rebranded to Resolution. Portfolio spans scalable oversight, learning theory (SLT, deep learning theory), mechanistic understanding and heuristic arguments, agent foundations, and model personas — with heavy investment in automating alignment research. Targeting 40–80 FTE researchers within two years.
institutions.threat_model: Misalignment and loss of control, approached through theory. The explicit bet is that theory unlocks automation of alignment research before capabilities outrun it.

routes.label: Legacy Timaeus site (redirects/announces the rebrand), Discord and GitHub
routes.note: timaeus.co now carries the banner 'Timaeus is now Resolution'. The old Timaeus Discord and github.com/timaeus-research remain the community entry points for SLT work.

institutions.reality_check: Brand-new and actively hiring, which makes it unusually open to technical newcomers right now. IMPORTANT for routing: do not address correspondence to 'Timaeus' — that name is retired. The SLT research community around it has historically been very welcoming to outside contributors via Discord and open seminars.
institutions.gov_channel: Indirect via the UK AISI alumni network; no formal advisory seat.

institutions.name: EleutherAI
institutions.remit: Grassroots-origin open research lab. Trains and releases open-source LLMs (GPT-NeoX, Pythia), maintains the LM Evaluation Harness used across the field, and researches interpretability (interpreting across training time), eliciting latent knowledge, alignment, and non-text modalities. Runs almost entirely in public on Discord.
institutions.threat_model: Mixed and openness-centric: the core thesis is that open models and public interpretability tooling are necessary for anyone outside the large labs to audit AI. Touches alignment (ELK, interpretability) but is not an x-risk organisation; it is frequently in tension with the pause/restriction wing.

routes.label: Discord — the actual organisation; research happens in public channels
routes.note: By far the most open research community in AI. Newcomers routinely join projects and end up as paper co-authors.

institutions.reality_check: The most genuinely open organisation in this entire list. An unaffiliated person with technical skill can join the Discord today and be contributing to alignment-relevant research within weeks. Caveat: it is a research community, not a complaints channel, and its open-release stance means it is not a natural home for a restrict-frontier-models concern.
institutions.gov_channel: Modest — EleutherAI has filed comments in US policy processes (notably on open models) and its researchers are cited on open-weight policy, but it has no advisory seat.

institutions.name: Conjecture
institutions.remit: For-profit AI company founded from the alignment community. Public agenda is Cognitive Emulation — building AI systems that follow bounded, auditable, human-like reasoning processes rather than opaque end-to-end learned policies. In practice the public site now emphasises task-specific training, modular AI components and workflow automation products.
institutions.threat_model: Loss of control via unbounded, uninterpretable general systems; the CoEm bet is that architecture-level boundedness is safer than post-hoc alignment. Its leadership has also been prominent in public advocacy against frontier scaling.

routes.label: Contact form
routes.note: No public email address is listed.

institutions.reality_check: Has become markedly more product-focused and less publicly research-transparent than in 2022–23. A commercial entity with a contact form. Low responsiveness to unsolicited outside input.
institutions.gov_channel: Indirect — its co-founder has been an active public voice in UK and EU AI policy debate, but the company holds no formal advisory role.

institutions.name: Goodfire
institutions.remit: For-profit interpretability research lab. Reverse-engineers causal mechanisms in neural networks; commercial product Silico for model understanding, debugging and training-time steering. Publishes interpretability research alongside the commercial offering.
institutions.threat_model: Interpretability as the enabling technology for oversight; the implicit model is that undiagnosable systems cannot be safely deployed. Commercially oriented toward debugging and control rather than catastrophic-risk mitigation.

routes.label: Research access request
routes.scope: Researchers — a genuine route for academics to get tooling access

institutions.reality_check: A company, not an advocacy body — note the domain moved from goodfire.ai to goodfire.com. No published email. The research-access programme and Discord are real routes for technical outsiders; there is no channel for raising a concern.
institutions.gov_channel: None formal.

institutions.name: Transluce
institutions.remit: Non-profit research lab building, in its words, 'the public tech stack for scalable oversight of AI'. Outputs include Docent (a platform for understanding model behaviours at scale), public behaviour reports (e.g. evaluating model responses in mental-health crisis scenarios), and research on activation oracles and surfacing behaviours third parties should monitor.
institutions.threat_model: Oversight capability gap — the concern that no one outside the labs has tooling to audit model behaviour. Spans near-term behavioural harms (crisis response, deception in deployment) and scalable-oversight/alignment concerns. Deliberately public-interest rather than x-risk framed.

routes.label: Behaviour reports — public catalogue of surfaced model behaviours
routes.scope: Public read; UNVERIFIED whether outside submissions are accepted
routes.note: Worth checking for a submission route — the framing is explicitly about what third parties should monitor.

institutions.reality_check: Small, open-source-first, and explicitly building infrastructure for outsiders to audit models — one of the better-aligned targets if your concern is a specific observed model behaviour you can document. Responsive relative to its size.
institutions.gov_channel: Indirect — its public behaviour reports have driven press coverage and company responses.

institutions.name: LawZero
institutions.remit: Non-profit founded by Yoshua Bengio in June 2025 to develop safe-by-design AI. Core technical bet is 'Scientist AI' — a non-agentic, uncertainty-quantifying system designed to understand and predict rather than to act, usable as a guardrail that monitors and vetoes unsafe actions by agentic systems.
institutions.threat_model: Loss of control from agentic AI with goals and self-preservation drives. Bengio's explicit thesis is that agency itself is the hazard and that non-agentic systems are the safe substrate.
institutions.reality_check: New and building. Two real published inboxes, which is more than most technical labs offer. Be aware that Bengio is spread across three major roles — reaching LawZero is not the same as reaching him, and volume to him is extremely high.
institutions.gov_channel: Very strong by proxy — Bengio chairs both the International AI Safety Report and co-chairs the UN Scientific Panel. LawZero itself has no formal advisory seat, but its founder is the single most connected individual in global AI safety governance.

institutions.name: FAR.AI
institutions.remit: Runs three distinct arms: in-house research on a portfolio of agendas (robustness, deception detection, red-teaming, safeguard vulnerabilities); a field-building events programme (Alignment Workshops, the Seoul and Cambridge workshops, verification workshops, technical-governance convenings); and FAR.Labs, a Berkeley co-working space for AI safety researchers, plus a grantmaking programme for academics and independent researchers.
institutions.threat_model: Broad frontier-risk portfolio — reward hacking, deception, jailbreaking through layered defences, and misuse. Deliberately agenda-agnostic; its comparative advantage is convening rather than a single thesis.

routes.label: Contact page
routes.note: No public email address is listed on the site.

routes.label: Grants for academics and independent researchers
routes.note: UNVERIFIED whether a specific open application window exists; the grantmaking programme is described on the site but application mechanics were not confirmed.

routes.label: FAR.Labs Berkeley co-working space
routes.note: Application-based.

institutions.reality_check: Genuinely a connector organisation and a good place for a technically credible outsider to get into the room via workshops or FAR.Labs. Weakness for routing purposes: no published email, only a form.
institutions.gov_channel: Indirect but useful — its workshops convene government, lab and academic participants, including around the safety-summit circuit.

institutions.name: Center for AI Safety (CAIS)
institutions.remit: Three pillars: technical and conceptual safety research; field-building (fellowships, the ML Safety course, and free access to its compute cluster for safety researchers); and safety standards/advocacy. Authored the one-sentence 2023 Statement on AI Risk signed by most leading AI scientists and lab CEOs. Paired with a separate 501(c)(4), the CAIS Action Fund.
institutions.threat_model: Societal-scale and catastrophic risk — malicious use, AI race dynamics, organisational risks and rogue AI, per its own taxonomy. Covers both misuse and loss of control; broader than MIRI, narrower than PAI.

routes.label: Compute cluster access for ML safety researchers — a concrete resource for unaffiliated researchers
routes.note: Free GPU access is a real and unusual offer to outsiders.

institutions.reality_check: Well-resourced and reads its inbox. The compute cluster and the ML safety course are the most tangible things any organisation here offers an unaffiliated technical person. Policy input is better routed to the Action Fund.
institutions.gov_channel: Strong via its Action Fund (see separate entry); CAIS itself was closely involved in California SB 1047 and subsequent state legislation.

institutions.name: Center for AI Safety Action Fund (CAIS AF)
institutions.remit: 501(c)(4) advocacy arm of CAIS. Nonpartisan lobbying and policymaker education. Stated policy focus areas: US leadership in AI chip manufacturing, compute security, preventing malicious use of AI, and global cooperation for safe and secure AI. Registered federal lobbyist; active in state legislation.
institutions.threat_model: Catastrophic misuse and national-security risk, plus compute governance. More security-and-competitiveness framed than the research arm.

routes.label: General enquiries
routes.note: Verified on action.safe.ai.

institutions.reality_check: If you want a catastrophic-risk concern carried into US legislative offices, this is one of about three organisations that can actually do it (with Encode and FLI). Contributions are not tax-deductible, which is the price of the lobbying capability.
institutions.gov_channel: Direct — registered federal lobbying disclosures (OpenSecrets, LegiStorm) and sustained state-legislature engagement. One of the few AI safety organisations that formally lobbies.

institutions.name: Centre for the Governance of AI (GovAI)
institutions.jurisdiction: United Kingdom (Oxford), with a US policy presence
institutions.remit: Research institute producing academic-quality AI governance research and, critically, a talent pipeline — GovAI Fellowships (biannual UK editions plus other cohorts), an Entrepreneur-in-Residence programme offering a salaried year plus ~$150k seed funding to launch new AI governance organisations, and policy roles. Research spans compute governance, corporate governance of labs, international institutions, and dual-use capability risk (e.g. bioterrorism risk from dual-use AI).
institutions.threat_model: Frontier and transformative-AI governance: dual-use misuse (especially bio), racing dynamics, institutional readiness, and loss of control. Long-termist in origin, increasingly mainstream-policy in output.

routes.label: Opportunities page — fellowships, roles, and the Entrepreneur-in-Residence programme
routes.note: EiR runs on a rolling basis — a genuinely open route for someone with a good new-organisation idea.

institutions.reality_check: Responsive and actively recruiting outsiders — the fellowship and EiR routes are real and competitive rather than nominal. It is a research and talent institution, not a complaints channel; it will engage with a well-argued governance proposal, not with a grievance.
institutions.gov_channel: Strong — GovAI alumni populate the UK AI Security Institute, the European Commission's AI Office, and frontier-lab policy teams. Its researchers advise governments directly.

institutions.name: Institute for AI Policy and Strategy (IAPS)
institutions.remit: Nonpartisan think tank producing policy research at the intersection of AI, national security and geopolitics. Focus areas include cyber autonomy and offence-defence balance, timely response mechanisms for AI security and public-safety risks, compute access and governance, and US-China strategic competition. Runs an AI Policy Fellowship.
institutions.threat_model: National-security-framed catastrophic risk: AI-enabled cyber and CBRN threats, compute proliferation, and strategic instability. Not a near-term-harms or civil-rights organisation.

routes.label: Contact form
routes.note: The contact page directs general enquiries to a form; no general email address is published.

routes.label: AI Policy Fellowship
routes.scope: Applicants; Spring 2027 cohort applications were open at time of checking
routes.note: The main open door for an outsider.

institutions.reality_check: Small and focused; the fellowship is the reliable route in. A form-only general contact suggests limited appetite for unsolicited correspondence.
institutions.gov_channel: Strong — DC-based, oriented to congressional and executive-branch audiences, with staff who move between IAPS and government.

institutions.name: RAND Center on AI, Security, and Technology (RAND CAST) — successor to the Technology and Security Policy Center (TASP)
institutions.remit: RAND's AI centre, formed by building on the Global and Emerging Risks division's inaugural centres — the Technology and Security Policy Center (TASP) and the Meselson Center. Research covers AI security, compute policy, AIxBio, bioresilience and transformative-technology risk. Runs a Fellows Programme and publishes reports that feed directly into US policy.
institutions.threat_model: National-security and catastrophic risk: securing model weights, AI-bio convergence, compute controls, and strategic surprise. Rigorously security-framed; loss of control is treated as one scenario among several.

routes.label: Get involved with RAND CAST
routes.note: Primary published route; contact form rather than email.

routes.label: CAST Fellows Programme
routes.note: The most tractable entry route.

institutions.reality_check: Institutionally large and effectively closed to unsolicited outside input; there is no meaningful public inbox. IMPORTANT for routing: 'TASP' is a legacy name — use RAND CAST. Influence here comes through the Fellows Programme or co-authorship, not correspondence.
institutions.gov_channel: Among the strongest of any organisation here — RAND briefs Congress and the executive branch routinely and operates FFRDCs for US government sponsors.

institutions.name: Center for Security and Emerging Technology (CSET), Georgetown University
institutions.remit: Data-driven, nonpartisan policy research at the intersection of security and technology, covering AI, advanced computing and biotechnology. Research lines include Applications, Assessment, Bio-Risk, Competition, CyberAI, Data and Workforce. Staff give congressional testimony and consult with policymakers; maintains large datasets (e.g. on Chinese AI research and chip supply chains).
institutions.threat_model: Great-power competition and national security, with sober empiricism about capability claims. Covers AI-enabled cyber and bio-risk; notably sceptical of both hype and doom framings. Not an x-risk organisation and not a civil-rights organisation.

routes.label: Publications and data tools
routes.note: CSET's open datasets and ETO tools are genuinely usable by outsiders.
