institutions.reality_check: A real published inbox but a large institution with a set research agenda; unsolicited concerns rarely change what it works on. Its public data tools are the highest-value thing an outsider can extract from it.
institutions.gov_channel: Very strong — congressional testimony is routine and CSET alumni staff senior executive-branch AI roles.

institutions.name: Ada Lovelace Institute
institutions.remit: Independent research institute (funded by the Nuffield Foundation) working on AI governance, policy and regulation; AI evaluation methods; public-sector AI; public participation and deliberation about AI; and law and policy. Notable for running genuine public deliberation exercises and for rigorous work on the limits of AI evaluation and audit.
institutions.threat_model: Near-term and structural: distributional justice, public legitimacy, regulatory capacity, and accountability for deployed systems. Explicitly NOT an existential-risk organisation — it has published critiques of the frontier-risk framing. Do not mislabel it as an alignment body.

routes.label: Contact page
routes.note: The page lists a general enquiries address and a media contact (George Lloyd-King), but the addresses are obfuscated against scraping and could not be read reliably — use the page itself. Phone: +44 (0)207 631 0566. Address: 100 St John Street, London EC1M 4EH.

routes.label: Public deliberation and participation programmes
routes.scope: Members of the public are recruited into deliberative exercises
routes.note: One of very few organisations that structurally involves ordinary members of the public in its method.

institutions.reality_check: Reputable and moderately responsive, with a genuine methodological commitment to public voice. Email addresses are deliberately obscured on the site, so use the form. UNVERIFIED: exact email addresses could not be confirmed — do not guess them.
institutions.gov_channel: Strong in the UK — regularly cited in parliamentary committee work and consulted on UK AI regulation; also active in EU debates.

institutions.name: AI Now Institute
institutions.remit: Independent policy research institute. Current agenda centres on the political economy of AI: market concentration and monopoly (co-executive director Amba Kak has testified before the congressional Monopoly Busters Caucus), data-centre expansion and its infrastructure harms, labour and the gig-ification of professions such as nursing, industry opacity, and AI security vulnerabilities. Publishes the Landscape reports.
institutions.threat_model: Concentration of corporate power and structural/political-economy harm — the thesis is that the danger is who controls AI and to what commercial end, not that AI will escape control. Sharply and deliberately opposed to the existential-risk framing.

routes.label: General enquiries — but see the caveat
routes.note: The contact page itself states: 'due to the high volume of inquiries, we are currently unable to guarantee a prompt response to general inquiries.'

institutions.reality_check: Publishes an email but explicitly warns it may not respond — take that at face value. Small team, high inbound. Route here only if your concern is corporate power, labour, or infrastructure; a misalignment concern will be actively unwelcome.
institutions.gov_channel: Real — congressional testimony, FTC and antitrust engagement, and strong influence on the competition-policy framing of AI.

institutions.name: Algorithmic Justice League (AJL)
institutions.remit: Founded by Joy Buolamwini. Combines art, research and advocacy to expose AI bias and harm — the Gender Shades audits of facial recognition, the Coded Bias documentary, and campaigns against biometric surveillance. Operates a public harm-reporting platform and builds the voice of the most-impacted communities.
institutions.threat_model: Near-term algorithmic harm to real people, especially racialised and gendered bias in facial recognition, biometrics and automated decision-making. Civil-rights framing throughout. Absolutely not an alignment organisation.

routes.label: Report an AI harm / share your story — a genuine public harm intake
routes.scope: Anyone who has experienced or witnessed algorithmic harm
routes.note: One of the very few public-facing harm-reporting channels run by a civil society organisation. If a person has been harmed by a deployed system, this is a primary route.

routes.label: General contact
routes.note: No public email address listed.

institutions.reality_check: Small, mission-driven, and one of the few organisations that has built an actual intake for individual harm stories and has a track record of acting on them. High responsiveness for in-scope harms; out of scope for anything frontier or speculative.
institutions.gov_channel: Real — AJL research has directly driven municipal facial-recognition bans, FTC and congressional attention, and corporate product withdrawals (IBM, Amazon, Microsoft facial recognition).

institutions.name: Access Now
institutions.jurisdiction: International (offices across all regions; RightsCon convener)
institutions.remit: Digital rights organisation defending users at risk. On AI, advocates binding, enforceable human-rights-based governance and works against rights-violating automated decision systems. Operates a 24/7 Digital Security Helpline for civil society, and convenes RightsCon, the largest global digital-rights summit.
institutions.threat_model: Human rights harms — surveillance, discrimination in ADM, censorship, and threats to activists, journalists and human rights defenders. Near-term and acute, with a strong Global Majority focus.

routes.label: Digital Security Helpline — 24/7, free, for civil society at risk
routes.scope: Activists, journalists, human rights defenders and civil society organisations facing a digital threat
routes.note: A real staffed emergency line, not a general inbox. https://www.accessnow.org/help/

routes.label: RightsCon
routes.scope: Summit participation; RightsCon runs an open session-proposal call each cycle
routes.note: The open call for RightsCon sessions is a genuine route to put a topic in front of the global digital-rights community.

institutions.reality_check: Among the most genuinely responsive organisations here, because it runs an actual operational helpline with staff obliged to answer. Scope is human rights and at-risk users; a frontier-alignment concern is out of scope.
institutions.gov_channel: Strong — formal engagement at the UN Human Rights Council, EU institutions, and national regulators; a recognised civil-society interlocutor in multiple multilateral processes.

institutions.name: Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF)
institutions.remit: Civil liberties organisation using litigation, pressure campaigns, technical analysis and advocacy. On AI it focuses on who uses AI and how — opposing government surveillance expansion, algorithmic policing, corporate data practices, and moves that would entrench incumbent platforms; also defends fair use and the right to build and study models.
institutions.threat_model: Civil liberties and power: state surveillance, corporate data extraction, algorithmic discrimination, and market concentration. Explicitly rejects the 'AI is magic' framing and treats AI as a general-purpose tool. Not an alignment or catastrophic-risk organisation, and often in direct opposition to restriction-oriented AI safety policy.

routes.label: Legal assistance request — EFF takes on impact cases
routes.scope: People facing a digital-rights legal problem; EFF also maintains a referral list of cooperating attorneys
routes.note: A real intake with real outcomes if your matter fits its docket.

routes.label: Action centre — campaigns and comment drives
Security/vulnerability matters
routes.note: EFF has a long record of defending security researchers facing legal threats.

institutions.reality_check: Large, well-staffed, and genuinely does read legal intake — but very selective, and its AI positions frequently cut against the AI-safety community's. Route surveillance, speech or researcher-protection concerns here; do not route frontier-risk concerns.
institutions.gov_channel: Strong — files amicus briefs, testifies, and litigates against federal and state agencies; comments in FTC, FCC and Copyright Office proceedings.

institutions.name: Electronic Privacy Information Center (EPIC)
institutions.remit: Public-interest research centre focused on privacy and algorithmic accountability. AI work spans law enforcement AI, chatbot harms, commercial AI in healthcare/education/hiring/housing, government AI use, risk assessments, and screening-and-scoring systems. Files FTC complaints, FOIA litigation, regulatory comments and amicus briefs, and drafts state AI legislation.
institutions.threat_model: Near-term privacy, due-process and discrimination harms from deployed automated systems. Regulatory-complaint oriented. Not a catastrophic-risk organisation.

routes.label: Calli Schroeder, Senior Counsel and AI/Human Rights lead
routes.scope: Direct subject-matter contact — the highest-yield route for an AI concern
routes.note: Named directly on EPIC's AI issue page.

routes.label: Contact page (phone: 202.483.1140; 1519 New Hampshire Ave NW, Washington DC 20036)
routes.note: EPIC has no dedicated public complaint portal; it originates FTC complaints itself from evidence it gathers.

institutions.reality_check: Genuinely responsive, and a named senior counsel for AI is published — unusual and valuable. If you have documentation of a company's unfair or deceptive AI practice affecting US consumers, EPIC is one of the few organisations that can convert it into a regulatory filing.
institutions.gov_channel: Strong — EPIC's FTC complaints have repeatedly triggered investigations, and it is a regular witness and commenter in federal and state proceedings.

institutions.name: Public Citizen
institutions.remit: Consumer advocacy organisation. AI work covers generative AI risks to consumers and democracy, model state AI legislation, campaigns against non-consensual deepfakes and political deepfakes, data-centre environmental and utility-cost impacts, AI companion products aimed at minors, and opposition to federal preemption of state AI laws. Maintains a tracker of state deepfake legislation.
institutions.threat_model: Near-term consumer protection and democratic integrity — deepfakes in elections, corporate accountability, environmental externalities of compute. Populist/consumer framing, not technical risk.

routes.label: Contact page
routes.scope: Anyone; Public Citizen has historically been receptive to consumer complaints that can seed campaigns
routes.note: No topic-specific email published on the AI page.

routes.label: Take action — petitions and comment drives

institutions.reality_check: Large, campaign-driven and genuinely populist in orientation — more willing than most DC organisations to take up an ordinary person's complaint if it illustrates a systemic pattern. Scope is consumer and democratic harm only.
institutions.gov_channel: Strong — long-standing congressional and regulatory presence, petitions agencies (FEC on political deepfakes, FTC on AI harms) and drafts state model bills.

institutions.name: Encode (formerly Encode Justice)
institutions.remit: Youth-founded AI advocacy organisation (Sneha Revanur). Legislative advocacy and coalition-building. Claimed wins include California SB 53, the New York RAISE Act, Illinois SB 315, defeating federal preemption of state AI laws, and securing AI-and-nuclear-command provisions in defence legislation. Self-describes as 'pro-human, pro-AI'.
institutions.threat_model: Unusually broad and deliberately bridging: bioweapons and loss of human control alongside child safety, companion-chatbot harms and erosion of liberty. One of the very few organisations that credibly spans catastrophic risk and near-term harm rather than picking a side.

routes.label: Get involved form on the homepage — explicitly invites people to find out how to participate
routes.scope: Anyone, especially students and young people
routes.note: Encode's chapter/volunteer model is its distinguishing feature; UNVERIFIED whether a formal chapter-application page currently exists.

institutions.reality_check: Small, young, hungry, and one of the most genuinely responsive organisations on this list — they actively want volunteers and will reply. If you are an individual wanting to convert a concern into legislative action in the US, this is among the best-value doors available.
institutions.gov_channel: Direct and disproportionately effective for its size — active in state legislatures and Congress; Sneha Revanur sits on FLI's AI Safety Index expert panel.

institutions.name: The Midas Project
institutions.remit: Watchdog non-profit holding AI companies to their own stated commitments. Projects: Watchtower (tracks changes to and violations of corporate AI safety policies), the Seoul Tracker (whether 16 organisations met the Seoul frontier-safety commitments), The OpenAI Files (documented governance, leadership and culture concerns at OpenAI), and Model Republic (industry influence on policymakers).
institutions.threat_model: Corporate accountability and commitment-drift — the concern that voluntary safety commitments quietly erode. Agnostic between threat models; it tracks whatever companies promised, which spans misuse, catastrophic risk and governance.

routes.label: Submit a tip — the best-designed whistleblower-adjacent intake in this list
routes.scope: Anyone with specific, non-public, evidence-backed information; they particularly want evidence of gaps between public statements and internal practice
routes.note: Accepts texts, emails, documents, photos, reports. Signal preferred for sensitive material.

routes.label: Signal (encrypted) — username
routes.note: Verified on the tips page. They warn no app protects a compromised device.

routes.label: General enquiries (explicitly NOT recommended for confidential material)

institutions.reality_check: Tiny, and it absolutely reads its inbox — the single best target in this list for someone with concrete non-public evidence about an AI company's conduct. Note their own advice: if you are an employee considering disclosure, contact the AI Whistleblower Initiative first for independent legal guidance before approaching any journalist or watchdog.
institutions.gov_channel: Indirect but potent — its findings get picked up by press and cited in policy debate; The OpenAI Files fed directly into scrutiny of OpenAI's restructuring.

institutions.name: AI Whistleblower Initiative (AIWI)
institutions.remit: Research, policy and direct support for frontier-AI employees considering disclosure. Founded by Karl Koch. Offers free consultations with specialist whistleblowing attorneys (pro bono or via a defence fund), an AI Whistleblower Defense Fund, a 'Third Opinion' service for independent expert assessment of a concern, privacy and security guidance, and a published AI Whistleblower Guide. Also does policy work on whistleblower protections for AI.
institutions.threat_model: Meta-level: the information asymmetry between frontier labs and the public. Agnostic as to which risk — it exists so that insiders with any credible safety concern can surface it safely.

routes.label: Contact Hub — connects to vetted specialist attorneys
routes.scope: Current and former employees of AI companies

routes.label: 'Third Opinion' — independent expert assessment of whether a concern is well-founded
routes.scope: Insiders unsure whether their concern warrants escalation
routes.note: Unusual and valuable: a way to get a concern sanity-checked before taking legal or public risk.

institutions.reality_check: Not on the original list but it is the single most important routing destination for anyone inside an AI company with a safety concern — every other watchdog here defers to it. Small, purpose-built, responsive. UNVERIFIED: no dedicated secure email or Signal channel was published on the homepage; use the Contact Hub.
institutions.gov_channel: Policy work on whistleblower protection statutes (e.g. proposed AI whistleblower protection legislation); no formal advisory seat.

institutions.name: AI Safety Asia (AISA)
institutions.jurisdiction: Asia-Pacific (Southeast, East and South Asia; listed activity in Cambodia, China, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, Republic of Korea, Singapore, Thailand)
institutions.remit: Non-profit working to harmonise international governance of safe and secure AI 'the Asia way'. Delivers AI governance training to government officials and civil society — including director-level officials in Indonesia and parliamentarians in Malaysia — conducts policy research (including with Brookings on Southeast Asian AI safety governance), and runs courses such as a 10-week cooperative AI course with the Cooperative AI Foundation. Listed in UNESCO's Global AI Ethics Observatory CSO directory and the WEF AI Global Alliance.
institutions.threat_model: Governance capacity and regional representation — the concern that AI safety norms are set in the West and imposed on Asia without local capability to evaluate them. Covers safety and security broadly rather than a specific technical threat.

routes.label: General enquiries
routes.note: Verified via the UNESCO Observatory CSO profile.

institutions.reality_check: Small and growing; the kind of organisation that reads its own email. Strongest value if your concern needs a hearing in an Asian jurisdiction where Western AI safety organisations have no standing. UNVERIFIED: an independent aisafety.asia homepage was not confirmed — the UNESCO profile is the verified reference.
institutions.gov_channel: Real and direct in-region — trains sitting officials and parliamentarians in several Asian states, which is unusually concrete access.

institutions.name: SaferAI
institutions.remit: Non-profit focused on AI risk management. Three arms: research (quantitative risk models — nine cyber risk models completed, expanding to loss of control and CBRN); ratings (independent grading of how well leading AI companies manage risk, across risk identification, severity assessment, safeguards and governance, published at ratings.safer-ai.org); and standards (leads AI risk management standards work in the EU and edits international red-teaming standards).
institutions.threat_model: Risk-management adequacy at frontier developers — explicitly covering cyber, loss of control and CBRN. Methodologically the most rigorous of the company-rating projects, borrowing from mature safety-critical industries.

routes.label: Company risk-management ratings portal
routes.note: UNVERIFIED whether they accept public submissions of evidence about a company's practices — worth asking via contact@.

institutions.reality_check: Small, technically serious and European — which matters, because it has standing in the EU standardisation processes that most US safety organisations do not. Responsive to substantive technical input on risk methodology.
institutions.gov_channel: Real in Europe — SaferAI staff serve as editors on international standards and participate in EU AI Act standardisation and the GPAI Code of Practice process.

institutions.name: ControlAI
institutions.jurisdiction: United Kingdom, with US, Canadian and German campaigns
institutions.remit: Campaigning organisation working for a prohibition on the development of superintelligent AI. Three functions: public education (newsletter with 148,000+ readers), grassroots advocacy (tooling that helps tens of thousands contact their elected representatives), and direct policymaker briefing — claims 400+ lawmakers briefed since November 2024, with 160+ cross-party UK MPs and Peers and 35+ Canadian lawmakers having endorsed its statement.
institutions.threat_model: Extinction risk from superintelligence, narrowly. Its stated position is that superintelligence could arrive before 2030 with no known containment method. No engagement with near-term harms.

routes.label: Take action — contact your representative
routes.scope: Anyone, especially UK, US, Canada and Germany
routes.note: The most operationally effective grassroots tool in this space — it has demonstrably produced lawmaker endorsements.

routes.label: General enquiries, briefing requests and funding enquiries
routes.scope: Anyone; note the email domain is controlai.com while the website is controlai.org
routes.note: Verified on controlai.org. They explicitly invite briefing requests — a legislator's office or an individual can ask for one.

institutions.reality_check: Small, fast-moving, and it answers its email. Best-in-class if your goal is to get a loss-of-control concern in front of a legislator. It will not engage with bias, privacy or labour concerns.
institutions.gov_channel: Direct and unusually effective for its size — its core product is legislator briefings, and it has secured named cross-party endorsements in three parliaments.

institutions.name: PauseAI
institutions.jurisdiction: International (volunteer network with national and local chapters)
institutions.remit: Volunteer grassroots movement calling for a halt to development of the most powerful general AI systems until safety is assured, and for 'a prohibition on the development of superintelligence, not lifted before there is broad scientific consensus'. Organises protests, lobbying days, letter-writing and local meetups; maintains extensive public explainer material.
institutions.threat_model: Existential risk from uncontrolled AI as the headline, but notably broader in its public messaging than MIRI or ControlAI — it also cites job displacement, democratic erosion and economic instability as reasons to pause.

routes.label: Discord — the organisational hub; anyone can join and start contributing immediately
routes.note: This is where the actual organising happens.

routes.label: Local communities directory — find or start a chapter
Contact form
routes.note: No public email address is listed.

institutions.reality_check: Maximally open — a volunteer can join the Discord today and be organising within a week. That openness is also its limit: it has little institutional access, and its confrontational framing means mainstream policy bodies keep it at arm's length. Good for mobilisation, poor for a targeted escalation.
institutions.gov_channel: Weak-to-moderate — organises lobbying days and has met individual legislators, but has no formal channel and is treated as an outside-game actor.

institutions.name: StopAI
institutions.remit: Grassroots direct-action movement. Calls for a permanent global ban on frontier AI development and proposes citizen oversight bodies empowered to regulate or dismantle threatening technologies. Operates on three fronts: public awareness, influencing decision-makers and legislation, and non-violent direct action — including blockades and civil disobedience at AI company offices, with members having been arrested.
institutions.threat_model: Extinction and human-dignity framing, combined — AI and Big Tech as threats to 'human dignity, freedom, democracy, and nature'. The most maximalist position in this list.

routes.label: General contact
routes.note: A Gmail address — an accurate signal of the organisation's scale and informality.

institutions.reality_check: Tiny and entirely open — anyone can turn up. Will certainly read your email. Has zero institutional access and association with it may actively reduce your credibility with policy bodies. Route here only if direct action is what you want.
institutions.gov_channel: None. It is explicitly an outside-game actor.

institutions.name: Center for AI Policy (CAIP)
institutions.remit: Was a nonpartisan advocacy group working with Congress from June 2023 to May 2025 on catastrophic AI risk — drafting model legislation, endorsing bills, hosting events and connecting policymakers with AI experts.
institutions.threat_model: Catastrophic risk from advanced AI, with an emphasis on giving government visibility, expertise and response authority.

routes.label: Jason Green-Lowe, Executive Director — legislative review service and revival/funding enquiries
routes.scope: Confidential expert feedback on pending or draft AI legislation — still offered
routes.note: One of two functions that survived the shutdown. Genuinely useful if you are drafting or reviewing a bill.

routes.label: Ivan — Grassroots Policy Advocacy Network
routes.scope: Training for young AI safety policy advocates — still operating

routes.label: Contact page
routes.note: Note aipolicy.us now redirects to centeraipolicy.org.

institutions.reality_check: LARGELY SHUT DOWN. Its own site states it 'has run out of funding and has ceased most of our active operations'. Two narrow services persist — the legislative review service and the grassroots advocacy training network — both reachable at the named personal addresses above. Do not treat CAIP as a live advocacy channel; it is now effectively two people offering two specific services.
institutions.gov_channel: Formerly strong congressional engagement; now residual.

institutions.name: Alignment Research Engineer Accelerator (ARENA)
institutions.jurisdiction: United Kingdom (London, hosted at LISA in Shoreditch)
institutions.remit: Intensive 4–5 week in-person bootcamp training people in the engineering skills for technical AI safety work — transformer internals, interpretability, RL, evals. Runs 2–3 cohorts a year (ARENA 9.0 scheduled 5 Oct – 6 Nov 2026). Covers travel, visas, accommodation and meals to remove financial barriers. Curriculum is public and self-studiable.
institutions.threat_model: Talent-pipeline intervention for technical alignment broadly — it is upstream of any particular threat model, though its curriculum is oriented toward interpretability, evaluations and alignment rather than near-term harms.

routes.label: Applications — three stages: form (<90 min), coding test (6 questions, 1 hour), 30-minute interview
routes.scope: Anyone with Python proficiency and foundational maths (linear algebra, calculus, probability); no institutional affiliation needed
routes.note: Financially supported, which makes it genuinely accessible.

institutions.reality_check: One of the most concretely open doors in the entire ecosystem for a technically-inclined individual with no credentials or connections — funded, structured, and explicitly designed to remove barriers. Competitive, but the curriculum is free online regardless.
institutions.gov_channel: None directly; alumni populate safety teams at labs and institutes.

institutions.name: Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI (HAI)
institutions.remit: University institute spanning research, policy and education. Publishes the AI Index (the most-cited annual measurement of AI progress, with the Global Vibrancy Tool), policy briefs, and runs policymaker education including Congressional Boot Camps for members and staff. Houses CRFM (see separate entry) and a large fellowship and seed-grant programme.
institutions.threat_model: Human-centred and broad: augmentation over replacement, healthcare, equity, governance capacity. The AI Index is deliberately descriptive rather than risk-framed. Not an alignment institute.

routes.label: Contact form
routes.note: No public email addresses are listed; only a form.

routes.label: AI Index — accepts data and methodology input between editions
routes.note: UNVERIFIED: a formal open call for AI Index contributions was not confirmed; contact via the form.

institutions.reality_check: Large, prestigious, form-only. Unsolicited outside input is very unlikely to get traction; the productive route is to reach an individual faculty affiliate directly through their Stanford page.
institutions.gov_channel: Strong — the Congressional Boot Camp is a rare structured channel into US legislative staff, and HAI scholars testify regularly.

institutions.name: Stanford Center for Research on Foundation Models (CRFM)
institutions.remit: Interdisciplinary centre spanning 10+ Stanford departments. Coined the term 'foundation models'. Outputs include HELM (Holistic Evaluation of Language Models — a widely used open benchmark suite), the Foundation Model Transparency Index (FMTI, which grades developers on transparency), Ecosystem Graphs, and Levanter. Works across technical foundations, beneficial applications, societal impact (transparency, openness, copyright, privacy, systemic risk) and AI policy.
institutions.threat_model: Systemic risk from homogenisation and opacity — the founding thesis is that a small number of foundation models become single points of failure across society. Transparency-centred. Covers near-term and structural risk; touches systemic risk but not loss of control.

routes.label: HELM — open benchmark; models and scenarios can be contributed via GitHub
routes.note: HELM is open source; contributing an evaluation scenario is a real route to influence how models are publicly measured.

routes.label: Foundation Model Transparency Index — developers respond to it, and the methodology is public
routes.note: UNVERIFIED: no public submission form for FMTI input was found.

routes.label: People directory — the practical contact route is an individual researcher
routes.note: No centre-level contact email is published.

institutions.reality_check: No centre-level inbox at all. Everything runs through named researchers or through open-source contribution to HELM, which is the genuinely open channel.
institutions.gov_channel: Real — CRFM has filed influential comments in US and EU processes (notably on the EU AI Act and on open foundation models) and its transparency work is cited by regulators.

institutions.name: MIT AI Alignment (MAIA)
institutions.remit: Student-and-researcher group at MIT running AI alignment education and research programmes — reading groups, technical bootcamps and supported research projects, feeding students into alignment research careers. Closely associated with MIT's Algorithmic Alignment Group.
institutions.threat_model: Technical alignment and loss of control — interpretability, evaluations, and scalable oversight.

routes.label: Programmes and application information
routes.note: UNVERIFIED — the site returned a 403 to automated fetching at time of checking. Do not assume an email exists; check the site in a browser.

institutions.reality_check: A student organisation, primarily serving MIT and Harvard affiliates. Not a channel for outside concerns; it is a talent-pipeline programme. UNVERIFIED across the board — I could not fetch the site.
institutions.gov_channel: None.

institutions.name: Center for Human-Compatible AI (CHAI), UC Berkeley
institutions.remit: Technical research lab founded by Stuart Russell, devoted to the theory, practice and policy of provably beneficial AI. Core research programme is assistance games / cooperative inverse reinforcement learning — designing AI that is uncertain about human objectives and defers to humans, rather than optimising a fixed specified objective. Interdisciplinary across CS, social science, law, philosophy, economics and governance. Runs an annual workshop and an internship programme.
institutions.threat_model: Misspecified objectives and loss of control — Russell's thesis that 'optimisation alone won't get us to humane AI' and that the standard model of AI (maximise a given objective) is structurally unsafe.

routes.label: General administrative contact
routes.note: Address: Bakar Gateway, 2300 Hearst Ave, Office 4438, Berkeley CA 94720-1660.

routes.label: Opportunities — internships and roles
routes.note: CHAI's internship programme has historically accepted applicants from outside Berkeley, which is a genuine route in.

institutions.reality_check: Publishes a real administrative inbox, which most academic labs do not. The internship route is genuinely open to outsiders. Russell himself is extremely over-subscribed; do not expect a personal reply.
institutions.gov_channel: Strong by proxy — Stuart Russell sits on the FLI AI Safety Index panel, advises the UN and numerous governments, and was a lead author on the International AI Safety Report.

institutions.name: Oxford Martin AI Governance Initiative (AIGI)
institutions.remit: Research initiative within the Oxford Martin School, co-directed by Robert Trager and Maike Osborne. Three research areas: frontier AI governance, international AI governance (including a China AI Governance programme and the Oxford AI Diplomacy Lab), and technical AI governance (including a Hardware AI Governance Lab working on compute verification and on-chip governance mechanisms). Files responses to government consultations.
institutions.threat_model: Frontier risk and international coordination failure — racing dynamics, verification and enforcement problems, and compute governance as the practical lever. Loss-of-control-aware but institutionally rather than technically framed.

routes.label: Oxford Martin School general enquiries (the published route for AIGI)
routes.note: Phone +44 (0)1865 287430. Oxford Martin School, 34 Broad Street, Oxford OX1 3BD.

routes.label: AIGI site — research, labs and news

institutions.reality_check: Contact runs through a shared Oxford Martin School inbox rather than a dedicated one, which dilutes it. Better to approach a named researcher. Technically credible and genuinely influential on compute governance.
institutions.gov_channel: Strong — files formal responses to US and UK government RFIs (e.g. to the US AI Action Plan RFI), and Trager sits on the FLI AI Safety Index panel and advises international processes.

institutions.name: Centre for the Study of Existential Risk (CSER), University of Cambridge
institutions.remit: Interdisciplinary research centre on risks that threaten human extinction or civilisational collapse — AI, biological risk, climate and ecological risk, and systemic/cascading risk. Now part of Cambridge's Institute for Technology and Humanity (ITH) alongside LCFI and the Centre for Human-Inspired AI. Runs education programmes, visitor and affiliate schemes.
institutions.threat_model: Global catastrophic and existential risk across multiple hazard classes; on AI, both loss of control and AI as a risk-amplifier for other hazards. Also strong on the governance of extreme risk generally.

routes.label: CSER general enquiries
routes.note: Verified via the ITH contact page, which explicitly invites direct contact with centre teams about education, visitor and affiliate programmes.

routes.label: Institute for Technology and Humanity (parent institute)
Visitor and affiliate programmes
routes.note: A real route for external academics to affiliate.

institutions.reality_check: A published, monitored inbox and an explicit invitation to contact centre teams about visiting and affiliation — notably more open than most academic centres. Academic pace; it will not act as a rapid-response channel.
institutions.gov_channel: Real in the UK — CSER researchers have given parliamentary evidence and advised on UK risk registers and international processes.

institutions.name: Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence (LCFI), University of Cambridge
institutions.jurisdiction: United Kingdom (Cambridge, with partners at Oxford, Imperial and Berkeley)
institutions.remit: Highly interdisciplinary centre — philosophy, computer science, law, politics, history, design — examining how AI reshapes human futures. Projects span AI ethics and narratives, kinds of intelligence, AI and gender/race, the political economy of AI, and AI in the arts. Now part of the Institute for Technology and Humanity.
institutions.threat_model: Conceptual and structural rather than technical: what AI does to human agency, epistemics, culture and power. Humanities-led. Not an alignment centre, and not a near-term-audit centre either — it sits deliberately outside both.

routes.label: LCFI general enquiries
routes.note: Verified via the ITH contact page.

routes.label: Visitor and affiliate programmes via ITH

institutions.reality_check: Real inbox, academic pace. Most useful if your concern is conceptual or about AI's cultural and epistemic effects rather than a specific technical or corporate issue.
institutions.gov_channel: Moderate — LCFI researchers contribute to UK policy consultations and international ethics processes.

institutions.name: NYU Alignment Research Group (ARG)
institutions.remit: A set of NYU researchers doing empirical work with language models aimed at longer-term concerns about deploying highly capable AI. Associated with Sam Bowman's group and collaborating across NYU's ML2, CILVR, the Center for Data Science and the Department of Linguistics. Known for work on debate and scalable oversight, chain-of-thought faithfulness, and benchmarks that resist saturation.
institutions.threat_model: Scalable oversight and honesty — how humans supervise models that exceed them, and whether stated model reasoning reflects actual computation. Alignment-focused, empirical rather than theoretical.

routes.label: People page — the only contact route is individual researchers
routes.note: No group-level email or contact form is published anywhere on the site.

institutions.reality_check: Effectively closed as an institution — it is a loose grouping of academics, not an entity with an inbox. Contact individual faculty via their NYU pages. Several ARG-affiliated researchers have since moved to frontier labs, so the group is less central than it was.
institutions.gov_channel: None directly.

institutions.name: Mila — Quebec AI Institute
institutions.remit: Research institute founded by Yoshua Bengio in 1993, uniting researchers from Université de Montréal, McGill, Polytechnique Montréal and HEC Montréal — 1,400+ researchers and 140+ affiliated professors. AI safety and governance work runs through an AI Governance, Policy and Inclusion division, the AI Policy Compass programme for policymakers, TRAIL responsible-AI training, and the AI4Good Lab, plus Indigenous-AI work.
institutions.threat_model: Broad. Bengio's presence anchors serious loss-of-control work, while the institutional programmes emphasise responsible AI, inclusion and policy capacity. Do not assume Mila as an institution shares Bengio's x-risk position — most of it does not.

routes.label: General information
routes.note: Address: 6666 St-Urbain #200, Montreal, Quebec H2S 3H1.

institutions.reality_check: Several real published inboxes, which is good. But it is a large general ML institute, not a safety organisation — most of its 1,400 researchers do capabilities work. Route safety concerns to LawZero or to Bengio's academic page rather than to Mila's general inbox.
institutions.gov_channel: Strong in Canada — Mila researchers advise the Canadian government and Bengio chairs both the International AI Safety Report and co-chairs the UN Scientific Panel.

institutions.name: Vector Institute
institutions.remit: Canada's Toronto-based AI institute — 1,488+ affiliated researchers and faculty, 30+ industry partnerships, 450+ papers. Focus is research excellence and accelerating AI adoption across Canadian industry and health systems, with a stated 'responsible AI leadership' strand and work on trustworthy AI frameworks and evaluation.
institutions.threat_model: Trustworthy-AI and adoption framing: reliability, privacy, fairness and deployment safety in regulated sectors, especially health. Not a catastrophic-risk institute.
institutions.reality_check: Published inbox, but an adoption-and-industry institute at heart. Its AI safety footprint is much smaller than its size suggests. Low yield for a safety concern.
institutions.gov_channel: Real in Canada — Vector is a federally and provincially funded pillar of the Pan-Canadian AI Strategy and advises on Canadian AI policy.

institutions.name: Institute for AI International Governance (I-AIIG), Tsinghua University
institutions.remit: Tsinghua's AI governance research institute. Conducts research on AI governance frameworks and international cooperation, hosts the International AI Cooperation and Governance Forum, runs talent programmes (including the AI for SDGs Global Youth competition), publishes annual reports and academic work, and coordinates with UN agencies and foreign governments. Tsinghua also hosts the Center for International Security and Strategy (CISS), which does AI-and-security track-II work, and co-launched a UNU Hub on ethical and responsible AI.
institutions.threat_model: International governance and cooperation framing; increasingly engages frontier risk and AI safety in dialogue with Western counterparts. Chinese AI safety discourse has moved noticeably toward frontier-risk framing, with Chinese scientists (including Andrew Yao and Zhang Ya-Qin) signing international statements.

routes.label: General enquiries
routes.note: Phone: +86 10 62794781. Tsinghua University, Haidian District, Beijing.

institutions.reality_check: A published inbox, but approaching a Chinese state-adjacent academic institute cold from abroad rarely works. The realistic route is via Concordia AI, which has existing relationships across Chinese AI safety institutions, or via the international forums Tsinghua co-hosts.
institutions.gov_channel: Strong within China — Tsinghua institutes advise Chinese ministries and participate in official international dialogues.

institutions.name: PKU Alignment Group / Center for AI Safety and Governance, Peking University
institutions.remit: PKU-Alignment is a student-organised research team at Peking University working on reinforcement learning, LLMs, world models and AI alignment. Widely known for open-sourcing alignment resources — PKU-SafeRLHF datasets, Safe-RLHF training code, BeaverTails and the Align-Anything framework — published at ACL, NeurIPS and ICLR, with collaborations including Anthropic, Google DeepMind, DeepSeek and Alibaba. PKU's Institute for AI separately hosts a Center for AI Safety and Governance.
institutions.threat_model: Value alignment of LLMs — safe RLHF, helpfulness/harmlessness tradeoffs, and increasingly scalable oversight. Genuinely alignment-focused, not a near-term-harms group.

routes.label: PKU Alignment Group general contact
routes.note: Location: West Ziyuan Building, Peking University, Haidian, Beijing.

routes.label: GitHub — open-source alignment datasets and frameworks, open to contribution
routes.note: The most practical route for technical engagement; these repositories are widely used internationally.

routes.label: PKU Center for AI Safety and Governance

institutions.reality_check: Notably open for a Chinese institution — a public Gmail address, open GitHub, and a public recruitment form. Its open-source alignment work is genuinely used worldwide, making GitHub the highest-bandwidth channel. Student-run, so responsiveness varies with cohort.
institutions.gov_channel: Indirect — PKU researchers feed into Chinese AI safety standards discussions and the China AI Safety and Development Network.

institutions.name: Seoul National University — AI policy and trustworthy AI centres
institutions.remit: Two relevant SNU bodies: the Center for Trustworthy AI (CTAI) at ctai.snu.ac.kr, and the SNU AI Policy Initiative (SAPI) at sapi.co.kr, which convenes the annual Seoul AI Policy Conference (SAIPCON, 2026 edition held). Korea is a significant venue — it hosted the 2024 Seoul AI Summit that produced the Frontier AI Safety Commitments, and operates its own AI Safety Institute.
institutions.threat_model: Trustworthy AI and AI policy/regulation, with Korea's own AI Framework Act as a focal point. Governance-framed rather than technical-alignment framed.

routes.label: Center for Trustworthy AI (CTAI)
routes.note: UNVERIFIED: no contact email confirmed.

routes.label: SNU AI Policy Initiative (SAPI)
routes.note: UNVERIFIED — the site returned a 403 to automated fetching. Check in a browser; do not assume an email address.

routes.label: Seoul AI Policy Conference (SAIPCON)
routes.note: An open conference is the most tractable route in.

Co-hosted the Global Conclave on Safe & Trusted AI with the IndiaAI Mission ahead of the India AI Impact Summit 2026, launching eight initiatives and reports. The IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar has approved 13+ projects on deepfakes, bias and related harms.
institutions.threat_model: Near-term and deployment harms in the Indian context — deepfakes, bias, consumer protection, explainability, and AI in public service delivery. Development-and-trust framing, not catastrophic risk.

institutions.name: Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI)
institutions.jurisdiction: United States (federal) — a center within NIST, US Department of Commerce
institutions.remit: RENAMED: was the 'U.S. AI Safety Institute' until 4 June 2025, when Commerce Secretary Lutnick renamed and re-scoped it as CAISI. Develops guidelines/best practices to measure and improve AI system security; leads unclassified evaluations of AI capabilities that may pose national-security risk (cybersecurity, biosecurity, chemical weapons); enters VOLUNTARY agreements with private AI developers and evaluators for pre/post-deployment testing; coordinates with DoD, DOE, DHS and the IC; represents US positions in international AI standards fora. Also runs an AI Agent Standards Initiative (announced Feb 2026).

institutions.reality_check: CAISI has NO enforcement power and no complaint route for the public. Its testing relationships with frontier labs are voluntary MOUs, so the lever is not correspondence — it is the Federal Register docket when CAISI/NIST publishes draft guidance or an RFI, and the named workshop mailbox (caisi-events@nist.gov) when a listening session is announced. A cold email to a general NIST inbox is routed to public affairs and effectively does not reach the evaluation staff. The rename also signals a substantive shift: 'safety' language was dropped in favour of security, national-security evaluation and 'AI dominance', so framing input as catastrophic-risk advocacy lands worse than framing it as measurement, standards or adversarial-nation risk.
institutions.notes: The rename is the single most important fact here. Separately, the AI Safety Institute Consortium (AISIC) was itself renamed the 'NIST AI Consortium' in May 2026 with scope widened to AI measurement, innovation and adoption — see the separate entry.

institutions.jurisdiction: United States (federal), US Department of Commerce
institutions.remit: Non-regulatory standards agency. Publishes the AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0) and its profiles (including Generative AI and critical-infrastructure profiles), measurement science, benchmarks and evaluation methods. Hosts CAISI and the NIST AI Consortium. In Dec 2025 NIST also launched centers for AI in manufacturing and critical infrastructure. Its outputs are voluntary but are widely incorporated by reference into procurement, insurance and state law.

institutions.reality_check: NIST's public-comment process is one of the genuinely effective US routes: comment periods on draft NIST AI publications are real, staff read and tabulate every submission, and substantive technical comments visibly change the text between draft and final. The trick is timing — you must catch the window, which is announced in the Federal Register and on the NIST AI page, not by writing in unsolicited. Technical specificity beats advocacy: NIST responds to measurement proposals, not to position statements.
institutions.notes: Non-regulatory by statute. NIST cannot compel, fine or investigate anyone.

institutions.name: NIST AI Consortium
institutions.remit: RENAMED: was the 'Artificial Intelligence Safety Institute Consortium (AISIC)'; renamed the 'NIST AI Consortium' in May 2026 with scope expanded from safety to 'AI measurement, innovation and adoption', building an AI evaluation ecosystem and promoting US-developed AI. It has NO regulatory authority — it directs agencies, it does not bind the public.

institutions.jurisdiction: United States (federal), with extraterritorial reach via the Export Administration Regulations

Rescinded the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule in 2025 and codified a revised advanced-chip licence review policy in Jan 2026 (see 91 FR, doc 2026-00789). Can deny licences, impose civil penalties, add parties to the Entity List / Denied Persons List, and refer criminal cases. This is the single hardest-edged US compute-governance lever.

If your concern is frontier compute proliferation, this is the agency with teeth — but frame it as a control violation, not as a safety argument.

institutions.remit: Runs the Genesis Mission (EO-established AI-for-science programme; DOE published 26 Genesis Mission national science and technology challenges and made awards through 2026) and operates the national laboratories (LLNL, Los Alamos, Sandia, Argonne, Oak Ridge). DOE/NNSA labs hold the classified expertise for nuclear and radiological risk and partner with CAISI on classified evaluations of frontier models for nuclear and radiological uplift. DOE has no general AI regulatory power over the public; its AI risk role is evaluation, classified red-teaming and compute provision.

Powers are largely voluntary/advisory toward the private sector, with administrative subpoena authority for vulnerability identification and binding operational directives that bind FEDERAL agencies only — not AI developers.

Its AI guidance documents are produced with industry partners and occasionally take comment via the Federal Register; that is the policy lever, the incident line is the operational one.

institutions.name: Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
institutions.remit: Enforces Section 5 of the FTC Act against unfair or deceptive acts and practices, plus COPPA, ROSCA and the Fair Credit Reporting Act. Applied to AI this means: deceptive claims about AI capability ('AI washing'), harms from AI products to children, deceptive chatbot design, and misuse of data for training. Can open investigations, issue compulsory process (civil investigative demands and 6(b) orders), sue in federal court, obtain injunctions and civil penalties, and impose consent decrees including algorithmic disgorgement (deletion of models built on unlawfully obtained data). It is the closest thing the US has to a general-purpose AI consumer regulator.

The FTC's AI work is squarely CONSUMER-HARM oriented — deception, children's safety, data misuse — and it has no theory of action for catastrophic or frontier risk. Do not route an existential-risk argument here.

institutions.name: Regulations.gov / the Federal Register (cross-cutting US public docket system)
institutions.jurisdiction: United States (federal) — operated by GSA's eRulemaking Program on behalf of ~300 agencies
institutions.remit: The single statutory channel through which any member of the public can submit a comment on a federal rulemaking, RFI, notice or guidance document, under the Administrative Procedure Act. Agencies must consider and respond to significant comments; failure to do so is grounds for a rule being vacated in court. Comments are published on the docket and are citable.

routes.scope: Every comment opportunity appears here first, with the docket ID and closing date.
routes.note: UNVERIFIED as fetched; individual FR document URLs cited elsewhere in this directory WERE confirmed via agency pages.

institutions.reality_check: THIS IS THE REAL US LEVER and it is systematically under-used by safety-focused groups. Unlike a letter to an agency, a docket comment creates a legal record the agency must address, and it is the evidentiary basis for later litigation. Practitioner consensus is: comment early in the window (late comments get less analytical attention), address the agency's specific questions in their order, provide data the agency does not already have, and file separately rather than signing a mass-comment campaign — agencies weigh unique substantive comments and count form letters. The OSTP AI Action Plan RFI drew 10,000+ comments and visibly shaped the output; mass identical submissions in that docket were counted, not read.
institutions.notes: Included as a routing entry rather than a body, because for most US agencies it is the only input channel that legally matters.
