institutions.reality_check: This subcommittee produced the most substantive US Senate AI oversight to date, but it has essentially no public front door — the /contact URL is dead. Access is entirely through member offices (the chair's and ranking member's personal staff) and through being invited as a witness. Practitioners get on witness lists by publishing work the staff already cite, then being introduced by a member's office; cold outreach to the committee does not work. Its framing is civil liberties, deepfakes and child safety rather than catastrophic risk.
institutions.notes: Verify the subcommittee's current name and leadership for the sitting Congress before relying on prior-Congress references.

institutions.name: Congressional Artificial Intelligence Caucus
institutions.jurisdiction: United States (federal legislature) — informal bipartisan, bicameral member organisation
institutions.remit: An informal caucus, NOT a committee. Exists to 'inform policymakers of the technological, economic, and social impacts of advances in AI' and to convene experts from academia, government and industry for member briefings. It has no jurisdiction, no staff of its own beyond member offices, no subpoena power and no ability to legislate as a body. Co-chairs announced vice-chairs and a core initiative in a recent Congress.

routes.label: Caucus contact (hosted on a co-chair's House site)
routes.value: (202) 225-4376 — 1226 Longworth House Office Building, Washington DC 20515
routes.scope: The caucus's about page publishes only this phone and address plus the X account https://x.com/AICaucus.
routes.note: VERIFIED at https://artificialintelligencecaucus-beyer.house.gov/about. NOTE: the caucus site is mirrored across several members' House domains (…-beyer, …-eshoo, …-olson), which change as membership changes — always check which mirror is current.

routes.label: Caucus email
routes.note: VERIFIED ABSENCE — the about page identifies no co-chairs by name and publishes no email, referring only generically to 'Chair offices'.

institutions.reality_check: A caucus is a briefing venue, not a decision-making body. The realistic use is offering a briefing: caucus staff programme lunch briefings and are receptive to a credible outside expert with a clear, short, non-partisan presentation. That contact runs through the co-chairs' personal office staff, reached by the phone number above, not through any caucus address. Nothing you send to a caucus creates a record or obliges a response. The separate House Bipartisan Task Force on AI (2024) produced a substantial report but was time-limited — check whether it still exists before citing it.
institutions.notes: The multiple House-domain mirrors are a genuine trap: several are stale and name former co-chairs.

institutions.name: California Attorney General — Catastrophic Risks in Artificial Intelligence Foundation Models (SB 53 / TFAIA enforcement)
institutions.jurisdiction: California, USA — but binding on frontier developers doing business in California, so de facto national
institutions.remit: Enforces the Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (SB 53, signed 29 September 2025). Large frontier developers must publish a Frontier AI Framework covering catastrophic-risk identification, mitigation and governance; all frontier developers must publish transparency reports before deployment; critical safety incidents must be reported to Cal OES within 15 days (24 hours if imminent danger). The AG can seek civil penalties of up to $1,000,000 per violation. SB 53 also creates whistleblower protection for covered employees and requires anonymous internal reporting channels. The AG must publish an annual anonymised, aggregated report on employee reports received.

routes.label: SB 53 covered-employee reports to the Attorney General
routes.scope: Complete the online contact form and select the category 'Catastrophic risks in AI foundation models – employee reports (SB 53)'. For employees and contractors of frontier developers reporting catastrophic risk or non-compliance.
routes.note: VERIFIED — quoted from https://oag.ca.gov/sb53. This dedicated category on a general form is easy to miss.

routes.label: Dedicated SB 53 email address
routes.note: VERIFIED ABSENCE — the AG's SB 53 page states submissions must go through the online form; no email is given.

institutions.reality_check: This is, as of now, the ONLY government channel anywhere in the US built specifically to receive reports about CATASTROPHIC risk from frontier models, with statutory whistleblower protection behind it and a $1m-per-violation penalty. It is a real lever and it is badly publicised — the route is a category buried in the AG's generic contact form. Covered employees are the intended users, but the form itself is open. The AG's annual aggregate report means submissions become part of a public record. If you have insider information about a frontier developer's safety practices, this is the highest-value single address in this directory.
institutions.notes: California's Department of Technology may recommend updates to statutory definitions such as the 'frontier model' compute threshold, so the covered set will shift over time.

institutions.name: California Governor's Office of Emergency Services (Cal OES) — Transparency in Frontier AI Act reporting, via the California Cybersecurity Integration Center
institutions.remit: Statutory recipient under SB 53 of critical safety incident reports from frontier AI developers (within 15 days of discovery; 24 hours where there is imminent risk of death or serious physical injury) and of periodic catastrophic-risk assessment summaries. SB 53 ALSO requires Cal OES to establish a mechanism for THE PUBLIC to report critical safety incidents. Cal OES does not fine or investigate developers itself; it receives, aggregates and refers, and reports to the legislature.

routes.label: TFAIA reporting portal (secure)
routes.scope: Submission of critical safety incidents and catastrophic-risk assessments. Cal OES describes it as a 'secure TFAIA Portal', also reachable by QR code from its page.
routes.note: VERIFIED — this exact URL is published on the Cal OES TFAIA reporting page. It is a third-party (Kaseware) hosted intake, which is why the URL looks unofficial; it is the one Cal OES publishes.

routes.label: Distinct public reporting channel
routes.note: VERIFIED PARTIAL ABSENCE — SB 53 requires a public reporting mechanism, but the Cal OES page presents a single portal without distinguishing a public-facing channel from the developer channel. In practice the portal above is the published route.

institutions.reality_check: Genuinely novel: a government incident-report inbox for frontier AI catastrophic risk that anyone can reach. It is brand new, thinly staffed, and sits inside the state's cyber-threat integration centre rather than an AI-specific unit, so expect reports to be triaged as security incidents. Its value is that filings here become part of the statutory record that feeds the AG's enforcement and the legislature's review. No email, no phone — the portal is the only published route, and reports are confidential.
institutions.notes: Buried four levels deep on the Cal OES site under Cal-CSIC; almost nobody finds it without the direct link.

institutions.name: California Privacy Protection Agency (CPPA)
institutions.remit: The only dedicated US privacy regulator. Enforces the CCPA/CPRA, including regulations on automated decisionmaking technology (ADMT), risk assessments and cybersecurity audits — the ADMT rules reach AI used for significant decisions about Californians. Can investigate, hold administrative hearings, issue orders and impose administrative fines (up to $2,500 per violation, $7,500 for intentional violations or violations involving minors). Conducts formal rulemaking with public comment.

routes.label: CPPA complaint form
routes.scope: Any consumer may complain about a business's handling of personal information, including ADMT and AI-driven decisions.
routes.note: VERIFIED on https://www.cppa.ca.gov/about_us/contact.html.

routes.label: Rulemaking — proposed regulations and comment periods
routes.scope: The ADMT, risk-assessment and cyber-audit regulations went through formal notice-and-comment here.
routes.note: VERIFIED as the page the CPPA's own contact page directs to for laws and regulations.

routes.label: Named staff email
routes.note: VERIFIED ABSENCE — CPPA publishes no email addresses and directs all contact to web forms. Phone 916-572-2900; fax 916-744-2560; post: 400 R Street Suite 350, Sacramento CA 95811.

institutions.reality_check: The complaint form genuinely initiates enforcement review and the CPPA has been willing to act. Its formal rulemaking is the better lever for policy input: California's Administrative Procedure Act requires the agency to publish and respond to every comment, and the ADMT regulations changed substantially across drafts in response to comments. Scope is data-protection and automated decisions about individuals — NOT frontier or catastrophic risk. Route those to the AG (SB 53) or Cal OES instead.
institutions.notes: ADMT obligations phase in over 2026-2027; check current compliance dates before relying on a deadline.

institutions.name: New York State Attorney General — RAISE Act (Responsible AI Safety and Education Act) enforcement
institutions.remit: Enforces the RAISE Act, signed by Governor Hochul (late 2025) and substantially amended/overhauled in April 2026; it takes effect 1 January 2027. Requires large frontier developers to write, publish and follow a safety protocol addressing unreasonable risk of critical harm, to report safety incidents, and bars deploying a model posing unreasonable risk of critical harm. Enforcement is exclusively by the NY Attorney General through civil penalties; there is no private right of action.

routes.label: NY Attorney General complaint forms
routes.scope: The AG's general complaint intake; as of now there is no RAISE-Act-specific category equivalent to California's.
routes.note: UNVERIFIED as fetched — the NY AG site was not directly retrieved. Do not assume a RAISE-specific route exists yet.

routes.label: RAISE Act incident reporting channel
routes.note: UNVERIFIED ABSENCE — the Act does not take effect until 1 January 2027 and no dedicated public reporting portal was located. Expect one to appear closer to the effective date.

institutions.reality_check: Not yet a live route. The law is on the books but does not bite until 1 Jan 2027, and unlike California there is no published AI-specific reporting channel and no equivalent of the SB 53 whistleblower category. Until the effective date, the real lever in New York is the legislature and the AG's rulemaking/guidance process, not a complaint form. Note also that the April 2026 overhaul materially changed the original 2025 text — any analysis based on the bill as first passed is out of date.
institutions.notes: RAISE sits directly in the path of the December 2025 federal preemption Executive Order and the DOJ AI Litigation Task Force; its survivability is contested.

institutions.name: Colorado Attorney General — Automated Decision-Making Technology Act and Chatbot Safety Act rulemaking
institutions.remit: RESTRUCTURED: the original Colorado AI Act (SB 24-205) was repealed and reenacted by SB 26-189 in 2026 after its predecessor's enforcement was blocked in federal court; the replacement regime is the Automated Decision-Making Technology (ADMT) Act, with provisions taking effect 1 January 2027, alongside a separate Chatbot Safety Act (passed May 2026) requiring disclosure of AI interaction, protection of minors from harmful content and safety protocols. The Attorney General has exclusive enforcement authority and rulemaking power; no private right of action.

routes.label: OPEN RULEMAKING: ADMT Act and Chatbot Safety Act proposed rules
routes.scope: Formal public comment on the draft rules filed 11 August 2026. Deadline 26 October 2026 at 11:59pm MST (or the last day of the formal hearing if extended); comments received by 4 September 2026 were considered for the revised draft.
routes.note: VERIFIED — the form URL and both deadlines are published at https://coag.gov/ai/.

routes.label: Public comment repository
routes.scope: All submitted comments are posted publicly here.
routes.note: VERIFIED — cited on the Colorado AG's AI page.

routes.label: Comment email
routes.note: VERIFIED ABSENCE — the AG's page states comments must be submitted via the form; no email address is given.

institutions.reality_check: An OPEN, PUBLISHED, NAMED comment window closing 26 October 2026 with a public comment repository — this is among the highest-value live levers in the US right now, and materially easier to influence than a federal docket because the volume is far lower. Colorado's AG is writing the operative definitions for 'consequential decision', chatbot safety duties and minors' protections from scratch. Scope is algorithmic discrimination and chatbot harms, NOT catastrophic risk. The 2026 repeal-and-reenact is critical: SB 24-205 analyses are obsolete.
institutions.notes: Colorado's reset was explicitly a pivot away from the EU model after federal pressure, including a White House callout.

institutions.name: Texas Attorney General — Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act (TRAIGA)
institutions.remit: Enforces TRAIGA, effective 1 January 2026. Prohibits AI developed or deployed to manipulate human behaviour to incite harm, social scoring by government, unlawful capture of biometric identifiers, AI intended to infringe constitutional rights, unlawful discrimination, and certain sexually explicit AI content; requires government agencies deploying consumer-facing AI to disclose it. The AG has exclusive enforcement, with a 60-day cure period, civil penalties and injunctive relief; there is no private right of action. TRAIGA also creates a regulatory sandbox and an AI Council.

routes.label: File an AI complaint online (Texas AG consumer protection portal)
routes.scope: Anyone may file an AI-specific complaint under TRAIGA. The AG's dedicated 'Consumer AI Rights' page links to this portal under the heading 'File An AI Complaint Online'.
routes.note: VERIFIED at https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/consumer-protection/file-consumer-complaint/consumer-ai-rights.

institutions.reality_check: One of the very few US state routes where an ordinary member of the public can file an AI-specific complaint that lands in an enforcement queue. The Texas AG has stood up a dedicated AI complaint intake and published consumer-facing guidance — a stronger operational posture than most states. But TRAIGA turns on INTENT for most prohibitions, which is a high bar, and the 60-day cure period blunts enforcement. Scope is manipulation, discrimination, biometrics and government use — explicitly not frontier or catastrophic risk.
institutions.notes: TRAIGA is the template the preemption-minded federal position points to as a preferred state model, so it is less exposed to the December 2025 Executive Order than California's or New York's regimes.

institutions.name: Illinois Department of Human Rights (IDHR)
institutions.remit: Enforces the Illinois Human Rights Act as amended by HB 3773 (effective 1 January 2026), which makes it a civil rights violation for an employer to use AI that discriminates on a protected characteristic, or to use zip code as a proxy for a protected class, and requires notice to employees and applicants when AI is used in employment decisions. IDHR investigates charges, makes substantial-evidence determinations, and cases proceed to the Illinois Human Rights Commission or to circuit court. Illinois also has BIPA (private right of action) and an AI Video Interview Act.

routes.label: File a charge of discrimination — intake email
routes.scope: Most employment and public-accommodation cases, including AI-in-hiring discrimination. Submit a Complainant Information Sheet (CIS) by email, post or fax.
routes.note: VERIFIED at https://dhr.illinois.gov/charge-process/filers.html. IDHR states email is the recommended method.

routes.label: Fair housing charges
routes.scope: Housing discrimination, including algorithmic tenant screening.
routes.note: VERIFIED on the same page.

routes.label: Intake phone
routes.note: VERIFIED. Deadlines: most cases within 2 years of the discriminatory act; housing within 1 year.

routes.label: Online filing portal
routes.note: VERIFIED ABSENCE — IDHR has no online charge-filing portal; filing is by form submitted via email, post or fax.

institutions.reality_check: A named, monitored intake email with statutory deadlines behind it — this is a functioning complaint route, not a suggestion box, and a charge triggers an investigation with a determination. But it is individual-remedy machinery: you must be a person who suffered discrimination. It has no application whatsoever to frontier or catastrophic risk. Note the 2-year deadline is unusually generous compared to the federal EEOC's 300 days.
institutions.notes: Illinois BIPA remains the more potent AI-adjacent lever in that state because it carries a private right of action and statutory damages, litigated in court rather than through IDHR.

institutions.name: AI Security Institute (AISI)
institutions.remit: RENAMED: was the 'AI Safety Institute'; renamed the AI Security Institute in February 2025 (announced by written ministerial statement, HLWS454, 24 February 2025), with the focus narrowed toward security, cyber, chemical/biological and criminal-misuse risks and away from bias and free-speech concerns. It is a DIRECTORATE OF DSIT, not an independent agency. Conducts pre-deployment and post-deployment testing of frontier models by voluntary agreement with developers, builds evaluation infrastructure, publishes a Frontier AI Trends Report, and advises government. It has NO statutory powers: it cannot compel access to a model, cannot fine, cannot require testing, and cannot stop a release.

routes.label: Data protection / privacy enquiries (DSIT DPO, covers AISI)
routes.scope: Privacy and data-protection questions only. Published on AISI's privacy policy and monitored by DSIT's Data Protection Officer.
routes.note: VERIFIED at https://www.aisi.gov.uk/privacy-policy. This is the ONLY email address AISI publishes anywhere on its site.

routes.label: AISI contact page
routes.note: UNVERIFIED — the page exists in AISI's navigation but could not be retrieved (permission/provenance failure on fetch). Its contents could not be confirmed, so do not assume an email is published there.

routes.label: Research collaboration and careers
routes.scope: AISI recruits researchers and runs grant programmes; this is the realistic route in for technical people.
routes.note: UNVERIFIED as fetched; the careers path is linked from the homepage, which WAS fetched.

routes.label: Public complaint or incident route
routes.note: VERIFIED ABSENCE — AISI is a research body with no complaints function, no regulatory remit and no public reporting channel.

institutions.reality_check: AISI publishes essentially no way for a member of the public to reach it — one data-protection address, maintained by its parent department. It is deliberately a research organisation, not a regulator, and there is nothing to complain to it about. What DOES reach AISI: publishing technical evaluation work it cites, applying to its research grant calls or open roles, and responding to DSIT consultations that shape its remit. The February 2025 rename was substantive, not cosmetic — 'safety' framing now lands less well than security, misuse and national-resilience framing. Because AISI is a DSIT directorate, parliamentary scrutiny of it happens through the Commons Science, Innovation and Technology Committee, which is where public evidence about AISI actually gets read.
institutions.notes: Frontier/catastrophic risk IS squarely in scope — chem/bio, cyber and autonomy evaluations — making it the UK body most focused on severe risk, but also the one least reachable.

institutions.name: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT)
institutions.remit: Lead UK department for AI policy. Parent of the AI Security Institute. Responsible for the UK's context-based, regulator-led AI approach (no cross-sector AI statute in force), the AI Opportunities Action Plan, AI and copyright policy (including the Section 137 Data (Use and Access) Act progress reporting), and online safety policy alongside Ofcom. DSIT sets policy and can sponsor legislation; it does not itself adjudicate or fine.

routes.label: DSIT ministerial correspondence form
routes.scope: General enquiries and correspondence to ministers.
routes.note: VERIFIED — this is the contact route published on DSIT's GOV.UK organisation page. No general DSIT email or phone number is published.

routes.label: DSIT consultations on GOV.UK
routes.scope: All DSIT open and closed consultations, with closing dates and response documents.
routes.note: VERIFIED as the URL DSIT's own GOV.UK page directs to; there is no dedicated DSIT consultations hub.

routes.label: All UK government open consultations
routes.scope: Cross-government listing; filter by keyword and department.
routes.note: VERIFIED — fetched and returned a live list of 24 open consultations. NOTE: a keyword filter for 'artificial intelligence' returned NO AI-specific open consultations at the time of checking, so AI consultation windows are episodic, not continuous.

routes.label: Data protection
routes.scope: Subject access requests and data-protection queries only.
routes.note: VERIFIED on DSIT's personal information charter. Postal address: 22-26 Whitehall, London SW1A 2EG.

institutions.reality_check: The ministerial correspondence form is the classic example of a route that is logged but not read by policy officials — it generates a templated reply from a correspondence unit. The real DSIT lever is a consultation window: responses are analysed, quoted in the government response document, and named organisations' positions are visible in the outcome. DSIT ran substantial AI and copyright and children's-online-experience consultations in 2025-26. Watch the GOV.UK consultation feed and respond inside the window; outside it, go via the Commons SIT Committee instead, where your evidence is published.
institutions.notes: The UK still has no general AI statute; a frontier AI bill has been repeatedly trailed and repeatedly deferred. Verify the current legislative position before assuming a bill exists.

institutions.name: Ofcom (Office of Communications)
institutions.remit: Independent regulator for communications and, under the Online Safety Act 2023, for user-to-user and search services. Ofcom has CONFIRMED that AI chatbots fall within the OSA where the service meets the Act's service definitions — a chatbot is out of scope only if it allows interaction with the chatbot alone and no other users, does not search multiple sites or databases when responding, AND cannot generate pornographic content. Powers: can require information, investigate, impose fines up to £18m or 10% of qualifying worldwide revenue, and seek business disruption measures (payment and access restrictions) against non-compliant services. Senior managers can face criminal liability for certain failures.

routes.label: Complain about online services, websites or apps
routes.scope: Public complaints about online services including AI chatbots falling within OSA scope.
routes.note: VERIFIED — the route is published on Ofcom's contact page and on its AI chatbots guidance page.

routes.label: General advice and complaints line
routes.note: VERIFIED on https://www.ofcom.org.uk/about-ofcom/contact-us/. Welsh 0300 123 2023; BSL video relay and text relay available.

routes.label: Ofcom consultations
routes.scope: Ofcom consults extensively on OSA codes of practice and guidance; responses are published.
routes.note: UNVERIFIED as fetched, though Ofcom's consultation programme is extensively documented. Confirm the current URL from the site navigation.

routes.label: Licensing mailboxes
routes.note: VERIFIED on the contact page. Ofcom publishes no general online-safety email.

institutions.reality_check: Ofcom is the UK's most powerful AI-adjacent regulator by a wide margin — it can fine 10% of global turnover and cut a service off from payment providers. Its OSA consultations are the single highest-leverage UK input route on AI: they run for months, every response is read and summarised, and Ofcom publishes detailed statements addressing arguments. Individual complaints matter less as individual remedies (Ofcom does not resolve your personal dispute) and more as evidence of systemic failure that supports an investigation. Ofcom is explicit about its limits: 'We can only take action on online harms covered by the Act, using the powers we have been granted' — so frontier and catastrophic risk is OUT OF SCOPE. This is content-harm regulation applied to generative AI, not model-level safety regulation.
institutions.notes: Ofcom's chatbot scoping is contested by practitioners — several categories of generative AI service sit ambiguously inside or outside the OSA.

institutions.name: Information Commissioner's Office (ICO)
institutions.remit: Independent data protection and information rights regulator. Enforces UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018, which govern AI training data, automated decision-making and profiling (Article 22 rights), and data subject rights. Can issue information notices and assessment notices, conduct audits, issue enforcement notices requiring a company to stop processing (including stopping a model's deployment), and fine up to £17.5m or 4% of global turnover. Also enforces PECR. Publishes AI and data protection guidance and runs a regulatory sandbox.

routes.label: Make a complaint
routes.scope: Complaints about how an organisation handled your personal information, including AI training on your data and automated decisions about you. Sub-routes include nuisance calls (https://ico.org.uk/for-the-public/nuisance-calls/) and FOI complaints.
routes.note: VERIFIED — page fetched; it is a hub that routes by complaint type. The ICO's contact pages are JavaScript-heavy and the helpline number could not be read off them directly.

routes.label: Concerns about how an organisation handled your information
routes.scope: The public-facing entry point for a data-protection concern.
routes.note: UNVERIFIED as fetched; appeared in ICO search results.

routes.label: ICO helpline and live chat
routes.scope: ICO operates a telephone helpline and live chat for the public.
routes.note: PARTIALLY VERIFIED — the page loaded and confirmed a helpline and live chat exist (it carried a notice about closure on specific bank holidays) but the phone number itself did not render to the retrieval tool. Read it from the page directly rather than trusting a remembered number.

routes.label: ICO calls for views and draft guidance consultations
routes.scope: The ICO consults on AI and data protection guidance, generative AI, and biometrics.
routes.note: UNVERIFIED as fetched; confirm from the ICO site navigation.

institutions.reality_check: The ICO complaint route is real and heavily used, but the practitioner experience is that individual complaints usually end in advice or a 'we have asked the organisation to improve' letter rather than enforcement; the ICO has been notably reluctant to fine large technology firms. The effective lever is the ICO's consultation and call-for-views process on AI guidance, where structured responses visibly move the text, and coordinated complaints that establish a pattern. Scope is personal data and automated decisions about individuals — NOT frontier or catastrophic risk. The ICO also has no jurisdiction over a model that harms no identifiable data subject.
institutions.notes: The Data (Use and Access) Act has altered parts of the UK automated-decision-making regime; check current Article 22 equivalents before relying on pre-2025 guidance.

institutions.name: Competition and Markets Authority (CMA)
institutions.remit: Competition and consumer protection regulator. Relevant to AI through foundation-model market studies, merger review of AI partnerships and acqui-hires, and the digital markets competition regime (Strategic Market Status designations under the DMCC Act, which allow the CMA to impose conduct requirements and pro-competition interventions on designated firms). Can compel information, conduct market investigations, block or unwind mergers, impose conduct requirements, and fine up to 10% of global turnover — and under the DMCC regime the CMA can now enforce consumer law directly with fines rather than going to court.

routes.label: Report a competition or market problem
routes.scope: Anyone can report suspected anti-competitive conduct, including in AI markets (compute access, model distribution, exclusive partnerships).
routes.note: VERIFIED — linked from the CMA's GOV.UK organisation page.

routes.label: General enquiries
routes.note: VERIFIED on https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/competition-and-markets-authority. Phone 020 3738 6000. Address: The Cabot, 25 Cabot Square, London E14 4QZ.

routes.label: Freedom of Information requests
routes.scope: FOI — a genuinely useful route for extracting CMA analysis of AI markets.
routes.note: VERIFIED on the same page.

routes.label: CMA consultations and market study calls for evidence
routes.scope: The CMA's foundation-model work proceeded via published calls for evidence with named response deadlines and email addresses per study.
routes.note: VERIFIED as the hub; individual study pages carry their own dedicated response mailbox.

institutions.reality_check: The CMA's foundation-model market study was unusually open: it published a call for evidence, set up a dedicated study mailbox, met respondents, and quoted submissions in its update reports. That per-study mailbox — not general.enquiries@cma.gov.uk — is where input lands. The general enquiries address is a correspondence unit. The CMA's AI framing is market power and consumer harm, with an explicit concern about concentration in compute and model supply; it has occasionally touched on safety as a competition concern (whether incumbents can be disciplined) but does not regulate model risk. FOI to the CMA is underused and productive.
institutions.notes: The DMCC regime materially expanded CMA powers; SMS designations are the mechanism to watch for AI-market intervention.

institutions.name: House of Commons Science, Innovation and Technology Committee
institutions.remit: Scrutinises DSIT — and therefore the AI Security Institute — its policy, administration and spending. Conducts inquiries, takes oral and written evidence, summons ministers and officials, and publishes reports to which the Government must respond within 60 days. It cannot legislate, fine or compel a private party in practice, but it can compel the attendance of officials and extract documents, and its reports set the terms of UK AI debate. Recent and current inquiries have included Low-energy computing (opened 16 April 2026), Neuroscience and digital childhoods (24 March 2026), Digital centre of government (3 February 2025), and Science diplomacy (3 April 2025).

routes.label: Written evidence to an open inquiry
routes.scope: Each open inquiry carries its own 'Submit evidence' link and deadline on the committee's inquiry page. Anyone may submit; accepted submissions are PUBLISHED on the committee website and become part of the formal record.
routes.note: VERIFIED — the committee page was fetched and lists its current inquiries. Note https://committees.parliament.uk/submit-written-evidence/ returns 404; submission is always via the specific inquiry's page.

routes.label: Committee staff
routes.scope: Correspondence with the committee team, including asking the clerk whether a submission is in scope.
routes.note: VERIFIED on the committee page. Postal: Science and Technology Committee, House of Commons, London SW1A 0AA.

institutions.reality_check: THIS IS THE UK'S BEST PUBLIC ROUTE and the clearest example of the contrast the question draws. Written evidence to an open select committee inquiry is read by the committee's specialist advisers and clerks, published under your name, indexed, quoted in the report, and cited afterwards by others — unlike a ministerial inbox, which produces a templated reply. Practitioner guidance (UCL Public Policy and others) converges on: keep it short and structured with numbered recommendations, answer the committee's published terms of reference point by point, submit before the deadline, and — the step most people skip — contact the clerk beforehand to check scope and signal availability to give oral evidence. The clerk, not the chair and not a minister, is the person who matters. Building a relationship with the clerk leads to future opportunities, including being called as a witness.
institutions.notes: Correct current name is 'Science, Innovation and Technology Committee' (committee ID 135). Do not confuse it with the House of Lords Science and Technology Committee (ID 193), which is a separate body.

institutions.name: House of Lords Communications and Digital Committee
institutions.jurisdiction: United Kingdom (House of Lords select committee)
institutions.remit: Considers the media, digital and creative industries. Has run the most substantial Lords work on AI, including its 'AI and copyright' inquiry (opened 3 November 2025; report published 6 March 2026; Government response published 15 May 2026) and earlier large language models and generative AI work. Currently running 'The Online Safety Act: implementation and impact' (opened 27 July 2026, written evidence deadline 21 September 2026). Takes evidence, reports, and obliges a Government response; no enforcement power.

routes.label: Written evidence to an open inquiry
routes.scope: Anyone may submit to an open inquiry via that inquiry's page; submissions are published. The OSA implementation inquiry's written evidence deadline was 21 September 2026.
routes.note: VERIFIED — committee page fetched, showing current inquiries and deadlines.

routes.label: Committee staff
routes.scope: Correspondence with the committee team and clerk.
routes.note: VERIFIED on the committee page. Postal: Communications and Digital Committee, House of Lords, London SW1A 0PW.

institutions.reality_check: Lords committees are, in practitioners' experience, MORE receptive to outside expertise than Commons committees: members are often subject-matter experts with no constituency workload, inquiries run longer, and the evidence base is read more carefully. The AI and copyright inquiry extracted a formal Government response within ten weeks of reporting. The same rules apply — submit to a live inquiry within its window, address the terms of reference, and contact the clerk. Scope is media, digital markets, copyright and online safety, not frontier risk; for severe-risk arguments the Commons SIT Committee scrutinising AISI is the better venue.
institutions.notes: Other Lords committees with adjacent AI remit include the Science and Technology Committee (ID 193) and the Constitution Committee on algorithmic decision-making in government; check which has a live inquiry before choosing.

institutions.name: UK Parliament and Government Petitions Service
institutions.remit: Statutory-adjacent petitions platform run jointly by the House of Commons Petitions Committee and the Government. A petition reaching 10,000 signatures receives a written Government response; one reaching 100,000 signatures is considered for a Westminster Hall debate by the Petitions Committee. Petitions are open to British citizens and UK residents. The Committee can also take evidence and hold sessions on petition topics.

routes.label: Start a petition
routes.scope: Any British citizen or UK resident. Requires five supporters before publication.
routes.note: VERIFIED — https://petition.parliament.uk/ was fetched and confirmed live, with both thresholds and the start URL.

routes.label: Browse and sign open petitions
routes.scope: Public signing; Government responses to petitions over 10,000 signatures are published on the site.
routes.note: VERIFIED.

institutions.reality_check: Honest assessment: the 10,000-signature Government response is almost always a restatement of existing policy drafted by the department, and is worth little on its own. The 100,000 threshold is different — a Westminster Hall debate creates a Hansard record, forces a minister to the despatch box, and generates press. For AI, no petition has yet moved policy. Its real utility is as a coordination and visibility device that makes a later select-committee submission or media campaign land harder, not as a lever in itself. Low cost, low expected value.
institutions.notes: Petitions close after six months and are rejected if they duplicate an existing petition or fall outside Government/Parliament responsibility.

institutions.name: European AI Office (within DG CONNECT, European Commission)
institutions.jurisdiction: European Union (extraterritorial: applies to providers placing models on the EU market wherever established)
institutions.remit: The AI Act's central enforcement body for general-purpose AI. Exclusive supervisory and enforcement competence over GPAI model providers. Can conduct inspections, require technical documentation and access to models to assess capabilities, request corrective action, RESTRICT THE PUBLIC AVAILABILITY OF A MODEL, and impose fines directly (up to 3% of global turnover or EUR 15m for GPAI provider breaches; up to 7% or EUR 35m for prohibited-practice breaches enforced elsewhere). Develops evaluation tools, methodologies and benchmarks. Serves as secretariat to the AI Board. Under the Digital Omnibus on AI its supervisory powers were expanded. GPAI obligations have applied since 2 August 2025; the AI Office's enforcement powers over GPAI became exercisable from 2 August 2026.

routes.label: AI Office general inquiries
routes.scope: General correspondence with the AI Office.
routes.note: VERIFIED — published on https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/ai-office.

routes.label: AI Office recruitment
routes.scope: Recruitment only; applications must go through the Expression of Interest form, not by email.
routes.note: VERIFIED on the same page.

routes.label: AI Act Service Desk (Single Information Platform)
routes.scope: Submit questions about the AI Act in any EU language and receive answers from a team of experts; includes interactive compliance-checker tools.
routes.note: VERIFIED — the Single Information Platform was fetched and this is the route it publishes.

routes.label: Commission consultations on AI Act implementing acts, guidelines and codes of practice
routes.scope: The AI Office has run multi-stakeholder consultations on the GPAI Code of Practice, the transparency code, GPAI guidelines and risk-classification guidance.
routes.note: UNVERIFIED as fetched; consultations are also mirrored on the Have your say portal.

institutions.reality_check: The AI Office is the most consequential AI-safety regulator on earth by formal power — it is the only body that can order a frontier model off the market and fine its provider — and it publishes a working email and a genuinely staffed multilingual service desk. But the service desk answers COMPLIANCE questions; it is not a complaints channel and not a policy channel. The real input levers are (1) the multi-stakeholder drafting processes for codes of practice and guidelines, which were genuinely open and where civil-society drafting comments visibly changed text, and (2) the Have your say portal when an implementing act is out for feedback. Systemic-risk GPAI is explicitly within the AI Office's mandate, making this the ONLY jurisdiction where frontier risk is a statutory supervisory duty rather than a research interest.
institutions.notes: CRITICAL 2026 UPDATE: the Digital Omnibus on AI — Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 — entered into force on 27 July 2026. It DEFERRED high-risk obligations (stand-alone Annex III systems to 2 December 2027; Annex I embedded systems to 2 August 2028) but did NOT defer the GPAI/systemic-risk regime, which has applied since 2 August 2025, and did NOT defer the Article 50 transparency obligations, which apply from 2 August 2026. So the frontier-model part of the AI Act is fully live; the consumer high-risk part is delayed.

institutions.name: European Artificial Intelligence Board
institutions.remit: Advisory and co-ordination body created by the AI Act, operational since the Act took effect on 1 August 2024. Composed of one representative per Member State, chaired by a Member State, with the EDPS and EEA-EFTA states as observers; the AI Office is its secretariat. Ensures consistent application of the AI Act, co-ordinates national competent authorities, issues opinions and recommendations, and endorses key documents — it endorsed the adequacy assessments of the GPAI Code of Practice and of the Transparency of AI-Generated Content code, and guidance on harmonised standards for high-risk systems. It advises; it does not itself fine or investigate.

routes.label: Register of Commission Expert Groups — AI Board entry (agendas, participants, minutes)
routes.scope: Public transparency record only. Agendas, membership and minutes are published here.
routes.note: VERIFIED — published on https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/ai-board.

routes.label: Direct public contact
routes.note: VERIFIED ABSENCE — the Commission publishes no email or form for the AI Board; correspondence would go via the AI Office as secretariat (CNECT-AIOFFICE@ec.europa.eu).

institutions.reality_check: NO PUBLIC INPUT ROUTE. The AI Board is a Member-State intergovernmental body; the public cannot address it. The only realistic influence is indirect — through your own national competent authority, which sits on the Board, or through the AI Office as secretariat. The expert-groups register is nonetheless valuable: minutes reveal what the Board is about to endorse, months before it appears as guidance, which is exactly when a national authority can still be lobbied.
institutions.notes: Distinct from both the Scientific Panel (independent experts) and the Advisory Forum (stakeholders). All three are separate AI Act bodies.

institutions.name: AI Act Scientific Panel of Independent Experts
institutions.remit: CONSTITUTED. Established under Article 68 of the AI Act and Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/454; 60 independent experts were recruited and named in 2026 (announced alongside the Advisory Forum around June 2026), serving renewable 24-month terms in a personal capacity, having signed confidentiality and commitment declarations. Its duties: alerting the AI Office to systemic risks, advising on GPAI classification and evaluation methodologies, and supporting market surveillance. Its sharpest instrument is the Article 90 QUALIFIED ALERT: where the panel suspects a GPAI model poses a concrete identifiable risk at Union level or meets the Article 51 systemic-risk conditions, it may issue a reasoned alert naming the provider, on receipt of which the AI Office may exercise its Article 91-94 powers (demand documentation, conduct evaluations, require remedial measures) and must inform the AI Board of measures taken.

routes.label: Public contact for the Scientific Panel
routes.note: VERIFIED ABSENCE — the Commission's Scientific Panel page names all 60 members but publishes no contact address, no submission mechanism and no route for outsiders to trigger consideration of a risk.

routes.label: Indirect route via the AI Office (panel secretariat)
routes.scope: The AI Office supports the panel; this is the only published address in the chain.
routes.note: VERIFIED on the AI Office page, not on the panel page. There is no guarantee correspondence reaches panel members.

institutions.reality_check: THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT GAP IN THE ENTIRE DIRECTORY. The Scientific Panel is the only body anywhere with a statutory mechanism to force regulatory scrutiny of a specific frontier model on systemic-risk grounds — the Article 90 qualified alert — and there is NO published way for an outside researcher, a whistleblower or a member of the public to bring evidence to it. No email, no form, no submission process. The realistic route is therefore personal: the 60 members are named publicly on the Commission's page, they are working academics with institutional addresses, and approaching an individual panel member with technical evidence is the only practical path. Membership renews on 24-month terms, and the Commission runs public calls for experts — applying is the other way in.
institutions.notes: Separate from the Advisory Forum. Do not confuse the two: the panel is 60 independent scientists with an alert power; the forum is 174 stakeholders with an opinion-giving role.

institutions.name: AI Act Advisory Forum
institutions.remit: CONSTITUTED. Established under Article 67 of the AI Act; 174 members selected from over 700 applications, representing civil society, academia, industry, SMEs and start-ups, serving two-year renewable terms; members were named in 2026. Five bodies hold permanent seats: the EU Agency for Fundamental Rights (FRA), ENISA, CEN, CENELEC and ETSI. It provides technical expertise and balanced stakeholder input to the Commission and the AI Board, works through plenary meetings and thematic subgroups, and prepares opinions and recommendations on request. Purely advisory.

routes.label: Register of Commission Expert Groups — Advisory Forum entry (members, agendas, meetings)
routes.scope: Public record of membership, meetings and documents.
routes.note: VERIFIED — this is the URL the Commission's Advisory Forum page directs stakeholders to.

routes.value: no open call at time of checking
routes.note: VERIFIED ABSENCE — the Commission's page carries no current call, no deadline and no contact email. The last call drew 700+ applications for 174 seats.

routes.label: Direct public contact
routes.note: VERIFIED ABSENCE.

institutions.reality_check: The Advisory Forum is the AI Act's designated civil-society channel, and it is a MEMBERSHIP channel, not an open one — 174 seats, no public submission route, no contact address. If your organisation is not a member, the practical approach is to work through one that is: the membership list is public on the expert-groups register, and forum members in the civil-society bloc actively solicit input for subgroup positions. Watch for the next call for applications, which is the only moment the door opens. Its remit is the whole AI Act, weighted toward fundamental rights and implementation practicality rather than frontier risk — the Scientific Panel is the severe-risk body.
institutions.notes: 174 seats from 700+ applicants means roughly a one-in-four success rate for applicants — better odds than most assume.

institutions.name: National market surveillance authorities under the AI Act (27 Member States)
institutions.remit: Supervise and enforce the AI Act's rules for AI SYSTEMS — prohibited practices and high-risk requirements — within their territory, using the powers in Regulation (EU) 2019/1020: request information, demand documentation, require corrective action, order withdrawal or recall from the market, and impose penalties set in national law (up to 7% of global turnover for prohibited practices). They do NOT supervise GPAI models; that is the AI Office's exclusive competence. Member States were required to designate them by 2 August 2025, and many have not: as of June 2026, only 9 Member States had fully designated both market surveillance and notifying authorities, 12 had partial clarity, and 6 had designated none at all.

routes.label: ARTICLE 85 — right to lodge a complaint with a market surveillance authority
routes.scope: 'Any natural or legal person having grounds to consider that there has been an infringement' of the AI Act may complain to the market surveillance authority of their Member State. The authority must handle it under its Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 procedures, alongside any other administrative or judicial remedy. APPLIES FROM 2 AUGUST 2026 (Article 113).
routes.note: VERIFIED — text and applicability date confirmed. Note this citation is to the widely used AI Act Explorer, a non-official but reliable consolidated text; the authoritative text is in the Official Journal.

routes.label: Commission list of national Single Points of Contact
routes.scope: The Commission page carries a table of designated Single Points of Contact by Member State, with links to some national authorities (e.g. Ireland's AI Office at aioffice.gov.ie).
routes.note: VERIFIED — BUT the page itself states 'The Commission is considering the notifications and will publish a list of Single Points of Contact in due time', i.e. the authoritative consolidated directory does NOT yet exist.

routes.label: Named national complaint portals
routes.value: varies by Member State; no consolidated EU directory published
routes.scope: Designated leads include Cyprus (Commissioner of Communications), Denmark (Danish Agency for Digital Government), Finland (Traficom as SPOC, decentralised model), Hungary (Minister for Enterprise Development), Ireland (15 designated bodies, SPOC is the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment), Italy (National Cybersecurity Agency, with AgID as notifying authority), Lithuania (Communications Regulatory Authority), Malta (Malta Digital Innovation Authority and the IDPC), Slovenia (Agency for Communication Networks and Services).
routes.note: VERIFIED via the AI Act national implementation tracker (updated 17 June 2026). Individual national complaint-form URLs were NOT verified and must be checked per country.

institutions.reality_check: Article 85 is the AI Act's single genuine citizen-facing right, live since 2 August 2026 — anyone with grounds may complain and the authority must process it. In practice it is badly broken at the point of use: six Member States have designated nobody, a third have only partial designations, Ireland split the function across fifteen bodies, and the Commission has still not published the consolidated contact directory it promised. So the right exists and the address often does not. Where an authority IS designated and is an existing regulator (Italy's ACN, Denmark's digital agency, Finland's Traficom), complaints land in a functioning inbox. Note the scope limit that catches people out: market surveillance authorities cannot act against a GPAI MODEL provider — that is the AI Office's exclusive competence — so a frontier-model complaint filed nationally will be bounced or forwarded.
institutions.notes: Around 2,000 bodies across the EU carry some market surveillance function, which is why no single directory works. Always verify your own Member State's designation before filing.

institutions.name: European Parliament Committee on the Internal Market and Consumer Protection (IMCO)
institutions.remit: One of the two lead committees (jointly with LIBE) that steered the AI Act through Parliament, and lead committee on the Digital Omnibus on AI. Remit covers single market rules, product safety, consumer protection and digital markets. Can amend and vote on legislation, hold hearings, commission studies and question the Commission. Legislative power is real — Parliament is a co-legislator — but individual committees cannot investigate or fine.

routes.scope: Agendas, minutes, draft reports and amendment tables are published; public hearings are streamed and occasionally invite written contributions.
routes.note: VERIFIED — page fetched; it confirms AI regulation is among IMCO's active files but publishes NO committee email or secretariat address.

Do NOT assume the commonly cited imco-secretariat@europarl.europa.eu pattern is correct without reading it off the page yourself.

routes.scope: The general public route into Parliament; the Citizens' Enquiries Unit answers questions and routes issues.
routes.note: UNVERIFIED as fetched — europarl.europa.eu/at-your-service pages are blocked by robots.txt. This form URL appeared in Parliament's own search results.

routes.scope: Follow the Digital Omnibus on AI and AI Act files, rapporteurs and shadow rapporteurs.
routes.note: UNVERIFIED as fetched. The Legislative Train for the Digital Omnibus on AI is at https://www.europarl.europa.eu/legislative-train/package-digital-package/file-digital-omnibus-on-ai (seen in search results).

institutions.reality_check: European Parliament committees do not run UK-style open written-evidence calls, and they publish no secretariat email — so there is no analogue to a select-committee submission. What actually works is the rapporteur system: each legislative file has a named rapporteur and shadow rapporteurs from each political group, all identifiable from the Legislative Observatory, and their policy advisers actively take meetings and written input during the amendment phase. That window — between the draft report and the committee vote — is the real lever, and it is short. Registering in the EU Transparency Register is a practical prerequisite for meetings. Ask EP is for citizens' questions, not policy influence.
institutions.notes: IMCO and LIBE shared the AI Act file; expect the same joint pattern on major AI files.

institutions.name: European Parliament Committee on Civil Liberties, Justice and Home Affairs (LIBE)
institutions.remit: Joint lead committee with IMCO on the AI Act. Described by its chair as 'the leading body of the European Parliament for shaping and overseeing EU legislation and policies that ensure EU citizens enjoy an area of freedom, security, and justice'. Responsibilities include rule of law, fundamental rights, anti-discrimination, data protection and privacy, asylum and migration, organised crime and citizen security. On AI it drove the prohibited-practices list, biometric surveillance restrictions and fundamental-rights impact assessments. Legislative co-decision power; no investigative or enforcement power over private parties.

routes.label: Committee pages, documents and public hearings
routes.scope: Agendas, draft reports, amendments and hearing streams.
routes.note: VERIFIED — page fetched. It references a 'Contacts' section but publishes NO email or postal address in the retrievable content.

routes.label: Committee on Petitions (PETI) — the Parliament's actual public channel
routes.scope: See the separate PETI entry; this is the route with a right of access, not LIBE.
routes.note: VERIFIED.

institutions.reality_check: Same structural reality as IMCO: no public evidence call, no published secretariat address, influence via named rapporteurs and shadow rapporteurs during the amendment window. LIBE is however the most receptive committee to civil-society and academic input on AI, and its members' offices routinely cite NGO analyses in amendments — several AI Act prohibitions trace directly to civil-society drafting. The practical sequence is: identify the shadow rapporteur from the political group closest to your position, contact their adviser, supply drafted amendment text rather than a position paper. LIBE's frame is fundamental rights and surveillance, not catastrophic risk.
institutions.notes: LIBE is also the committee for GDPR and law-enforcement AI, so biometric and predictive-policing concerns belong here rather than IMCO.

institutions.name: European Parliament Committee on Industry, Research and Energy (ITRE)
institutions.remit: Opinion-giving committee on AI files, with lead responsibility for industrial policy, research (Horizon Europe), telecommunications and energy — including the compute and data-centre dimension of AI, the AI Continent Action Plan, AI gigafactories and EuroHPC. On the AI Act it gave an opinion rather than leading. Co-legislative power on files within its own competence.

routes.label: Committee pages and documents
routes.scope: Agendas, opinions, draft reports and public hearings.

institutions.reality_check: The least useful of the three committees for AI risk input and the most useful for AI infrastructure and compute policy. Same rapporteur-centric access model. If your concern is compute governance, chip supply or data-centre siting in the EU, ITRE is the committee; if it is model risk, it is not.
institutions.notes: ITRE's AI work is growth- and sovereignty-framed; safety arguments land poorly here unless recast as strategic-autonomy or resilience arguments.

institutions.name: European Parliament Committee on Petitions (PETI)
institutions.remit: Handles petitions submitted under the Treaty right of petition — a fundamental right of every EU citizen and resident. Examines admissibility, may ask the Commission for information or a legal opinion, can hold hearings, conduct fact-finding visits, and report to plenary. Through petitions it 'conducts an ongoing reality check on the way in which European legislation is implemented'. It cannot legislate or fine, but it can force the Commission to answer in writing on a specific implementation failure.

routes.label: Submit a petition to the European Parliament
routes.scope: Open to 'all European citizens and residents'. Petitions must concern a matter within the EU's fields of activity and affect the petitioner directly. Submission is online via the portal's 'Start a petition' route.
routes.note: VERIFIED — portal fetched and confirmed live, with eligibility and process guides ('How do I submit a petition?', 'How is my petition treated?').

routes.label: Petitions FAQ
routes.note: UNVERIFIED as fetched; URL appeared in Parliament's own search results.

institutions.reality_check: Underrated and genuinely open — unlike a UK petition, a single EU petition from one person can succeed on its merits with no signature threshold at all. If declared admissible, the Commission must respond in writing, the petition is discussed in committee, and MEPs can question the Commission on it. For AI this is a viable route to force an official answer on, say, a Member State's failure to designate a market surveillance authority, or non-enforcement of a prohibited practice. The constraints are real: it must fall within EU competence and affect you directly, and the process is slow (often a year or more). But it creates an official record that nothing else at EU level gives an individual.
institutions.notes: Distinct from the European Citizens' Initiative, which proposes new law and needs a million signatures. A petition complains about existing EU law or its implementation and needs one person.

institutions.name: European Citizens' Initiative (ECI)
institutions.remit: Treaty-based participatory instrument administered by the European Commission. Allows citizens to 'call on the European Commission to propose new laws'. On reaching one million valid signatures across a minimum number of Member States within the collection period, the Commission must meet the organisers, the Parliament holds a public hearing, and the Commission must respond formally setting out what action it will take and why. The Commission is NOT obliged to legislate.

routes.label: Find, sign or register an initiative
routes.scope: Public signing and organiser registration. Official Commission portal.
routes.note: VERIFIED as live — the site was fetched and confirms the one-million-signature rule, though the landing page is a language selector and the procedural detail sits on deeper pages.

routes.label: Organisers' register
routes.scope: Where a citizens' committee registers a proposed initiative for Commission admissibility screening.
routes.note: UNVERIFIED as fetched; referenced from the verified ECI find-initiative page.

routes.label: Open AI-related initiatives
routes.note: UNVERIFIED — the initiative database could not be read (the listing pages returned navigation shells only). No AI-related open initiative was found, but absence could not be confirmed.

routes.label: Submission page
routes.scope: Proposals for EU legal acts in areas where the Commission has power to propose legislation.
routes.note: Form an organising group of at least 7 EU citizens resident in 7 different Member States, register the initiative, then collect at least 1 million signatures from EU citizens old enough to vote in European elections (16 in some countries), meeting minimum country thresholds in at least 7 Member States.

institutions.reality_check: High cost, low probability, occasionally decisive. Fewer than a dozen ECIs have ever reached a million signatures in the instrument's lifetime, and the Commission has declined to legislate even on several that did. It requires a citizens' committee from seven Member States, a year of collection, national ID-number verification in many countries, and real money. It is not a route for an individual or a small group. Where it pays off is agenda-setting and the mandatory Parliament hearing, which produces a public record and press. For AI, no initiative has yet been mounted; the more efficient EU routes by an order of magnitude are a PETI petition, a Have your say consultation response, or direct rapporteur engagement.
institutions.notes: Do not confuse with a PETI petition (no threshold, complains about existing law) or with the Ombudsman (maladministration only).

institutions.name: European Commission 'Have your say' portal
institutions.remit: The Commission's single public feedback and consultation platform under the Better Regulation framework. Every Commission initiative — call for evidence, draft delegated or implementing act, public consultation, evaluation — is published here with a feedback window, and all feedback received is published alongside. The Commission must publish a synopsis report summarising and responding to feedback. This is the formal EU equivalent of the US regulations.gov docket.

routes.label: Have your say — give feedback on EU initiatives
routes.scope: Open to anyone worldwide, though respondents are asked to identify themselves and their category (citizen, company, NGO, public authority). Feedback is published publicly with the respondent's name unless anonymity is requested.
routes.note: VERIFIED as live and as the Commission's own canonical URL. The landing page is a language gateway; individual initiative pages carry the actual feedback forms and deadlines. No AI-specific item was visible from the landing page.

routes.label: Legacy Better Regulation URL (redirects)
routes.scope: Older link still in wide circulation.
routes.note: VERIFIED as resolving to the Have your say portal.

institutions.reality_check: THE MAIN FORMAL EU LEVER, and the AI Act's implementing machinery runs through it — codes of practice, guidelines on GPAI, risk-classification guidance and delegated acts all pass through a feedback window here. Feedback is published, attributed and answered in a synopsis report, which makes it far more consequential than a letter. The caveats practitioners repeat: windows are short (often four weeks) and poorly publicised, the Commission weights structured, evidence-bearing responses from identifiable organisations much more heavily than individual comments, and a response that does not engage the specific questions asked is summarised away in one line. Set up an alert on the portal for the AI Act rather than checking periodically — most people miss the window entirely.
institutions.notes: Complements rather than replaces the AI Office's own targeted multi-stakeholder consultations, which have been the more substantive route for the GPAI Code of Practice.

institutions.name: European Ombudsman
institutions.remit: Investigates maladministration by EU institutions, bodies, offices and agencies — which includes the European Commission and therefore the AI Office, DG CONNECT, and the AI Act's governance bodies. Can open own-initiative inquiries, demand documents from institutions, make findings of maladministration and issue recommendations; can refer a refusal to comply to the European Parliament. It CANNOT overturn a decision, fine anyone, or act against private companies or Member State authorities.

routes.label: Online complaint form — the ONLY accepted channel
routes.scope: Open to 'a citizen of the European Union', 'a resident of a Member State', or 'a legal person having your registered office in a Member State'. Must be within two years of becoming aware of the facts, and you must first have tried to resolve the matter with the institution concerned.
routes.note: VERIFIED — and note the explicit warning: 'Only complaints submitted using the online complaint form below will be processed. Please note that complaints sent by email will not be accepted.'

routes.label: Complaint by email
routes.note: VERIFIED ABSENCE — the Ombudsman expressly refuses email complaints.

routes.label: General contact (not complaints)
routes.scope: General enquiries. Phone +33 3 88 17 23 13. Post: Médiateur européen, 1 avenue du Président Robert Schuman, CS 30403, F-67001 Strasbourg Cedex. Offices at Bâtiment Václav Havel, Allée Spach, F-67000 Strasbourg and Bâtiment Froissart, 87 rue Froissart, B-1000 Bruxelles.
routes.note: VERIFIED.

institutions.reality_check: A real and surprisingly effective route, but only for a specific complaint type: that an EU institution handled something badly — refused access to documents, failed to consult properly, missed a legal deadline, or had an undeclared conflict of interest. Applied to AI, that means the Ombudsman is the address if the AI Office refuses your document request, or if a consultation was run unfairly, or if expert-group appointments were opaque. The Ombudsman has previously found maladministration in Commission expert-group composition and in access-to-documents refusals, which is directly relevant to the Scientific Panel and Advisory Forum selection processes. It is NOT an address for complaining about an AI system, a company, or the content of EU law. Note the two mandatory preconditions: prior contact with the institution, and the two-year limit — complaints fail on these more often than on the merits.
institutions.notes: Pair it with an access-to-documents request under Regulation 1049/2001 first: the refusal is what creates the admissible Ombudsman complaint.

institutions.name: AI Act Service Desk / Single Information Platform
institutions.remit: Commission-run help service operated by the AI Office. Described as 'a central initiative to help stakeholders navigate the AI Act requirements', providing interactive tools to determine whether a given actor falls within the Act's obligations, and a staffed desk where anyone can 'submit questions about the AI Act and receive answers from a team of experts' in their own language. It gives guidance; it does not take complaints, does not enforce, and its answers are not legally binding.

routes.label: AI Act Service Desk — ask a question
routes.scope: Open to anyone, in any EU language. Compliance and interpretation questions about the AI Act.
routes.note: VERIFIED — the Single Information Platform was fetched and publishes this as its question route.

routes.label: AI Office (behind the service desk)
routes.note: VERIFIED on the Single Information Platform page.

institutions.reality_check: Genuinely staffed and genuinely useful — the only place in the EU AI governance architecture where a non-expert can ask a question and get a human answer. But its purpose is compliance navigation, not risk reporting: if you write to it about a dangerous model it will answer a question about legal classification, not open a case. For an actual complaint use the Article 85 route to your national market surveillance authority (AI systems) or, for GPAI models, there is no public complaint route at all — only the AI Office's general inbox.
institutions.notes: Included because it is the most reachable EU AI address for an ordinary person, and because it is frequently mistaken for a complaints channel.

institutions.name: General-Purpose AI Code of Practice and its Signatory Taskforce
institutions.remit: Co-regulatory instrument under Article 56 of the AI Act, published by the Commission in its final form in July 2025 and assessed as adequate by the AI Board and the Commission. Signing is voluntary, but signature is the presumptive route to demonstrating compliance with GPAI obligations, which have applied since 2 August 2025; non-signatories must demonstrate compliance by other means and face greater scrutiny. It has three chapters — Transparency, Copyright, and Safety and Security — with the Safety and Security chapter applying only to providers of models with SYSTEMIC RISK. A Signatory Taskforce, convened by the AI Office, holds ongoing meetings with signatories on implementation. institutions.name: Digital Omnibus on AI — Regulation (EU) 2026/1744
institutions.remit: NOT A BODY — included because it changed the legal facts every other EU entry depends on, and because prior knowledge of the AI Act timeline is now wrong. Provisional political agreement was reached between Council and Parliament on 7 May 2026; the regulation was published in the Official Journal and ENTERED INTO FORCE ON 27 JULY 2026. It DEFERS the AI Act's high-risk obligations: stand-alone Annex III high-risk systems move from 2 August 2026 to 2 DECEMBER 2027, and Annex I high-risk systems embedded in regulated products to 2 AUGUST 2028. The deferral is limited to Chapter III and does NOT extend to other obligations — notably the Article 50 transparency obligations, which still applied from 2 August 2026. It did NOT defer the GPAI/systemic-risk regime, which has applied since 2 August 2025. It also expanded the AI Office's powers to supervise GPAI providers and certain very large online platforms.

institutions.reality_check: The single most important 2026 correction for anyone working from earlier knowledge. Two errors are now common: believing the AI Act's high-risk regime went live in August 2026 (it did not — December 2027 and August 2028), and believing the omnibus also delayed the frontier-model rules (it did not — GPAI and systemic-risk obligations have been live since August 2025, and the AI Office's enforcement powers over them since August 2026). Practically: the frontier-AI part of the EU regime is the part that is actually operating, and the consumer-protection part is the part that slipped. Anyone arguing about EU AI enforcement should check which of the two they mean.
