Practical problem: as of March 2026 only 8 of 27 Member States had notified a single point of contact, so identifying the correct national authority is genuinely difficult in most of the EU. Where you cannot identify one, use the Commission's AI Act complaints tool instead and ask for referral.

institutions.reality_check: Legally real and newly in force, but immature. The absence of designated authorities in most Member States means enforcement capacity lags the right. Parliamentary research flags 'uneven enforcement' as a structural risk of the decentralised model. Best used as a formal, citable act that creates a record and can be escalated or publicised — not as a fast route to action.
institutions.accepts: Complaints from 'any natural or legal person' with grounds to consider there has been an infringement of the AI Act. No standing requirement, no need to be personally harmed, no institutional affiliation required. Applies without prejudice to other administrative or judicial remedies.
institutions.does_not_accept: Matters outside the AI Act. It is a complaint right, not a right to a remedy — the Act does not give the complainant a personal entitlement to redress, damages or a specific outcome.
institutions.how: Submit to the market surveillance authority of your Member State. The authority must take complaints into account under Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 and handle them under its established procedures. Practical problem: as of March 2026 only 8 of 27 Member States had notified a single point of contact, so identifying the correct national authority is genuinely difficult in most of the EU. Where you cannot identify one, use the Commission's AI Act complaints tool instead and ask for referral.
institutions.format: No prescribed EU-wide format. In practice: identify the AI system, the provider/deployer, the specific AI Act provision you say is breached, the country where it occurred, and attach evidence.
institutions.after: The authority considers the complaint as part of its market surveillance activities and may open an investigation. There is no guaranteed individual response or published outcome under Article 85 itself.
institutions.operator: National market surveillance authorities of EU Member States; coordinated by the European AI Board and Commission AI Office

institutions.name: EU AI Act complaints tool (AI Office)
institutions.remit: Complaints from individuals and organisations about alleged AI Act infringements falling within the exclusive competence of the AI Office, under Article 85. All official EU languages. Supporting detail and a stated country of incident are required.

routes.label: Submission page
routes.scope: Complaints from individuals and organisations about alleged AI Act infringements falling within the exclusive competence of the AI Office, under Article 85. All official EU languages. Supporting detail and a stated country of incident are required.
routes.note: Web form at ai-act-complaints.integrityline.app, reached from the Commission's AI Act complaints tool page. State the country, describe the alleged infringement in detail, identify yourself.

institutions.reality_check: This is the single most usable EU route for an unaffiliated person, because it solves the 'which national authority?' problem: you file centrally and the AI Office refers onward with your consent. It is brand new, so there is no outcome track record. The non-anonymity requirement is a real constraint for anyone with an employment relationship to the target — use the whistleblower tool instead in that case.
institutions.accepts: Complaints from individuals and organisations about alleged AI Act infringements falling within the exclusive competence of the AI Office, under Article 85. All official EU languages. Supporting detail and a stated country of incident are required.
institutions.does_not_accept: Infringements outside the AI Act's scope; breaches of other EU or national law; matters under Articles 53–55 (GPAI model obligations from downstream providers, which have a separate channel); and matters covered by Article 89(2). Submissions are NOT anonymous — complainant identification is required.
institutions.how: Web form at ai-act-complaints.integrityline.app, reached from the Commission's AI Act complaints tool page. State the country, describe the alleged infringement in detail, identify yourself.
institutions.format: Structured online form, any official EU language, with attachments.
institutions.timing: Rolling. The Commission page was last updated 31 July 2026.
institutions.after: The AI Office treats complaints confidentially and will notify you if your complaint falls outside its jurisdiction. With your prior consent it may refer the complaint on to national market surveillance authorities or fundamental rights enforcement bodies.
institutions.operator: European Commission — AI Office / DG CNECT; hosted on EQS Integrity Line

institutions.name: EU AI Act Whistleblower Tool (AI Office)
institutions.remit: Reports of harmful practices or other AI Act violations, from 'individuals who are professionally connected to providers of general-purpose AI (GPAI) models or of AI systems' within the AI Office's enforcement scope. Supporting documents may be attached.

routes.label: Submission page
routes.scope: Reports of harmful practices or other AI Act violations, from 'individuals who are professionally connected to providers of general-purpose AI (GPAI) models or of AI systems' within the AI Office's enforcement scope. Supporting documents may be attached.
routes.note: Anonymous submission via the hosted portal, available in all EU languages. You receive a secure inbox so you can track progress and answer follow-up questions while remaining anonymous. The AI Office states it maintains a high standard of confidentiality with documented internal procedures to maximise protection of reporter identity.

institutions.reality_check: Strong on mechanics — genuine anonymity with two-way follow-up is rare and is exactly what the Right to Warn signatories asked for. Legally reinforced by AI Act Article 87, which applies the EU Whistleblower Directive (EU) 2019/1937 to AI Act infringement reporting from 2 August 2026, giving confidentiality and anti-retaliation protection. No outcome data yet; the AI Office's enforcement capacity is unproven.
institutions.accepts: Reports of harmful practices or other AI Act violations, from 'individuals who are professionally connected to providers of general-purpose AI (GPAI) models or of AI systems' within the AI Office's enforcement scope. Supporting documents may be attached.
institutions.does_not_accept: Matters outside the AI Office's enforcement remit. Note the professional-connection framing: this is an insider channel, not a general public complaint route (use the complaints tool for that).
institutions.how: Anonymous submission via the hosted portal, available in all EU languages. You receive a secure inbox so you can track progress and answer follow-up questions while remaining anonymous. The AI Office states it maintains a high standard of confidentiality with documented internal procedures to maximise protection of reporter identity.
institutions.format: Structured online form plus free text and attachments.
institutions.after: The report enters AI Office handling; the whistleblower monitors progress and receives communications through the secure inbox.
institutions.operator: European Commission — AI Office; hosted on EQS Integrity Line (ai-act-whistleblower.integrityline.app)

institutions.name: EU AI Act Article 73 — serious incident reporting
institutions.remit: Serious incidents as defined in Article 3(49), reported by the provider. Deadlines: immediately after establishing a causal link and in any case not later than 15 days after awareness; 2 days for widespread infringement or certain serious incidents; and for a death, immediately after establishing or suspecting a causal relationship and within 10 days maximum. Incomplete initial reports are permitted, followed by a complete report.

routes.label: Submission page
routes.scope: Serious incidents as defined in Article 3(49), reported by the provider. Deadlines: immediately after establishing a causal link and in any case not later than 15 days after awareness; 2 days for widespread infringement or certain serious incidents; and for a death, immediately after establishing or suspecting a causal relationship and within 10 days maximum. Incomplete initial reports are permitted, followed by a complete report.
routes.note: Indirect only, and this is the practically important point: a member of the public cannot trigger Article 73 directly, but can (a) notify the provider, which starts the provider's own awareness clock and creates evidence of when they knew, and (b) file an Article 85 complaint with the market surveillance authority alleging a serious incident went unreported — failure to report is itself an infringement the authority can act on.

institutions.reality_check: Real legal force but a closed circuit for outsiders. The leverage for an ordinary person is asymmetric and underused: putting a provider on written notice of a serious incident converts their silence into a reportable regulatory breach. That is a stronger move than the complaint itself.
institutions.accepts: Serious incidents as defined in Article 3(49), reported by the provider. Deadlines: immediately after establishing a causal link and in any case not later than 15 days after awareness; 2 days for widespread infringement or certain serious incidents; and for a death, immediately after establishing or suspecting a causal relationship and within 10 days maximum. Incomplete initial reports are permitted, followed by a complete report.
institutions.does_not_accept: Reports from members of the public. The duty sits on providers and deployers only. A member of the public cannot file an Article 73 report and cannot directly compel one.
institutions.how: Indirect only, and this is the practically important point: a member of the public cannot trigger Article 73 directly, but can (a) notify the provider, which starts the provider's own awareness clock and creates evidence of when they knew, and (b) file an Article 85 complaint with the market surveillance authority alleging a serious incident went unreported — failure to report is itself an infringement the authority can act on.
institutions.format: Commission draft guidance and a reporting template were consulted on (responses due 7 November 2025) ahead of the August 2026 application date.
institutions.timing: Obligations for high-risk AI apply from 2 August 2026.
institutions.after: National competent authorities immediately notify the Commission.
institutions.operator: Providers (and in some cases deployers) of high-risk AI systems, reporting to national market surveillance authorities; Commission draft guidance and template consulted in late 2025

institutions.name: EU AI Act Article 87 — protection of persons reporting infringements
institutions.remit: Reports of AI Act infringements by workers in the broad sense covered by the Whistleblower Directive.

routes.label: Submission page
routes.scope: Reports of AI Act infringements by workers in the broad sense covered by the Whistleblower Directive.
routes.note: Its single operative sentence: 'Directive (EU) 2019/1937 shall apply to the reporting of infringements of this Regulation and the protection of persons reporting such infringements.' In practice this means internal channels first, then the competent national authority, with external/public disclosure protected in defined circumstances. The AI Office's whistleblower tool is the EU-level external channel.

institutions.reality_check: This is the most substantive statutory AI whistleblower protection in force anywhere as of September 2026 — notably stronger than the US position, where the federal AI Whistleblower Protection Act remains stuck in committee. Its weakness is that it covers AI Act infringements, not 'AI is dangerous' concerns that break no specific provision.
institutions.accepts: Reports of AI Act infringements by workers in the broad sense covered by the Whistleblower Directive.
institutions.does_not_accept: Does not create a new standalone AI whistleblower regime; it imports the existing Directive wholesale.
institutions.how: Its single operative sentence: 'Directive (EU) 2019/1937 shall apply to the reporting of infringements of this Regulation and the protection of persons reporting such infringements.' In practice this means internal channels first, then the competent national authority, with external/public disclosure protected in defined circumstances. The AI Office's whistleblower tool is the EU-level external channel.
institutions.format: As per national implementations of the Directive.
institutions.after: Confidentiality safeguards and anti-retaliation protection apply; remedies are pursued under national implementing law.
institutions.operator: European Commission / Member States, applying Directive (EU) 2019/1937

institutions.name: EU AI Act Service Desk
institutions.remit: Questions about AI Act interpretation and compliance; routes users to the complaints tool and whistleblower tool.

routes.label: Submission page
routes.scope: Questions about AI Act interpretation and compliance; routes users to the complaints tool and whistleblower tool.
routes.note: Browse the AI Act Explorer, Compliance Checker, guidelines and templates; contact the AI Office at CNECT-AIOFFICE@ec.europa.eu; or follow the links to the complaint and whistleblower tools. Available in English, Spanish, German, French, Italian and Polish.

institutions.reality_check: Useful as the authoritative starting point for anyone trying to work out which EU route applies to their concern, and as the canonical index of open AI Act consultations. Not itself a lever.
institutions.accepts: Questions about AI Act interpretation and compliance; routes users to the complaints tool and whistleblower tool.
institutions.does_not_accept: It is a help desk and resource hub, not an enforcement intake in its own right.
institutions.how: Browse the AI Act Explorer, Compliance Checker, guidelines and templates; contact the AI Office at CNECT-AIOFFICE@ec.europa.eu; or follow the links to the complaint and whistleblower tools. Available in English, Spanish, German, French, Italian and Polish.
institutions.format: Web resources and email.
institutions.timing: Rolling; hosts periodic public consultations on implementation topics.
institutions.after: Response from the AI Office, or referral to the appropriate tool.
institutions.operator: European Commission (AI Office / DG CNECT)

institutions.name: GDPR Article 77 — complaint to a data protection supervisory authority
institutions.remit: Complaints from any data subject who considers that processing of their personal data infringes the GDPR. You may complain to the authority in your Member State of habitual residence, your place of work, or the place of the alleged infringement.

routes.label: Submission page
routes.scope: Complaints from any data subject who considers that processing of their personal data infringes the GDPR. You may complain to the authority in your Member State of habitual residence, your place of work, or the place of the alleged infringement.
routes.note: File with the chosen supervisory authority, usually via their online form. Frame the concern in data protection terms — lawful basis, accuracy, transparency, Article 22 automated decision-making — because a concern framed as 'this AI is unsafe' will be rejected as out of scope, while the same facts framed as a data protection issue may be entertained.

institutions.reality_check: The most battle-tested adjacent route, with a real enforcement record against AI systems (the Italian Garante's ChatGPT actions being the best-known). Its power is the duty to inform you of progress and outcome — a stronger procedural guarantee than Article 85 of the AI Act gives. Its limit is that it only bites where personal data is involved.
institutions.accepts: Complaints from any data subject who considers that processing of their personal data infringes the GDPR. You may complain to the authority in your Member State of habitual residence, your place of work, or the place of the alleged infringement.
institutions.does_not_accept: Concerns that do not involve processing of personal data. This is the key limit for AI safety work: it reaches training data, inference on personal data, profiling, automated decision-making and accuracy of personal data, but not model capability, misuse potential or catastrophic risk.
institutions.how: File with the chosen supervisory authority, usually via their online form. Frame the concern in data protection terms — lawful basis, accuracy, transparency, Article 22 automated decision-making — because a concern framed as 'this AI is unsafe' will be rejected as out of scope, while the same facts framed as a data protection issue may be entertained.
institutions.format: Authority-specific form; identify the controller, the processing, the provision breached, and the effect on you.
institutions.after: The supervisory authority must inform the complainant of the progress and outcome of the complaint, and of the possibility of a judicial remedy under Article 78. Without prejudice to other remedies.
institutions.operator: National data protection authorities (EU/EEA); ICO in the UK

institutions.name: UK ICO data protection complaint
institutions.remit: Complaints about how an organisation has handled your personal information. General customer service complaints only if combined with a data protection concern.

routes.label: Submission page
routes.scope: Complaints about how an organisation has handled your personal information. General customer service complaints only if combined with a data protection concern.
routes.note: Raise it with the organisation first and give them a chance to put things right, then complain via ico.org.uk/make-a-complaint. Expect the ICO to ask what the organisation said.

institutions.reality_check: Be realistic: the modal outcome is that your complaint is logged as intelligence. Its value is cumulative and systemic — the ICO acts on patterns, so a well-evidenced complaint contributes to a case file even when your individual outcome is nil. Do not expect personal redress.
institutions.accepts: Complaints about how an organisation has handled your personal information. General customer service complaints only if combined with a data protection concern.
institutions.does_not_accept: Non-data-protection grievances. The ICO does not award compensation or obtain individual redress — outcomes are regulatory, not remedial. Compensation requires a court claim.
institutions.how: Raise it with the organisation first and give them a chance to put things right, then complain via ico.org.uk/make-a-complaint. Expect the ICO to ask what the organisation said.
institutions.format: Online form; concise factual narrative plus the organisation's response.
institutions.timing: Rolling. Where you ask the ICO to review how it handled your complaint, a reviewing officer writes to you within 30 calendar days.
institutions.after: Outcomes range from recording the complaint for intelligence purposes, to confirming the organisation complied, to asking the organisation to improve practice, to regulatory action in appropriate cases. Most complaints end at the first two.
institutions.operator: Information Commissioner's Office

institutions.name: Ofcom — individual complaint about an online service
institutions.remit: Complaints about phone, broadband and postal services; TV, radio and on-demand programmes; wireless interference; something you have seen on an online service, website or app; and premium rate services.

routes.label: Submission page
routes.scope: Complaints about phone, broadband and postal services; TV, radio and on-demand programmes; wireless interference; something you have seen on an online service, website or app; and premium rate services.
routes.note: Contact the service provider first, then report via Ofcom's online complaints portal at ofcom.org.uk/make-a-complaint.

institutions.reality_check: Explicitly symbolic at the individual level — Ofcom says so. It is a data point in a monitoring dataset. The mechanism with actual teeth is the super-complaint, which individuals cannot use.
institutions.accepts: Complaints about phone, broadband and postal services; TV, radio and on-demand programmes; wireless interference; something you have seen on an online service, website or app; and premium rate services.
institutions.does_not_accept: Ofcom cannot investigate individual cases or mandate removal of specific content. It will not resolve your dispute with a platform.
institutions.how: Contact the service provider first, then report via Ofcom's online complaints portal at ofcom.org.uk/make-a-complaint.
institutions.format: Online form.
institutions.after: Reports feed Ofcom's monitoring and evidence base for Online Safety Act supervision and enforcement against systemic failures.
institutions.operator: Ofcom

institutions.name: Ofcom Online Safety super-complaints
institutions.remit: Complaints from eligible entities about a feature or conduct of one or more regulated services presenting a material risk of significant harm, of significant adverse impact on freedom of expression, or other significant adverse impacts. For a single-service complaint you must additionally explain its particular importance or the scale of user impact.

routes.label: Submission page
routes.scope: Complaints from eligible entities about a feature or conduct of one or more regulated services presenting a material risk of significant harm, of significant adverse impact on freedom of expression, or other significant adverse impacts. For a single-service complaint you must additionally explain its particular importance or the scale of user impact.
routes.note: Written submission to Ofcom with organisational contact details, description of the feature or conduct, identification of the services/providers, and evidence of material risk. Supporting evidence must be current, objective and verifiable. An unaffiliated individual's realistic route is to supply evidence to an eligible organisation rather than to file directly.

institutions.reality_check: This is the UK's real lever on platform-level AI harms, with binding response timescales — a sharp contrast to individual complaints, which Ofcom will not investigate. The whole design assumes intermediation by civil society. For a playbook, the actionable instruction is: package your evidence to Ofcom's stated standard (current, objective, verifiable) and hand it to an eligible body.
institutions.accepts: Complaints from eligible entities about a feature or conduct of one or more regulated services presenting a material risk of significant harm, of significant adverse impact on freedom of expression, or other significant adverse impacts. For a single-service complaint you must additionally explain its particular importance or the scale of user impact.
institutions.does_not_accept: Individuals cannot bring super-complaints. The entity must represent the interests of users, the public or a specific group; be independent of regulated services; be a significant expert contributor to public online safety discussion; and have regard to Ofcom's guidance.
institutions.how: Written submission to Ofcom with organisational contact details, description of the feature or conduct, identification of the services/providers, and evidence of material risk. Supporting evidence must be current, objective and verifiable. An unaffiliated individual's realistic route is to supply evidence to an eligible organisation rather than to file directly.
institutions.format: Written submission per Ofcom's super-complaints guidance; evidence-led.
institutions.after: Ofcom decides eligibility within 30 days of a completed submission, and responds to an admissible complaint usually within 90 days (extendable if further information is needed).
institutions.operator: Ofcom, under the Online Safety Act 2023

institutions.name: US FTC — ReportFraud.ftc.gov
institutions.remit: Reports of fraud, scams and bad business practices — which covers AI-related deception: false capability claims, deceptive AI marketing, undisclosed AI use, AI-enabled impersonation. The FTC has brought AI-deception cases under its Section 5 unfair-or-deceptive-practices authority.

routes.label: Submission page
routes.scope: Reports of fraud, scams and bad business practices — which covers AI-related deception: false capability claims, deceptive AI marketing, undisclosed AI use, AI-enabled impersonation. The FTC has brought AI-deception cases under its Section 5 unfair-or-deceptive-practices authority.
routes.note: Online at reportfraud.ftc.gov. Note: at the time of this research the site was returning a government shutdown notice and was unable to offer the reporting service, directing users to consumer.ftc.gov instead — verify availability before relying on it. An alternative framing for AI-safety-adjacent harms is a complaint to a State Attorney General.

institutions.reality_check: Purely aggregate. A single report is a statistic. Its real utility is when many reports converge on one practice, or when a report accompanies a documented, novel AI deception pattern that the FTC has signalled interest in. Do not present an FTC report as equivalent to a regulatory complaint with a duty to respond.
institutions.accepts: Reports of fraud, scams and bad business practices — which covers AI-related deception: false capability claims, deceptive AI marketing, undisclosed AI use, AI-enabled impersonation. The FTC has brought AI-deception cases under its Section 5 unfair-or-deceptive-practices authority.
institutions.does_not_accept: The FTC does not resolve individual complaints and will not obtain redress for you in the ordinary case. Reports feed the Consumer Sentinel Network, a law enforcement intelligence database shared with federal, state and international enforcers.
institutions.how: Online at reportfraud.ftc.gov. Note: at the time of this research the site was returning a government shutdown notice and was unable to offer the reporting service, directing users to consumer.ftc.gov instead — verify availability before relying on it. An alternative framing for AI-safety-adjacent harms is a complaint to a State Attorney General.
institutions.format: Structured web form: what happened, who, when, amounts, documents.
institutions.timing: Rolling (subject to the availability issue above).
institutions.after: Data enters Consumer Sentinel and is used to spot patterns and build cases. No individual case is opened and you get no case outcome.
institutions.operator: Federal Trade Commission

institutions.name: California Attorney General — consumer complaint
institutions.jurisdiction: California (reaches most major AI developers, which are California-domiciled)
institutions.remit: Complaints about businesses, including AI companies. The AG investigates where complaints suggest patterns of consumer harm or systematic violations of consumer protection law.

routes.label: Submission page
routes.scope: Complaints about businesses, including AI companies. The AG investigates where complaints suggest patterns of consumer harm or systematic violations of consumer protection law.
routes.note: Online web form at oag.ca.gov, or download, print and mail the form. Forms available in English, Spanish, Chinese and Vietnamese. Provide your contact details, the business's details, the product/service, transaction dates, names of representatives, your desired resolution, and evidence of prior contact attempts with the business.

institutions.reality_check: Worth more than its bureaucratic appearance because of jurisdiction: California's AG has direct reach over OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta, and California has become the lead US AI regulator via SB 53. A well-documented complaint alleging a pattern lands in the office with both the authority and the demonstrated appetite to act. Still: no individual remedy, no guaranteed response.
institutions.accepts: Complaints about businesses, including AI companies. The AG investigates where complaints suggest patterns of consumer harm or systematic violations of consumer protection law.
institutions.does_not_accept: The form is explicit: 'The Attorney General cannot provide you with legal advice or represent you in personal legal actions' and 'cannot act as my personal lawyer.' It will not adjudicate your individual dispute.
institutions.how: Online web form at oag.ca.gov, or download, print and mail the form. Forms available in English, Spanish, Chinese and Vietnamese. Provide your contact details, the business's details, the product/service, transaction dates, names of representatives, your desired resolution, and evidence of prior contact attempts with the business.
institutions.format: Structured form; up to 5 supporting documents, max 50MB each, PDF/DOC.
institutions.after: Review; possible investigation if a pattern emerges; possible referral to a more appropriate agency.
institutions.operator: California Department of Justice, Office of the Attorney General

institutions.name: UK select committee written evidence
institutions.remit: Evidence drawn from research, professional expertise or personal experience. You explicitly do not need to be a formal expert or have any institutional affiliation. Address the questions in the call for evidence; you need not answer all of them.

routes.label: Submission page
routes.scope: Evidence drawn from research, professional expertise or personal experience. You explicitly do not need to be a formal expert or have any institutional affiliation. Address the questions in the call for evidence; you need not answer all of them.
routes.note: Find an inquiry currently accepting evidence via the committees portal filter (committees.parliament.uk/inquiries/ with 'Currently accepting evidence'), then submit through that inquiry's online portal. At the time of this research 27 inquiries were accepting evidence and none was specifically AI-focused — but AI-relevant evidence is regularly submitted to inquiries on employment, financial services, human rights and public services, and recent AI inquiries (Business and Trade Committee on AI and the future workforce; Treasury Committee on AI in financial services; JCHR on human rights and AI regulation) show the pattern.

institutions.reality_check: The highest-value consultation route available to an unaffiliated individual, and the clearest counterexample to 'petitions are pointless.' Evidence is published under your name, is permanently citable, is read by clerks and specialist advisers, and is routinely quoted in reports that government must respond to. Two privacy options exist: anonymity (published without your name — 'provides some protection but is not failsafe') and confidentiality (informs members privately, neither name nor contribution published — described by Parliament as 'the safest way' if you fear identification).
institutions.accepts: Evidence drawn from research, professional expertise or personal experience. You explicitly do not need to be a formal expert or have any institutional affiliation. Address the questions in the call for evidence; you need not answer all of them.
institutions.does_not_accept: Evidence about active court proceedings; individual complaints or personal grievances (you are told to contact your MP instead); previously published material — submissions must be original and created specifically for the committee; defamatory statements likely to harm reputations; personal data you would not want made public. House of Lords committees require you to declare substantial AI-generated content.
institutions.how: Find an inquiry currently accepting evidence via the committees portal filter (committees.parliament.uk/inquiries/ with 'Currently accepting evidence'), then submit through that inquiry's online portal. At the time of this research 27 inquiries were accepting evidence and none was specifically AI-focused — but AI-relevant evidence is regularly submitted to inquiries on employment, financial services, human rights and public services, and recent AI inquiries (Business and Trade Committee on AI and the future workforce; Treasury Committee on AI in financial services; JCHR on human rights and AI regulation) show the pattern.
institutions.format: Single editable file (Word, ODT or RTF), max 25MB. No PDFs, no logos, no decorative graphics, no repeated headers/footers. Usually no more than 3,000 words. Numbered paragraphs and section headings. Plain language with technical terms explained. Cite published sources with links.
institutions.timing: Hard deadlines set per inquiry, typically 4–10 weeks from launch. Check the specific inquiry page.
institutions.after: The committee decides whether to accept and publish. Published evidence becomes part of the permanent parliamentary record and remains publicly accessible indefinitely; you cannot request changes or removal afterwards. Do not self-publish until the committee authorises it. Submissions may be quoted and cited in the committee's report. You are responsible for accuracy — deliberately misleading a committee is a contempt of Parliament.
institutions.operator: House of Commons and House of Lords select committees, UK Parliament

institutions.name: UK Parliament — find an inquiry accepting written evidence
institutions.remit: N/A — this is the discovery tool.

routes.scope: N/A — this is the discovery tool.
routes.note: Filter the inquiries list with 'Currently accepting evidence' set to true. Each result shows 'Written evidence: Accepting' and the deadline. This is the correct first step before drafting anything, because evidence must respond to a live call.

institutions.reality_check: Essential plumbing. The most common failure mode for outside contributors is writing a submission with no open inquiry to send it to.
institutions.accepts: N/A — this is the discovery tool.
institutions.does_not_accept: N/A

institutions.name: US federal rulemaking comments — Regulations.gov
institutions.remit: Comments from anyone, including non-US persons, on proposed rules, requests for information and requests for comment. No affiliation required.

routes.label: Submission page
routes.scope: Comments from anyone, including non-US persons, on proposed rules, requests for information and requests for comment. No affiliation required.
routes.note: Search the docket number on regulations.gov, click 'Comment Now!', complete the fields and attach or type your comment. Live AI-relevant examples at the time of this research: NIST-2026-0100 (Modernizing the National Vulnerability Database in the Age of AI, comments due 13 October 2026) and NIST-2025-0035 (Security Considerations for AI Agents, closed 9 March 2026 with 937 comments).

institutions.reality_check: Genuinely high-leverage and widely underrated for an unaffiliated person, precisely because of the legal duty to respond to significant comments — no other consultation mechanism in this list carries an enforceable response obligation. A single well-evidenced technical comment on a low-volume AI docket can shape a final rule. A form letter does nothing.
institutions.accepts: Comments from anyone, including non-US persons, on proposed rules, requests for information and requests for comment. No affiliation required.
institutions.does_not_accept: It is not a vote. Identical mass comments carry no extra weight: 'multiple identical comments are not likely to be more persuasive than if the comment had been sent only once,' and the number of comments for or against does not determine whether a rule proceeds.
institutions.how: Search the docket number on regulations.gov, click 'Comment Now!', complete the fields and attach or type your comment. Live AI-relevant examples at the time of this research: NIST-2026-0100 (Modernizing the National Vulnerability Database in the Age of AI, comments due 13 October 2026) and NIST-2025-0035 (Security Considerations for AI Agents, closed 9 March 2026 with 937 comments).
institutions.format: No length limit, but substance over volume. What works: explain concretely how the policy would affect a specific situation, supply reasoning and evidence, or offer a perspective the agency has not previously considered. What fails: bare statements of support or opposition. Agencies invite 'concrete examples, best practices, case studies, and actionable recommendations.'
institutions.timing: Typically a 30–60 day window after a proposed rule is issued; the deadline is stated in the preamble of each notice. RFIs vary.
institutions.after: Comments are posted publicly on the docket. Agencies must respond to significant, relevant comments when publishing a final rule, and may explain how comments changed the rule. Inadequate response to significant comments is a ground for legal challenge.
institutions.operator: eRulemaking Program (US federal government); individual agencies own each docket

institutions.name: UK Parliament e-petitions
institutions.remit: Petitions from British citizens and UK residents that ask for a clear action from the UK Government or Parliament on a matter within their responsibility.

routes.label: Submission page
routes.scope: Petitions from British citizens and UK residents that ask for a clear action from the UK Government or Parliament on a matter within their responsibility.
routes.note: Draft the petition, secure 5 supporters, submit for standards review, and if approved it is published and open for signatures for 6 months.

institutions.reality_check: Largely symbolic, and should be labelled as such. The 10,000 threshold buys a departmental form response drafted to restate existing policy; the 100,000 threshold buys, at best, a sparsely-attended Westminster Hall debate that binds nobody. It is not remotely equivalent to written evidence to a select committee, which is published under your name, permanently citable and quoted in reports the Government must formally answer. Use petitions for public attention and media hooks, not for influence.
institutions.accepts: Petitions from British citizens and UK residents that ask for a clear action from the UK Government or Parliament on a matter within their responsibility.
institutions.does_not_accept: Local council matters; anything not calling for a clear action; petitions failing the standards check. Only petitions created on petition.parliament.uk qualify — petitions hosted elsewhere (Change.org, 38 Degrees) receive no government response and no committee consideration whatsoever.
institutions.how: Draft the petition, secure 5 supporters, submit for standards review, and if approved it is published and open for signatures for 6 months.
institutions.format: A short, single, clearly-actionable request.
institutions.after: At 10,000 signatures the Government publishes a written response. At 100,000 the petition is considered for a Westminster Hall debate — the Petitions Committee retains discretion and may decline if the topic was recently debated or is already scheduled.
institutions.operator: UK Government and Parliament, overseen by the Commons Petitions Committee

institutions.name: California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act) — whistleblower protections and public incident reporting
institutions.remit: Two distinct things. (1) Whistleblower protection: employees and contractors of frontier developers are protected against retaliation for reporting activity connected to catastrophic risks — defined around foreseeable risks of a frontier model causing death or serious injury to 50+ people, enabling weapons creation, engaging in criminal conduct without meaningful human intervention, or evading developer control. Employers must give notice of these rights and maintain anonymous internal reporting channels. (2) Developer reporting: frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to OES within 15 days of discovery, or 24 hours where there is imminent danger of death or serious injury.

routes.label: Submission page
routes.scope: Two distinct things. (1) Whistleblower protection: employees and contractors of frontier developers are protected against retaliation for reporting activity connected to catastrophic risks — defined around foreseeable risks of a frontier model causing death or serious injury to 50+ people, enabling weapons creation, engaging in criminal conduct without meaningful human intervention, or evading developer control. Employers must give notice of these rights and maintain anonymous internal reporting channels. (2) Developer reporting: frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to OES within 15 days of discovery, or 24 hours where there is imminent danger of death or serious injury.
routes.note: Employees: use the employer's mandated anonymous internal channel, and take legal advice before external disclosure. Critically for this playbook: SB 53 requires OES to establish a mechanism for the public to report critical safety incidents — meaning a member of the public, not just an insider, has a statutory route to a state emergency agency. Verify the current status and URL of that OES mechanism directly with OES before relying on it; implementation detail was not published in the sources reviewed.

institutions.reality_check: The most concrete AI-specific whistleblower protection actually in force in the United States, and materially more than the federal position. Two honest caveats: the catastrophic-risk threshold is high and excludes most real concerns, and the public reporting mechanism's practical operation is unproven. It applies only to large frontier developers, though that captures most of the companies that matter.

institutions.does_not_accept: Concerns below the catastrophic-risk threshold are outside the protected category. Ordinary product-safety, bias or misuse concerns are not covered by the whistleblower provisions.

institutions.after: Incidents go to OES; whistleblower retaliation claims are pursued under the statute.

institutions.name: Government Accountability Project
institutions.remit: People who have discovered illegality, gross mismanagement or waste of funds, or threats to health and safety in their employment. Focus is on widespread, systemic issues affecting the public interest.

routes.label: Submission page
routes.scope: People who have discovered illegality, gross mismanagement or waste of funds, or threats to health and safety in their employment. Focus is on widespread, systemic issues affecting the public interest.
routes.note: Complete the intake form at intake.whistleblower.org. Reviewed by staff, with a response typically within about a month. Important: contacting them does not create legal representation and does not toll any statute of limitations — you bear responsibility for your own filing deadlines, which range from 30 days to three years depending on claim type, and GAP will not alert you to them during the application process.

institutions.reality_check: The most established US whistleblower legal organisation, with decades of litigation record and demonstrated willingness to fight identity subpoenas. The deadline warning is the single most important operational fact for anyone in this position: waiting for GAP's one-month review can itself blow a 30-day filing window. Take that as an instruction to identify your deadlines independently and immediately.
institutions.accepts: People who have discovered illegality, gross mismanagement or waste of funds, or threats to health and safety in their employment. Focus is on widespread, systemic issues affecting the public interest.
institutions.does_not_accept: Explicitly: small-scale issues lacking broad public concern; Section 8 housing fraud; EEOC employment discrimination claims; benefit denial cases unless whistleblower-related; scam victim cases.
institutions.how: Complete the intake form at intake.whistleblower.org. Reviewed by staff, with a response typically within about a month. Important: contacting them does not create legal representation and does not toll any statute of limitations — you bear responsibility for your own filing deadlines, which range from 30 days to three years depending on claim type, and GAP will not alert you to them during the application process.
institutions.format: Online intake application.
institutions.timing: Rolling; roughly one month to a response. Your legal deadlines run regardless.
institutions.after: Possible representation. Services at a 'greatly reduced public interest rate'; pro bono for those unemployed and without resources until reemployment; litigation costs assessed on financial capacity and typically recoverable on a win or settlement. Communications are attorney-client privileged, and GAP has successfully resisted subpoenas seeking whistleblower identities in federal court.
institutions.operator: Government Accountability Project (US nonprofit legal organisation)

institutions.jurisdiction: United States; covers publicly traded companies and securities-law violations
institutions.remit: Original information about potential violations of the federal securities laws. institutions.reality_check: The only route in this entire list that pays the whistleblower substantial money and has a long, documented record of doing so. The critical mechanic: you may submit anonymously, but only if you are represented by an attorney who provides their contact information — anonymity and award eligibility both depend on having counsel. Requires reframing an AI safety concern as an investor-disclosure concern, which is a genuine constraint but often achievable where a company has made public safety claims.
institutions.accepts: Original information about potential violations of the federal securities laws. institutions.name: UK Public Interest Disclosure Act — protected disclosure to a prescribed person
institutions.remit: Qualifying disclosures by workers, in the public interest, to a prescribed person with responsibility for the relevant subject matter — giving statutory protection against detriment and dismissal.

routes.label: Submission page

routes.note: Identify the correct prescribed person for the subject matter and disclose to them. Relevant to AI: the Public Interest Disclosure (Prescribed Persons) (Amendment) Order 2026 (SI 2026/478), in force 2 June 2026, added the Secretary of State for Science, Innovation and Technology as a prescribed person — the first explicitly AI/digital-policy route — and expanded the scope for existing regulators including Ofcom and the FCA. The ICO remains prescribed for data protection matters.

institutions.reality_check: Meaningful but reactive: PIDA does not stop retaliation, it gives you a claim after it happens. The 2026 addition of DSIT is a genuine and underpublicised development, creating for the first time a UK prescribed route for technology-policy disclosures. Take legal advice on which prescribed person covers your concern before disclosing — getting this wrong forfeits the protection.
institutions.accepts: Qualifying disclosures by workers, in the public interest, to a prescribed person with responsibility for the relevant subject matter — giving statutory protection against detriment and dismissal.
institutions.does_not_accept: Disclosures to a body that is not prescribed for that subject matter do not attract the same protection. This is the most common and most costly error.

institutions.name: 'The perils of AI safety's insularity' — why outside contributions get ignored
institutions.remit: N/A

routes.label: Submission page
routes.note: N/A — read as diagnosis. Its claims: AI safety has built a parallel research universe outside academia that trades external scrutiny for speed; the network is geographically and financially concentrated (Berkeley/San Francisco, EA-aligned funders); researchers do not meaningfully engage with mainstream ML venues and consequently reinvent existing methods; funding shapes research direction more than consensus does; and there is a reported lower publication bar for optimistic than for critical claims about AI. It cites work arguing 'scheming' research risks repeating failures ape-language researchers made 50 years ago, and Dan Hendrycks calling mechanistic interpretability misguided.

institutions.reality_check: Include this in the playbook as the honest counterweight. It explains structurally why a good submission from an unaffiliated person often lands nowhere: the field's absorption mechanisms are social and network-based, not procedural. The practical implication is that formal mechanisms with published duties — select committee evidence, regulations.gov comments, regulatory complaints, a permanent AIID record — are more reliable for an outsider than trying to be heard inside the field, because they do not depend on already being known.

Owns the FTC (consumer protection, unfair/deceptive AI practices), NIST and the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), NTIA, NSF, NOAA, the FCC, interstate commerce generally, and commercial data privacy. Send here: general-purpose/frontier AI regulation, AI safety testing and evaluation mandates, federal preemption of state AI laws, AI transparency and disclosure rules, chatbots and minors, deepfakes/NCII, AI standards, commercial data privacy, autonomous vehicles, and AI in telecom. committees_and_bodies.parent: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: NIST, CAISI, NSF and the standards/measurement side of AI. Send here: AI evaluation science and benchmarks, AI standards development, the National AI Research Resource, AI workforce and education, AI in manufacturing, and US-vs-China AI competitiveness framing. If your concern is 'who measures whether a model is safe', this is the authorizing subcommittee (the money is in Appropriations CJS).
committees_and_bodies.business: VERIFIED: 3 Mar 2026 subcommittee hearing chaired by Sen. Budd evaluating innovative deployment of AI to support workforce, healthcare and industry (commerce.senate.gov/2026/3/senator-budd-chairs-subcommittee-hearing-to-evaluate-innovative-deployment-of-ai-to-support-workforce-healthcare-and-industry). Full-committee hearing 'Measuring What Matters: Science, Standards, and Strategic Competition' (21 Jul 2026) covers the same NIST/standards terrain.

committees_and_bodies.body: Senate Committee on the Judiciary
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: Rights, remedies and law enforcement. Send here: whether AI companies can be sued (duty of care, product liability, Section 230), AI and copyright/right of publicity, AI-generated CSAM and deepfakes as crimes, DOJ and FBI use of AI, antitrust in AI and cloud/compute markets, AI and immigration adjudication, and constitutional/civil-liberties questions. This is the liability door; Commerce is the regulation door.
committees_and_bodies.business: VERIFIED: S.2937 AI LEAD Act (Durbin/Hawley, introduced 29 Sep 2025) — first federal AI duty-of-care/product-liability bill, referred to this committee. S.1367 NO FAKES Act of 2026 (Coons) — digital replicas/voice and likeness — referred here and now on the Senate Legislative Calendar. Hearing 'Examining the Harm of AI Chatbots' (S.Hrg. 119-256, 16 Sep 2025, Crime and Counterterrorism Subcommittee). Hearing 'The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly: AI-Generated Deepfakes in 2025' (S.Hrg. 119-171). Prior series 'Oversight of AI' including 'Oversight of AI: Insiders' Perspectives'.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: VERIFIED: no /contact page exists on judiciary.senate.gov. Routes are the chair's and ranking member's own Senate offices (Grassley: 202-224-3744; Durbin: 202-224-2152) and the committee's published rules at https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/about/committee/rules. Committee main line 202-224-5225 (Dirksen 224).
committees_and_bodies.note: Chair/ranking verified 2026-09-22 against senate.gov committee_memberships_SSJU.htm.

committees_and_bodies.body: Subcommittee on Privacy, Technology, and the Law
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: The named AI-oversight subcommittee of Senate Judiciary and the venue that produced the 2023-2024 'Oversight of AI' hearing series. Send here: AI and civil liberties, government and corporate surveillance, biometric and facial recognition, AI transparency and audit obligations framed as a legal duty, and whistleblower accounts from inside AI labs. Distinct from Commerce's consumer subcommittee: this one frames AI as a rights-and-rule-of-law problem rather than a marketplace problem.
committees_and_bodies.business: VERIFIED: this subcommittee ran the 'Oversight of AI' hearing series including 'Oversight of AI: Rules for Artificial Intelligence' and 'Oversight of AI: Insiders' Perspectives' (whistleblower testimony from former frontier-lab staff). 2026 work centers on a federal privacy framework and AI data use. Note: the Sept 2025 'Examining the Harm of AI Chatbots' hearing was held by the Crime and Counterterrorism Subcommittee (Hawley), not this one — chatbot-harm work has partly migrated there.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: Through full-committee routes and the two members' own offices (Blackburn 202-224-3344; Klobuchar 202-224-3244).
committees_and_bodies.note: Chair/ranking verified 2026-09-22 from senate.gov SSJU subcommittee roster. Blackburn chairs both this subcommittee and Senate Commerce's consumer/tech subcommittee — a single office is the pivot for much Senate AI work.

committees_and_bodies.body: Subcommittee on Intellectual Property
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: AI training data and copyright, licensing of creative works for model training, patentability of AI-assisted inventions, digital replicas and voice/likeness rights. If you are an author, musician, performer, visual artist or publisher whose work was used in training data, this is your door in the Senate.
committees_and_bodies.business: VERIFIED: S.1367 NO FAKES Act of 2026 (Coons, with Tillis, Blackburn and Klobuchar) is the central vehicle — referred to Senate Judiciary 9 Apr 2025 and since placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar (Calendar No. 446), making it one of the few AI bills past committee in the Senate.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: Full-committee routes plus the members' own offices (Tillis 202-224-6342; Schiff 202-224-3841).
committees_and_bodies.note: Verified 2026-09-22 from senate.gov SSJU subcommittee roster.

committees_and_bodies.body: Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: Criminal misuse of AI and, in the 119th Congress, the de facto venue for AI chatbot harms to children and vulnerable users. Also AI-enabled fraud and impersonation, AI-generated CSAM, and AI in terrorism and bioweapon uplift framed as a criminal matter.
committees_and_bodies.business: VERIFIED: hearing 'Examining the Harm of AI Chatbots' (S.Hrg. 119-256, 16 Sep 2025), at which Durbin previewed the AI LEAD Act; S.2937 AI LEAD Act introduced 29 Sep 2025 by Durbin and Hawley. Hawley is also lead sponsor of S.2938 Artificial Intelligence Risk Evaluation Act of 2025 (referred to Commerce, not here).
committees_and_bodies.public_route: Full-committee routes; Hawley 202-224-6154, Durbin 202-224-2152. Hawley's office has actively solicited accounts from families harmed by AI chatbots.
committees_and_bodies.note: Verified 2026-09-22 from senate.gov SSJU subcommittee roster. Worth knowing because the FLI guide points chatbot-harm concerns at the Privacy/Technology subcommittee, but the actual 119th Congress hearing and bill came out of this one.

committees_and_bodies.body: Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: How the federal government itself buys, builds and uses AI, plus DHS and CISA. Send here: federal AI procurement rules and contract terms, agency Chief AI Officers, AI risk management inside agencies, AI in federal benefits and enforcement decisions, government use of AI for surveillance or content moderation, GSA and OMB AI policy, federal AI workforce, and AI threats to critical infrastructure on the DHS side. NOT the place for rules on private-sector AI products.
committees_and_bodies.business: VERIFIED: S.3410 (Kim, D-NJ) to establish federal agency technology and AI talent teams — referred here. Peters is the committee's long-running AI-in-government legislator; his PREPARED for AI Act (risk-based federal AI procurement, Chief AI Officers, high-risk contract terms) was reported by this committee in the 118th Congress as S.4495 and remains the template for 119th Congress procurement work. Chairman Paul's AI emphasis is the opposite direction — restricting government use of AI for surveillance and speech moderation. UNVERIFIED: no specific 2026 full-committee AI hearing title confirmed; the committee's 2026 AI-adjacent activity is mostly bill referrals and oversight letters.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: VERIFIED contact page https://www.hsgac.senate.gov/contact (also /about/contact/). Committee: 340 Dirksen, Washington DC 20510, 202-224-4751. The committee also runs a whistleblower/tips intake — HSGAC and its Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations actively accept documents and allegations from the public, including from non-constituents, which makes it an unusually real door for someone with inside information about federal AI misuse.
committees_and_bodies.note: Chair/ranking verified 2026-09-22 against senate.gov committee_memberships_SSGA.htm. The chair holds unilateral subpoena authority in this committee, which is why oversight requests land here.

committees_and_bodies.body: Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations
committees_and_bodies.parent: Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: The Senate's standing investigative body, with subpoena power. Not an AI-jurisdiction subcommittee by name, but the correct destination for evidence-backed allegations about an AI company's conduct, federal AI contracting abuse, or AI-enabled fraud schemes. If you have documents rather than an opinion, this is the door.
committees_and_bodies.business: UNVERIFIED for AI-specific 2025-2026 investigations. Blumenthal, as ranking member here, is co-sponsor of S.2938 Artificial Intelligence Risk Evaluation Act and a co-author of the bipartisan AI framework work with Hawley.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: Via HSGAC contact page https://www.hsgac.senate.gov/contact and the subcommittee's majority/minority staff. PSI accepts information from the public and from whistleblowers regardless of state of residence.
committees_and_bodies.note: Leadership verified 2026-09-22 from senate.gov SSGA roster.

committees_and_bodies.body: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: Export controls and financial-sector AI. This committee owns the Export Control Reform Act and the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security — so every question about AI chip export controls, location verification on advanced chips, and smuggling to China lands here, not in Foreign Relations. Also: AI in credit decisions, underwriting, insurance and fraud detection, algorithmic discrimination in lending, AI and financial stability, and CFIUS review of AI investments.
committees_and_bodies.business: VERIFIED: S.1705 Chip Security Act (Cotton) referred here 8 May 2025 and still pending; its House companion H.R.3447 (Huizenga) was ordered reported by House Foreign Affairs 42-0 on 26 Mar 2026 and, on reaching the Senate, was referred to this committee — so this committee is the chokepoint for AI chip export legislation. Hearing 'AI and the American Dream: Promoting Innovation, Affordability, and American Dominance' (June 2026), chaired by Scott, focused on affordability, innovation and national security. 8 Jun 2026: Warren letter pressing Chairman Scott to hold an additional AI hearing with senior administration officials on data-center costs borne by ratepayers.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: VERIFIED contact page https://www.banking.senate.gov/contact. Committee: 534 Dirksen, Washington DC 20510; majority 202-224-7391, minority 202-224-5842 (numbers listed on the contact page).
committees_and_bodies.note: Chair/ranking verified 2026-09-22 against senate.gov committee_memberships_SSBK.htm. The export-control jurisdiction here is the single most commonly misrouted AI issue in Congress.

committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: The export-control workbench within Banking: BIS authorities and resourcing, entity-list designations, chip and semiconductor-tooling controls, outbound investment screening, and sanctions touching AI supply chains.
committees_and_bodies.business: UNVERIFIED for AI-specific 2026 subcommittee hearings; the Chip Security Act (S.1705) work is being handled at full-committee level.

committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: Newly created in the 119th Congress. Relevant to AI where AI agents transact — autonomous agents holding or moving assets, AI-driven trading, AI-enabled financial fraud, and identity/authentication for machine actors.
committees_and_bodies.business: UNVERIFIED for AI-specific activity; included because it is the Senate counterpart to the House Financial Services subcommittee that has 'Artificial Intelligence' in its name.

committees_and_bodies.body: Senate Committee on Armed Services
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: Military AI and, through the NDAA, the one must-pass annual vehicle that reliably carries AI policy. Send here: autonomous weapons, AI in nuclear command and control, DoD AI adoption and the Chief Digital and AI Office, DARPA, military AI testing and evaluation, AI-enabled cyber operations, and DoD compute and data-center buildout. Also covers the nuclear weapons parts of the Department of Energy.
committees_and_bodies.business: VERIFIED: the FY2026 NDAA carried a substantial set of AI and cyber provisions (see CRS In Focus IF13197, 'Cyber and Artificial Intelligence Provisions in the FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act'), and House and Senate AI provisions went to conference in late 2025. The Senate NDAA process has also been the vehicle for tightening AI chip export controls. FY2027 NDAA work ran through 2026.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: VERIFIED: https://www.armed-services.senate.gov/contact and, unusually helpful, a published staff directory at https://www.armed-services.senate.gov/about/committee-staff — this committee names its professional staff members, so a member of the public can address the staffer who actually handles emerging technology. Committee: 228 Russell, 202-224-3871.

committees_and_bodies.body: Subcommittee on Cybersecurity
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: AI-enabled offensive and defensive cyber operations, CYBERCOM, AI model security and adversarial attacks on defense systems, and the security of AI supply chains inside DoD.
committees_and_bodies.business: VERIFIED by association: Rounds is co-chair of the Senate AI Caucus and one of the four authors of the Senate's bipartisan AI roadmap, making this subcommittee chair a principal Senate Republican AI interlocutor.

committees_and_bodies.body: Subcommittee on Emerging Threats and Capabilities
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: DARPA, DoD science and technology accounts, special operations, and emerging-technology threat assessment — including AI-enabled bio and chemical threats, and frontier-model capability risks framed as national security.

committees_and_bodies.body: Senate Committee on Foreign Relations
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: AI diplomacy, not AI regulation. Send here: international AI governance bodies and treaties, State Department AI policy and the Bureau of Cyberspace and Digital Policy, AI provisions in bilateral technology agreements, AI and human rights abroad, foreign assistance involving AI, and confirmation of relevant ambassadors and State officials. Note that the statutory export-control authority sits in Banking, not here — Foreign Relations gets the diplomacy and the sanctions framing.
committees_and_bodies.business: UNVERIFIED for a named 2026 AI hearing. The committee's AI-relevant work in the 119th Congress has run through nominations, China technology-competition oversight, and its Subcommittee on East Asia, the Pacific, and International Cybersecurity Policy.

committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: China AI competition, allied coordination on AI and semiconductor controls, international cyber norms and their extension to AI, and AI in the Indo-Pacific.
committees_and_bodies.business: UNVERIFIED for a named 2026 AI hearing. Coons is separately the lead sponsor of S.1367 NO FAKES Act, so his office engages AI issues in both committees.

committees_and_bodies.body: Senate Select Committee on Intelligence
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: Intelligence Community use of AI and AI as an intelligence target. Send here: IC adoption of frontier models, AI in signals and open-source intelligence, foreign adversary AI capabilities assessments, AI-enabled foreign influence operations, and counterintelligence risk to US AI labs (including insider threat and foreign talent access). Proceedings are largely classified, so the public route is narrow and mostly one-way.
committees_and_bodies.business: VERIFIED by referral: Cotton is lead sponsor of S.1705 Chip Security Act (referred to Banking). The committee's AI work is carried in the annual Intelligence Authorization Act. UNVERIFIED for open 2026 AI hearing titles — most sessions are closed.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: VERIFIED: https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/about-the-committee/contact/. Committee: 211 Hart, Washington DC 20510, 202-224-1700. This committee also operates the statutory Intelligence Community whistleblower channel, which is the realistic route for someone with classified or contractor-side AI concerns.
committees_and_bodies.note: Chair verified 2026-09-22 against senate.gov committee_memberships_SLIN.htm; the minority leader of this committee holds the title Vice Chairman, not Ranking Member.

committees_and_bodies.body: Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: The power behind AI. Send here: data-center electricity demand and who pays for it, grid interconnection queues, DOE national laboratories as AI compute and evaluation venues, DOE AI programs, nuclear and geothermal siting for AI loads, and ratepayer protection when utilities serve hyperscale data centers. This has become one of the busiest AI-adjacent committees because energy is the binding constraint on AI buildout.
committees_and_bodies.business: VERIFIED: the committee has held hearings on AI data centers and electricity demand (C-SPAN program record 662912). March 2026: Ranking Member Heinrich published an energy-affordability agenda tied to data-center load growth. September 2026: legislation to curb AI data-center utility costs stalled in the Senate (CNBC, 17 Sep 2026). Heinrich is also co-chair of the Senate AI Caucus, so this committee's ranking member is a principal Senate AI actor. Separately, Heinrich, Whitehouse and Van Hollen sent March 2026 letters to AI companies about gas-powered data centers through the Environment and Public Works Committee.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: VERIFIED: https://www.energy.senate.gov/contact and a help page at https://www.energy.senate.gov/help. Committee: 304 Dirksen, Washington DC 20510, 202-224-4971.

committees_and_bodies.body: Subcommittee on Energy
committees_and_bodies.parent: Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: DOE programs, the national laboratories, grid reliability and electricity markets — the subcommittee-level venue for data-center load growth, transmission, and DOE's role in AI compute and model evaluation.
committees_and_bodies.business: UNVERIFIED for a named 2026 subcommittee AI hearing; AI-and-energy work has largely been at full committee.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: Full-committee contact page https://www.energy.senate.gov/contact.
committees_and_bodies.note: Leadership verified 2026-09-22 from senate.gov SSEG subcommittee roster. Note S.2938 would site an advanced-AI risk evaluation program at DOE, which would put frontier-model testing into this subcommittee's orbit.

committees_and_bodies.body: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: AI where it touches work, health and school. Send here: AI and job displacement, worker surveillance and algorithmic management, AI in hiring and employment discrimination (with EEOC), FDA regulation of AI medical devices and clinical decision support, AI in drug development, AI in K-12 and higher education, and AI literacy. If your concern is 'my employer is using AI on me' or 'an AI tool is making medical decisions', this is the door.
committees_and_bodies.business: VERIFIED: Cassidy released a committee white paper on artificial intelligence (https://www.help.senate.gov/help-committee-gop-final-ai-white-paper) covering AI in health care, education, labor and the FDA, and solicited stakeholder responses — an explicit, documented public-comment opportunity. Hearing 'The Impact of AI on the Workforce' (https://www.help.senate.gov/hearings/the-impact-of-ai-on-the-workforce). Sanders as ranking member has made AI-driven job displacement and a shorter work week a signature theme.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: VERIFIED: there is no committee-wide /contact page. Published routes are the chair's and ranking member's own Senate offices — Cassidy at https://www.cassidy.senate.gov/contact and Sanders press at https://www.sanders.senate.gov/contact/press-inquiries/. Committee: 428 Dirksen, Washington DC 20510, 202-224-5375.
committees_and_bodies.note: Chair/ranking verified 2026-09-22 against senate.gov committee_memberships_SSHR.htm.

committees_and_bodies.body: Senate Committee on Appropriations
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: Money, and therefore the real leverage over AI agencies. Appropriations bills carry both funding levels and policy riders for NIST/CAISI, NSF, DOE labs, DHS/CISA, DoD AI programs and the FTC. Also the only committee in Congress that formally invites written testimony from the general public every year.
committees_and_bodies.business: VERIFIED: the committee accepted public written testimony for FY2027, with the Commerce, Justice, Science subcommittee deadline of 22 May 2026. Subcommittee markup of the FY2027 Commerce, Justice, Science and Related Agencies Appropriations Act held in 2026.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: VERIFIED: the /contact page is retired (returns HTTP 410). Working routes: committee office S-128, The Capitol, Washington DC 20510, 202-224-7257, and the FAQ page https://www.appropriations.senate.gov/about/faqs. Hearings are open to the public subject to space.

committees_and_bodies.body: Subcommittee on Commerce, Justice, Science, and Related Agencies
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: THE subcommittee that funds NIST and, within it, the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI, the former US AI Safety Institute). Also funds NSF (including the National AI Research Resource), NASA, NOAA, DOJ and the FTC. If your concern is whether the US government has the capacity to evaluate frontier models at all, the number that decides it is written here.
committees_and_bodies.business: VERIFIED: subcommittee markup of the FY2027 Commerce, Justice, Science and Related Agencies Appropriations Act held in 2026; public written testimony for FY2027 accepted through 22 May 2026. See CRS report R48929, 'Overview of FY2027 Appropriations for Commerce, Justice, Science, and Related Agencies (CJS)', for the NIST and NSF lines.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: Committee office S-128, The Capitol, 202-224-7257; subcommittee guidance is posted annually on the subcommittee page.
committees_and_bodies.note: Leadership verified 2026-09-22 from senate.gov SSAP subcommittee roster. This is the answer to the brief's question about 'the subcommittee funding NIST/CAISI' on the Senate side.

committees_and_bodies.body: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: The broadest authorizing jurisdiction in the House and the main House counterpart to Senate Commerce. Owns the FTC, FCC, NTIA, interstate commerce, consumer protection, telecommunications, electricity and the grid, and health (FDA/HHS). Send here: comprehensive federal AI legislation and preemption of state AI laws, commercial data privacy, AI consumer protection and deceptive practices, AI and kids, AI's electricity demand and ratepayer impact, AI in health care, and communications infrastructure for AI.
committees_and_bodies.business: VERIFIED: 'AI Regulation and the Future of US Leadership' (Commerce, Manufacturing and Trade Subcommittee, 21 May 2025, 2322 Rayburn). 'Seizing America's AI Opportunity' (CMT Subcommittee). 'AI and the Grid: Meeting Growing Power Demand While Protecting Ratepayers' (Energy Subcommittee). Communications and Technology Subcommittee hearing on network infrastructure demands for AI and AI in media and entertainment; a separate C&T hearing on AI and communications infrastructure. CMT hearing on AI in American manufacturing, 3 Jun 2026 (docket HHRG-119-IF17-20260603). The committee was also the House locus of the 2025 fight over a federal moratorium on state AI laws.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: VERIFIED: https://energycommerce.house.gov/contact-us. Committee: 2125 Rayburn House Office Building, Washington DC 20515, 202-225-3641; press 202-226-4972. Minority site: https://democrats-energycommerce.house.gov/ (separate Democratic staff and contact).

committees_and_bodies.body: House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: Non-defense federal R&D. Owns NIST (and therefore CAISI), NSF, OSTP, NASA, and the civilian side of DOE including the national labs. Send here: AI standards and measurement science, AI testing and evaluation methods, AI safety research funding, the National AI Research Resource, AI workforce and education, AI incident and flaw reporting, and federal AI R&D coordination. In the 119th Congress this committee has produced more reported AI legislation than any other House committee.

Send here: AI standards, model evaluation methodology, AI safety and security research, AI flaw and incident reporting, AI education and workforce, and oversight of the federal AI Action Plan.

Erin Houchin, released the ~270-page bipartisan 'Great American AI Act' discussion draft — codifying CAISI at $100M/year through FY2029, frontier-developer critical-safety-incident reporting, AI testbeds at DOE/NIST/NSF, codification of NAIRR, and preemption of most state frontier-AI regulation.

committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: Courts, DOJ, FBI, copyright and patent law, antitrust, immigration, and constitutional questions. committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: DHS, CISA, TSA and DHS Science and Technology. committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: CISA's authorities and budget; AI-enabled offensive cyber operations against US critical infrastructure; securing AI systems and model supply chains; automated vulnerability discovery; and the cyber-information-sharing framework as applied to AI incidents.

committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: The dedicated AI-and-emerging-technology subcommittee of HASC. Send here: DoD AI adoption and CDAO oversight, military cyber operations, defense software acquisition reform, AI test and evaluation inside DoD, and commercial AI companies' defense contracts.

committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: The House counterpart to Senate HSGAC: how the federal government itself uses AI. committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: The House door for AI export controls and AI diplomacy. committees_and_bodies.body: Congressional Artificial Intelligence Caucus
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: Not a jurisdictional body — no bills are referred here and it cannot hold official hearings or markups. Its function is member education and cross-committee coordination: briefings for members and staff, sign-on letters, and building bipartisan support before a bill reaches a committee of jurisdiction. Useful to a member of the public as a way to reach AI-attentive offices in bulk, and as a signal of who is engaged.

Eshoo's site (artificialintelligencecaucus-eshoo.house.gov), which is now legacy.

committees_and_bodies.body: Senate Artificial Intelligence Caucus
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: Bipartisan member-education and coordination body founded in 2019. No referral jurisdiction. Its value is that its two co-chairs sit on the committees that matter — Heinrich is ranking member of Energy and Natural Resources and sits on Intelligence; Rounds chairs Armed Services' Cybersecurity subcommittee and sits on Banking — so the caucus functions as a bridge between the energy, defense and financial AI conversations.

Heinrich, Schumer, Rounds and Young were the four authors of the Senate's bipartisan AI policy roadmap. Heinrich, Young, Rounds and Booker reintroduced legislation to expand access to AI research (the CREATE AI / NAIRR line of work) in the 119th Congress. Rounds and Heinrich introduced legislation on AI for pandemic preparedness and response.

Rounds' office (https://www.rounds.senate.gov/, 202-224-5842). Rounds publishes his caucus memberships at https://www.rounds.senate.gov/issues/caucus-membership. Membership is senators only.

committees_and_bodies.body: House Bipartisan Task Force on Artificial Intelligence
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: A leadership-appointed, time-limited body — not a committee — created by Speaker Mike Johnson and Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries in February 2024 and co-chaired by Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Ted Lieu (D-CA). It produced a comprehensive final report in December 2024 that remains the House's closest thing to a shared AI framework, organized by sector rather than by committee.
committees_and_bodies.business: VERIFIED: final report delivered December 2024 (118th Congress). NOT VERIFIED AS RECONSTITUTED IN THE 119th CONGRESS — no official announcement of a re-established task force was found as of 22 Sep 2026, and the 16 Sep 2026 bipartisan letter from Beyer, Obernolte, Lieu and seven others urging House leaders to act on AI is itself evidence that members are pressing leadership for renewed structured action. The live successor vehicle is the bipartisan 'Great American AI Act' discussion draft released 4 Jun 2026 by Trahan, Obernolte and Houchin.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: The task force has no standing office. Reach the former co-chairs: Obernolte at https://obernolte.house.gov/ (202-225-5861) and Lieu at https://lieu.house.gov/ (202-225-3976). For substantive AI policy input right now, the open channel is GAAIA@mail.house.gov, the public feedback address for the Great American AI Act draft.
