committees_and_bodies.body: European Commission — European AI Office (within DG CNECT)
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: The EU's central AI regulator and the enforcement body for the AI Act's rules on general-purpose AI models. Three functions: (1) AI Act implementation and enforcement, including 'developing tools, methodologies and benchmarks for evaluating capabilities' of GPAI models and investigating possible violations; (2) fostering trustworthy AI, including sandboxes and real-world testing; (3) international AI governance coordination. Over 125 staff across 6 units plus 2 adviser posts.

chair.role: Head of the AI Office — not named on the official AI Office page as at this check

committees_and_bodies.key_people: Governance bodies that carry outside voices into the AI Office: the AI Board (Member State representatives); the Scientific Panel of independent experts; the Advisory Forum, which is explicitly designed for balanced stakeholder representation including civil society; the AI Pact for business; and the Apply AI Alliance.
committees_and_bodies.business: GPAI model oversight, AI Act guidelines (including on high-risk classification and transparency obligations), the Code of Practice process, and implementation of the changes made by the Digital Omnibus on AI.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: Four concrete routes: (1) general enquiries to CNECT-AIOFFICE@ec.europa.eu; (2) the AI Act Service Desk for regulatory questions; (3) the Expression of Interest form for collaboration, which is how outside experts get onto drafting and consultation groups; (4) respond to AI Office consultations on draft guidelines, which are announced on the Shaping Europe's Digital Future consultations page. The Advisory Forum is the formal civil-society seat.
committees_and_bodies.format_rules: Consultations on draft AI Act guidelines are typically 4–8 weeks and run through structured online questionnaires. Responses may be published. Recent examples VERIFIED on the consultations page: 'Targeted consultation on the draft guidelines for the classification of high-risk artificial intelligence systems' (19 May – 23 July 2026); 'Consultation on the draft guidelines on transparency obligations under the AI Act' (8 May – 3 June 2026); 'European Commission survey: AI in healthcare and pharmaceuticals' (2 – 26 June 2026). All three have closed; the page is the live index to whatever is open now.

committees_and_bodies.body: European Commission — 'Have your say' consultation portal
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: The single entry point for public input to every EU legislative initiative before it is proposed, including all AI initiatives. Each initiative passes through a 'call for evidence' stage and often a full public consultation, both open to comment.

chair.role: Not applicable — administered by the Commission's Secretariat-General

committees_and_bodies.business: AI-related initiatives that have used the portal include 'Artificial intelligence strategy for the cultural and creative sectors' (initiative 18592) and the Apply AI Strategy consultation. Open/closed status changes constantly — the portal's own search is the only reliable source.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: Anyone in the world may register an EU Login account and submit feedback on any published initiative. This is the least gatekept formal channel in the entire EU system: no residency, nationality, or organisational requirement.
committees_and_bodies.format_rules: Feedback is limited to 4,000 characters plus an attachment (normally one document up to 1MB). Calls for evidence typically run 4 weeks; full public consultations 12 weeks. Feedback is PUBLISHED on the initiative's feedback page with your name, your organisation and your country; organisations must supply an EU Transparency Register number. Anonymity can be requested.

committees_and_bodies.body: Members of the European Parliament — direct correspondence
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: Every MEP can table amendments, ask written questions of the Commission (which must be answered and are published), sign motions, and speak in committee. On AI, a single MEP's written question can force the Commission to state a position on the record.

chair.role: 720 MEPs

committees_and_bodies.key_people: For AI specifically: Michael McNamara (Renew, IE), Brando Benifei (S&D, IT), Arba Kokalari (EPP, SE), Reinier van Lanschot (Greens/EFA, NL), plus the four committee chairs listed separately.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: Find MEPs at the MEP directory, which searches by member name and by country. Each MEP's individual page publishes their Brussels and Strasbourg office addresses, phone numbers and email. CRUCIAL POINT FOR OUTSIDERS: MEPs are elected from multi-member constituencies (often the whole country) under proportional representation, so you have many MEPs, not one. There is no constituency-service convention equivalent to the UK's — MEPs routinely accept and act on correspondence from people who are not their voters, including from other Member States and from outside the EU, and they are not obliged to refuse it. In practice the group and the committee portfolio matter far more than geography: write to the MEP who holds the AI file, whatever country they represent. Parliament also runs a general citizens' enquiry service ('Ask EP') for questions about the EU and Parliament's work.
committees_and_bodies.format_rules: No limits. Correspondence is not published. Replies are at the MEP's discretion; a specific, short, evidenced request to a policy adviser gets a far higher response rate than a mass-campaign email.
committees_and_bodies.note: VERIFIED 2026-09-22: the MEP directory and the 'Write to us' / Ask EP form are both live official European Parliament pages. The statement that MEPs generally accept non-constituent correspondence reflects the structure of EU elections (no single-member constituencies) rather than a written rule I could cite.

committees_and_bodies.body: House of Commons Standing Committee on Industry and Technology (INDU)
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: The lead Commons committee for AI. Industry, science, technology, telecommunications, competition and innovation policy. It was the committee that studied Bill C-27 (which contained the Artificial Intelligence and Data Act) clause by clause, and it is now running a dedicated AI study.

chair.name: Ben Carr, MP (Liberal, Winnipeg South Centre, Manitoba)
chair.role: Chair

committees_and_bodies.key_people: Vice-Chairs: Raquel Dancho (Conservative, Kildonan—St. Paul) and Gabriel Ste-Marie (Bloc Québécois, Joliette—Manawan). Members: Parm Bains, Karim Bardeesy, Doly Begum, Adam Chambers (CPC), Harb Gill (CPC), Jason Groleau (CPC), Leslyn Lewis (CPC), Michael Ma, Bienvenu-Olivier Ntumba, Dominique O'Rourke.
committees_and_bodies.business: Four active studies as at 22 Sep 2026, including 'Opportunities, Risks, and Regulation of AI in Canada's Strategic Industries'. The others: Financial Fraud and Scams in Canada; Federal Government's Electric Vehicle Policies; U.S. Tariffs and the Canadian Metallurgical Sector.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: Submit a brief. Canada's brief system is the most open of the five jurisdictions here: 'Any individual or organization may submit a brief to a committee of the House of Commons, even if they are not given the opportunity to appear.' You do not need an invitation and you do not need to be Canadian. Send it to the committee clerk by email or through the online form; contact details are on the committee page.
committees_and_bodies.format_rules: EXACT RULES: a brief should not exceed 10 pages. If longer, you must include a summary of no more than 500 words, which the committee may translate and distribute INSTEAD of the full document — so the 500-word summary is the part that actually gets read. May be submitted in either official language; the clerk coordinates translation, so submit early. Identify the author/organisation clearly on the cover; put your personal contact details in the covering email, NOT on the cover page. Support claims with concise factual information; put specific, summarised recommendations at the end; cite all quoted material in footnotes or a bibliography; visuals in black and white and preferably bilingual. Briefs become part of the committee's public archives, may be posted on the committee website, and submitters are listed in committee reports.
committees_and_bodies.note: VERIFIED 2026-09-22 from the INDU committee page and the official 'Guide for submitting briefs to House of Commons Committees' at ourcommons.ca/procedure/guides/brief-e.html.

committees_and_bodies.body: House of Commons Standing Committee on Access to Information, Privacy and Ethics (ETHI)
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: Privacy, data protection and ethics oversight — the committee that handles algorithmic and automated decision-making from a rights and privacy angle, facial recognition, and government use of AI tools. The natural home for AI-and-privacy work now that AIDA is dead and the privacy half of Bill C-27 has been reintroduced separately.

chair.name: John Brassard, MP (Conservative, Barrie South—Innisfil, Ontario)
chair.role: Chair

committees_and_bodies.key_people: Vice-Chairs: Linda Lapointe (Liberal, Rivière-des-Mille-Îles) and Luc Thériault (Bloc Québécois, Montcalm).
committees_and_bodies.business: Statutory Review of the Lobbying Act; a study on the connection between the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and Alto; Main Estimates 2026-27. No AI-titled study was active as at this check.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: Same brief system as INDU — any individual or organisation may submit, unsolicited, at any time.
committees_and_bodies.format_rules: Max 10 pages, or a 500-word summary if longer; either official language; published on the committee website and listed in reports.
committees_and_bodies.note: VERIFIED 2026-09-22 from the ETHI committee page. Note the chair is an opposition (Conservative) MP — ETHI is one of the committees chaired by the Official Opposition under Canadian practice.

committees_and_bodies.body: House of Commons of Canada — committee brief submission system (the public route)
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: The mechanism, not a body. Every Commons standing, special and legislative committee accepts briefs from the public on any study it is conducting.

chair.role: Administered by each committee's clerk

committees_and_bodies.public_route: Go to the committee's page, find the active study, and send a brief to the clerk by email or the online form. No invitation is needed. This is genuinely underused: most Canadian committee studies receive a small number of briefs, so a well-made one is disproportionately likely to be quoted in the report. You may also ask to appear as a witness — the request is made to the clerk in the same email.
committees_and_bodies.format_rules: Maximum 10 pages. Longer briefs require a summary of no more than 500 words, and the committee may translate and circulate only that summary. English or French; the clerk arranges translation, and members will not receive the brief until it exists in both languages — so submit well before the study's hearings end. Author identified on the cover, personal contact details in the email only. Briefs become public archives, may be published online, and authors are listed in the committee's report.
committees_and_bodies.note: VERIFIED 2026-09-22 against the official procedural guide at ourcommons.ca/procedure/guides/brief-e.html.

committees_and_bodies.body: Government of Canada — Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: Canada's dedicated AI portfolio. Owns the national AI strategy and the federal government's response to the collapse of AI legislation.

chair.name: The Hon. Evan Solomon
chair.role: Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation (also Minister responsible for the Federal Economic Development Agency for Southern Ontario)

committees_and_bodies.business: AIDA'S STATUS AND WHAT REPLACED IT: the Artificial Intelligence and Data Act was Part 3 of Bill C-27 (Digital Charter Implementation Act, 2022). It died on the Order Paper when Parliament was prorogued in January 2025 and was never reintroduced. Canada therefore has NO general AI statute as at September 2026. What replaced it is not a law but a strategy plus targeted bills: 'AI for All', Canada's national AI strategy, launched by Prime Minister Mark Carney on 4 June 2026, built on three pillars (trust, opportunity, sovereignty), targeting a rise in AI adoption from 12% to 60% by 2034 and 250,000 new AI-related jobs over five years. Alongside it: the Protecting Victims Act (introduced December 2025) to prohibit distribution of non-consensual sexual deepfakes, and new legislation tabled in June 2026 on children's data and privacy. Commitments to modernise digital frameworks cover deepfakes and surveillance pricing.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: Write to the minister; respond to Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada consultations; or, more effectively, put the point into an INDU brief where it enters the parliamentary record.
committees_and_bodies.format_rules: Ministerial correspondence is not published and has no set format.
committees_and_bodies.note: VERIFIED 2026-09-22 from the Prime Minister of Canada's official news release of 4 June 2026 launching AI for All, which names Evan Solomon in that portfolio. AIDA's death by prorogation is well established; I did not find any successor AI bill, and I am explicitly NOT claiming one exists.

committees_and_bodies.body: Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: Australia's principal current AI inquiry body, appointed by resolution of BOTH the House of Representatives and the Senate on 20 August 2026. Its terms of reference are unusually broad and are the best single statement of Australian AI policy scope: AI's contribution to resilience, productivity, competitiveness and living standards; spreading benefits to suburbs and regions; AI and robotics in research, new industries and exports (agriculture, resources, health and medical research, advanced manufacturing, financial services, defence industry); rate and barriers to adoption by SMEs and family businesses; sovereign AI capability and its commercialisation, R&D, investment and talent; data sovereignty and narrow domain-specific models trained on Australian data; workforce and skills implications including job creation and displacement and job quality and security; adoption of AI by Commonwealth departments and agencies and the transparency and accountability measures applying to it; THE ADEQUACY OF AUSTRALIA'S EXISTING LAWS AND REGULATORY FRAMEWORKS AS THEY APPLY TO AI AND WHETHER THERE ARE GAPS WARRANTING REFORM; AI's interaction with intellectual property and copyright law including use of Australian creative, cultural and media content in training; risks and harms including fraud and scams, deepfakes and risks to children and vulnerable Australians; national security and cyber security opportunities and foreign interference risks including supply chains and critical infrastructure; and the implications of emerging AI capability for national security and strategic resilience, including the ability of regulators, THE AUSTRALIAN AI SAFETY INSTITUTE and the intelligence and security community to identify and respond to emerging risks.

chair.name: Ms Jo Briskey MP (Australian Labor Party, Maribyrnong, VIC)
chair.role: Chair

committees_and_bodies.key_people: Deputy Chair: Senator the Hon Jonathon Duniam (Liberal Party, TAS). Members: Senator Ross Cadell (Nationals, NSW); Ms Kate Chaney MP (Independent, Curtin WA); Senator Josh Dolega (ALP, TAS); Hon Andrew Hastie MP (Liberal, Canning WA); Ms Zaneta Mascarenhas MP (ALP, Swan WA); Senator David Pocock (Independent, ACT); Senator Tony Sheldon (ALP, NSW); Senator Marielle Smith (ALP, SA); Mr Aaron Violi MP (Liberal, Casey VIC); Hon Tim Watts MP (ALP, Gellibrand VIC). Late submissions are sometimes accepted at the secretariat's discretion — ask. Secretariat: Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence, PO Box 6100, Parliament House, Canberra ACT 2600; phone +61 2 6277 3863; ai.joint@aph.gov.au.
committees_and_bodies.format_rules: The committee's own instruction: 'Given the timeframe for this inquiry, the committee would appreciate submissions to be kept as brief as possible, ideally around 5-6 pages.' It also draws attention to the advice that 'if you are making a submission to a committee, you are responsible for the quality and accuracy of the content of that submission, including where AI tools have been used' — an explicit warning against AI-generated submissions. Submissions are published only after the committee accepts and authorises them; you may not disclose your own submission until then.

committees_and_bodies.body: Parliament of Australia — public submission system (the public route)
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: The mechanism by which any person reaches any Australian parliamentary committee, including all the AI inquiries above.

chair.role: Administered by each committee secretariat

committees_and_bodies.business: Live index of every Senate, House and Joint inquiry currently accepting submissions is maintained at the Submissions_Open pages.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: EXACT PROCESS, from the Parliament's own guidance: 'Any interested individual or organisation can make a submission to a parliamentary committee. Several people or organisations can make a joint submission. Organisations and people from other countries can make submissions to an inquiry' — though parliamentary privilege 'cannot be enforced outside Australia'. Lodge online via the link on the inquiry home page after creating a free My Parliament account (name and valid email only); or send directly by email or post to the committee secretariat. You can upload multiple documents, e.g. a covering letter, a public submission and a confidential attachment. An acknowledgement is emailed on receipt. If you cannot meet the deadline, a short extension is often possible — contact the secretariat.
committees_and_bodies.format_rules: No word limit in general (individual committees may ask for brevity — the Joint Select Committee on AI asked for 5–6 pages). Upload as Word, PDF or plain text. PROCESS AND PUBLICATION: the secretariat assesses the submission, then the COMMITTEE decides whether to accept it and authorise publication, and may publish only part of it. Once authorised, personal details are removed and it is placed on the website and forms part of the formal record. YOUR OBLIGATIONS: 'After a submission is received by a committee, you cannot publish or disclose it to any other person unless or until the committee has authorised its publication' — this is a real constraint, breach of which can be a contempt. You cannot withdraw or alter a submission without the committee's permission. Confidential submissions may not be shared with anyone. If you submit by an organisation, the organisation is published as the author, not an individual.
committees_and_bodies.note: VERIFIED 2026-09-22 by direct fetch of aph.gov.au 'Making a submission to a committee inquiry'. All quoted text is from that page.

committees_and_bodies.body: Department of Industry, Science and Resources — AI policy function, National AI Centre and AI Expert Group
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: The Commonwealth department that owns AI policy: the safe and responsible AI consultation and the Government's interim response, the proposed mandatory guardrails for high-risk AI, the AI Adopt Program, and coordination of Australia's international AI engagement including GPAI. The National Artificial Intelligence Centre, hosted at CSIRO's Data61, 'coordinates Australia's AI expertise and capabilities to address barriers for small and medium enterprises'. A temporary AI Expert Group advised on testing, transparency and accountability for high-risk AI.

committees_and_bodies.business: Government response to the Senate Select Committee on Adopting AI report is published at industry.gov.au/publications. AI Adopt Program; work on high-risk AI guardrails.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: Respond to DISR consultations when open (the department has run a 'safe and responsible AI' consultation with a published interim response). More reliably, put the same material into a submission to the Joint Select Committee on AI, where it enters the parliamentary record and cannot be quietly filed.
committees_and_bodies.format_rules: Departmental consultations set their own rules and usually publish submissions.

committees_and_bodies.body: Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee (54th Parliament)
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: The New Zealand select committee whose subject area covers AI. Its stated remit: 'business development, tourism, Crown minerals, commerce, consumer protection and trading standards, research, science, innovation, intellectual property, broadcasting, communications, and information technology.' AI sits inside 'research, science, innovation' and 'information technology', and AI-and-copyright inside 'intellectual property'. This is New Zealand's default destination for an AI bill, petition or briefing.

chair.name: Dr Parmjeet Parmar, MP (ACT Party, List)
chair.role: Chairperson

committees_and_bodies.key_people: 8 members in total; the full list is on the committee's members page.
committees_and_bodies.business: Bills and items referred by the House plus briefings and petitions. No AI-titled inquiry was listed as open for submissions on 22 Sep 2026.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: Two routes. (1) Make a submission when the committee calls for them on a bill or inquiry — the live list of items open for submissions is on the select committees home page. (2) Petition the House: a petition can be lodged by any person, goes to the Petitions Committee, and is then routinely referred to the relevant subject committee such as this one. Committee secretariat: edsi@parliament.govt.nz.
committees_and_bodies.format_rules: No word limit. You may write in English or in Māori. Submissions can be released by the committee at any time, which makes them public on the Parliament website — this can take a few months. You may ask to make an oral submission in person, by phone or by video conference; remote appearance is explicitly offered to people outside Wellington and to disabled submitters. If the meeting is livestreamed your submission will appear publicly. Advisers read and analyse all submissions and summarise them for the committee in a departmental report, which is also published.
committees_and_bodies.note: VERIFIED 2026-09-22 by direct fetch of the committee's own page on parliament.nz, which names the chairperson and states the subject remit verbatim.

committees_and_bodies.body: Education and Workforce Committee (54th Parliament)
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: Remit: 'education, training, employment, immigration, industrial relations, health and safety, and accident compensation.' This is where AI's labour-market effects land in New Zealand — automation and job displacement, AI in workplaces and workplace surveillance, and AI in education and training. It has produced MPs' reporting on AI and business returns.

committees_and_bodies.format_rules: Same New Zealand rules: no word limit, English or Māori, published by the committee, oral submissions available including remotely.

committees_and_bodies.body: Petitions Committee (54th Parliament)
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: No AI subject matter of its own, but it is the door through which a member of the public — including a single individual — puts a new issue such as AI regulation onto Parliament's agenda when no inquiry is open. It can refer a petition to a subject committee such as Economic Development, Science and Innovation, refer it to a Minister for response, or nominate it for debate in the House.

chair.name: Greg O'Connor, MP (Labour Party, Ōhāriu)
chair.role: Chairperson

committees_and_bodies.key_people: 4 members in total.
committees_and_bodies.business: A rolling caseload — 318 petitions listed in the committee's business index as at 22 September 2026, with new petitions presented that same day.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: Anyone may start a petition to the House of Representatives — there is no signature threshold for presenting one, and petitions with a single signature are accepted. The committee's own advice: 'If you would like to start your own petition, it is strongly recommended that you contact Petitions Committee staff before you begin collecting signatures. The staff will help you with guidance to ensure that your petition meets the rules for form and content.' Secretariat: petitions@parliament.govt.nz. In considering a petition the committee can group similar petitions, refer it to a Minister, refer it to another select committee or consider it jointly, request assistance from the Ombudsman, work with the petitioner to collect more evidence, invite the petitioner to speak in person, and nominate it for a House debate.
committees_and_bodies.format_rules: The committee either publishes a report to Parliament on every petition it considers, or asks a subject committee or a Minister to do so; its report can recommend law or policy changes. Note: 'The committee does not always ask for submissions on the petitions it is considering.' Petitions and reports are published.

committees_and_bodies.body: New Zealand House of Representatives — select committee submission system (the public route)
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: The mechanism for reaching any New Zealand select committee, including on any future AI bill.

chair.role: Administered by the Office of the Clerk

A special Committee of TDs and Senators, the Committee on Public Petitions, will consider your petition. The Committee will publish your petition and may invite you to speak directly to them.' No signature threshold — an individual may petition.
committees_and_bodies.format_rules: Petitions are PUBLISHED by the committee. The petitioner may be invited to address the committee in person. The matter must be one on which the Houses have power to act.
committees_and_bodies.note: VERIFIED 2026-09-22 by direct fetch of the committee's Oireachtas membership page and the Oireachtas 'Making a submission' page, from which the quoted description is taken.

committees_and_bodies.body: Houses of the Oireachtas — committee submission and consultation system (the public route)
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: The mechanism for reaching any Oireachtas committee, including the Joint Committee on Artificial Intelligence and the AI-adjacent committees (Enterprise, Tourism and Employment; Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science; Arts, Media, Communications, Culture and Sport; Justice, Home Affairs and Migration; Finance, Public Expenditure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation, and Taoiseach).

chair.role: Administered by each committee's secretariat

committees_and_bodies.business: Current calls for submissions are indexed on the Oireachtas public consultations page.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: Official wording: 'Committees give people the opportunity to input directly into the work of the Oireachtas, usually by sending a written submission. A Committee may hold a public consultation on a specific matter and issue a call to the public to send submissions relating to it... ANYONE WHO WISHES TO RAISE A MATTER WITH A COMMITTEE MAY WRITE OR SEND A SUBMISSION TO THE COMMITTEE AT ANY TIME.' That last sentence is the important one: unlike the UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand, Ireland does not require an open call for evidence before you can write in. Separately: petition the Oireachtas through the Committee on Public Petitions; and there is a formal remedy, 'Utterances having an adverse effect', if a statement made about you in a committee meeting was not addressed.
committees_and_bodies.format_rules: Follow the Oireachtas guidance note 'Making Witness Submissions and Oral Presentations to Oireachtas Committees'. Submissions accepted by a committee are typically published on the committee's Documents page. Witnesses invited to appear are normally asked to supply a written submission in advance.
committees_and_bodies.note: VERIFIED 2026-09-22 by direct fetch of oireachtas.ie/en/committees/making-a-submission/; all quoted text is from that page.

committees_and_bodies.body: Government of Ireland — Minister of State with the AI brief, Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: The Irish ministerial holder engaging the Oireachtas AI committee. Ireland's AI policy sits in the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment, which is also the department that leads on EU AI Act implementation and the designation of national competent authorities.

chair.name: Niamh Smyth
chair.role: Minister of State at the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment

committees_and_bodies.business: Appearing before the Joint Committee on Artificial Intelligence on 23 September 2026 at 16:30.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: Raise the matter in writing with the Joint Committee on Artificial Intelligence ahead of a ministerial session — committees regularly put constituent-raised points to ministers directly — or contact the Minister through a TD.
committees_and_bodies.format_rules: No formal rules for ministerial correspondence; not published.
committees_and_bodies.note: VERIFIED 2026-09-22 from the Oireachtas AI committee's own scheduling entry, which names her as 'Minister Niamh Smyth, Minister of State at the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment'. I did NOT independently verify the precise title of her delegated AI responsibility on gov.ie, so the exact wording of her AI-specific brief is UNVERIFIED.

committees_and_bodies.body: Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology (Department-Related Parliamentary Standing Committee No. 18)
committees_and_bodies.local_name: संचार और सूचना प्रौद्योगिकी संबंधी स्थायी समिति
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: Oversight of MeitY, Ministry of Communications and Ministry of Information & Broadcasting. Covers AI policy, IndiaAI Mission budgets, IT Rules, deepfakes/AI-generated content, data protection, telecom. It examines Demands for Grants and can self-select AI subjects; it has no power to amend rules, only to report.

chair.name: Nishikant Dubey
chair.role: Chairperson (BJP, Lok Sabha, Godda constituency)

committees_and_bodies.business: 2025-26 committee (31 members: 21 Lok Sabha + 10 Rajya Sabha per current LS practice; PRS lists 28 as 20+8 — the exact count is disputed between sources, see note). Reported in March 2026 on the impact of the emergence of artificial intelligence. Also active on Make in India in electronics (meeting 25 June 2026), fake news/misinformation and telecom. VERIFIED that Dubey chaired as of June 2026 via ANI; committees are normally reconstituted each September, so a 2026-27 reconstitution may have occurred in the days around this date — re-check before citing.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: Two routes. (1) When a committee takes up a subject or a Bill it issues a Press Communiqué through PIB and on sansad.in inviting memoranda from 'individuals, organisations, experts and stakeholders', usually 15-21 days, submitted by post or email to the Committee Branch, Lok Sabha Secretariat. (2) Writing directly to the Chairperson or the Committee's Director/Additional Director at any time. There is no standing online submission portal for DRSCs.
committees_and_bodies.format_rules: None. No signature or supporter threshold. Acceptance of a memorandum is entirely at the Chairperson's discretion, and there is no obligation to acknowledge or publish it.
committees_and_bodies.language: English and Hindi. Submissions accepted in either. No other languages served.
committees_and_bodies.realistic: Partly usable. An ordinary person can post or email a memorandum and it costs nothing, but there is no tracking, no acknowledgement and no publication of unsolicited submissions. Oral evidence invitations go almost exclusively to industry bodies, ministries and a small set of established think tanks. A non-Indian or an unaffiliated individual is very unlikely to be called. The realistic value is written input that may be cited anonymously in a report.
committees_and_bodies.note: Chair verified via ANI reporting (June 2026) and PRS India committee page. The official sansad.in per-committee deep link returns HTTP 500 intermittently; the eParlib composition PDF for 2025-26 is at https://eparlib.sansad.in/bitstream/123456789/3017142/1/18_Communications_and_Information_Technology_25.pdf. Membership counts differ between PRS (28) and Lok Sabha rules (31) — treat as UNVERIFIED on that specific number.

committees_and_bodies.body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)
committees_and_bodies.local_name: इलेक्ट्रॉनिकी और सूचना प्रौद्योगिकी मंत्रालय
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: The primary AI policy ministry. Owns the IndiaAI Mission, the India AI Governance Guidelines (Nov 2025), the IT Act and IT Rules including the 2026 AI-labelling/deepfake amendments, the DPDP Act rules, and the India AI Impact Summit. Any future Indian AI statute will originate here.

chair.name: Ashwini Vaishnaw
chair.role: Union Minister for Electronics and Information Technology (also Railways and Information & Broadcasting). Minister of State: Jitin Prasada. Secretary, MeitY: S. Krishnan.

committees_and_bodies.business: Implementation of the India AI Governance Guidelines (released Nov 2025, foregrounded at the Feb 2026 Summit, 'seven sutras' framework). Operating the AIGEG/TPEC structure constituted 16 April 2026. Draft IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Second Amendment Rules 2026 on AI-generated content labelling — consultation ran 30 March to 29 April 2026 (extended from 14 April); notified thereafter. Reported to be studying a graded, risk-based AI law rather than a single AI Act.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: MeitY does not use a single standing portal. Its actual mechanism is: it publishes a draft plus a one-page 'inviting comments' notice as a PDF under meity.gov.in/documents or /ministry/whats-new, and names a consultation-specific email address. Comments go to that address as .docx or .pdf. Some consultations are additionally mirrored on MyGov (mygov.in) as a 'Discussion' or 'Consultation' with a comment box. Worked example: the Draft IT Amendment Rules 2026 consultation took comments at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in, rule-by-rule, in MS Word or PDF, deadline extended to 29 April 2026.
committees_and_bodies.format_rules: None. Any person or organisation may email comments. India's Pre-Legislative Consultation Policy 2014 notionally requires 30 days, but MeitY has repeatedly used shorter windows and civil society (IFF, SFLC.in) has formally objected.
committees_and_bodies.language: English (Hindi notionally accepted; in practice all drafts and responses are in English).
committees_and_bodies.realistic: Genuinely usable, and one of the easier routes in this list — a single email with a PDF attached is the whole procedure. Two honest caveats: MeitY frequently states that submissions are 'held in fiduciary capacity' and will not be published, so you cannot see what others said or whether you were read; and windows are often short and announced with little notice. Set an alert on meity.gov.in/whats-new rather than expecting to be notified. Note that meity.gov.in is JavaScript-rendered, so its consultation listing does not load for simple scrapers or link-preview tools.
committees_and_bodies.note: Consultation mechanism and the itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in address VERIFIED from the MeitY notice PDF at https://www.meity.gov.in/static/uploads/2026/04/964ca48ac7d0c92e3bba5d32d9a59fcb.pdf and corroborated by SFLC.in. As of 2026-09-22 I could not confirm an open consultation window; the most recent verified one closed 29 April 2026. The /documents/public-consultation landing URL is given as the standing entry point but renders client-side.

committees_and_bodies.body: IndiaAI Mission (IndiaAI Independent Business Division)
committees_and_bodies.local_name: इंडियाAI मिशन
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: Executing agency for India's national AI programme (approx. INR 10,372 crore). Seven pillars including Compute Capacity, Foundation Models, Datasets (AIKosh), Application Development, Future Skills, Startup Financing, and Safe & Trusted AI. Runs the compute tenders, GPU allocation, model-development grants, and the Safe & Trusted AI research portfolio.

chair.name: Saurabh Vijay
chair.role: Chief Executive Officer, IndiaAI Mission (IAS 1998, Maharashtra cadre; concurrently CEO, UIDAI). Chief Operating Officer: Sudeep Shrivastava, Joint Secretary, MeitY.

committees_and_bodies.business: Structured as an Independent Business Division (IBD) of Digital India Corporation, a Section 8 company under MeitY — not a statutory body, which matters: its decisions are corporate/administrative, not subject to parliamentary rule-making scrutiny. As of July 2026, 13 projects approved under the Safe & Trusted AI pillar addressing deepfakes and bias. Nationwide AI skilling programme (target 1 million youth) launched January 2026.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: No formal comment mechanism. Practical routes: (a) respond to its Expressions of Interest and calls for proposals published at indiaai.gov.in — these are open to academia, startups and non-profits and are the only route with a defined process; (b) general contact form/email on indiaai.gov.in; (c) reach it indirectly through a MeitY consultation.
committees_and_bodies.format_rules: Calls for proposals impose eligibility thresholds — typically Indian-registered legal entity, sometimes minimum turnover or institutional affiliation. Individuals generally cannot apply.
committees_and_bodies.language: English.
committees_and_bodies.realistic: Not usable as a policy-influence route by an ordinary person. This is a delivery body, not a deliberative one. It consults industry and academia through invited roundtables. An individual's realistic option is to apply to a funding call if eligible, or to raise IndiaAI issues through the MeitY consultation route or the Standing Committee instead.
committees_and_bodies.note: CEO appointment VERIFIED via ANI, 5 June 2026. The DIC/IBD corporate structure is VERIFIED from MeitY recruitment advertisements issued under 'India AI Division, Digital India Corporation'. I did not find a published board or governing-council membership list — treat the internal governance above the CEO/COO level as UNVERIFIED.

committees_and_bodies.body: AI Governance and Economic Group (AIGEG)
committees_and_bodies.local_name: एआई गवर्नेंस एंड इकोनॉमिक ग्रुप
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: India's central institutional mechanism for AI governance policy development and inter-ministerial coordination. Mandate covers cross-sectoral AI governance, policy alignment across government, and labour-market impacts of AI. This is the seat where an Indian AI law would be shaped before it reaches Cabinet.

chair.name: Ashwini Vaishnaw
chair.role: Chairperson (Minister of Electronics and IT, Railways, and I&B). Vice-Chairperson: Jitin Prasada, Minister of State for Electronics & IT and Commerce & Industry.

committees_and_bodies.business: Constituted 16 April 2026. Composed of senior Government of India stakeholders across policy development, science and technology, security and economic affairs. Supported by a Technology and Policy Expert Committee (TPEC) which advises it on global developments, emerging technologies, risks and regulation. Operationalises the India AI Governance Guidelines.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: None. There is no public submission mechanism, no published meeting calendar, no minutes. Indirect routes only: a MeitY consultation, the Parliamentary Standing Committee, or an RTI application to MeitY for AIGEG records.
committees_and_bodies.format_rules: RTI application fee INR 10. RTI is restricted to Indian citizens — foreign nationals cannot file.
committees_and_bodies.language: English.
committees_and_bodies.realistic: Not usable directly. This is a closed inter-ministerial body of serving officials. Be honest with anyone planning engagement: the only handle an outsider has is RTI (citizens only) or influencing MeitY upstream. Membership of the TPEC is by invitation and the criteria are not published.
committees_and_bodies.note: Chair, vice-chair, constitution date and the TPEC relationship VERIFIED from PIB Press Release PRID 2252739. Full membership list is stated in the release to be in a linked annex PDF which I did not retrieve — individual members beyond the chair and vice-chair are UNVERIFIED.

committees_and_bodies.body: India AI Impact Summit 2026
committees_and_bodies.local_name: भारत एआई इम्पैक्ट शिखर सम्मेलन 2026
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: Host of the fourth in the series of global AI summits (after Bletchley, Seoul, Paris). Held 19-20 February 2026 at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi. Organised by MeitY/IndiaAI under a 'Sutras and Chakras' framework. Set the agenda for Global South AI positioning; the India AI Governance Guidelines were foregrounded there.

chair.name: Ashwini Vaishnaw
chair.role: Minister responsible (MeitY); hosted by Prime Minister Narendra Modi

committees_and_bodies.business: Concluded 20 February 2026. Current business is implementation and follow-through of summit outcomes. The Summit ran a formal pre-summit stakeholder consultation in June 2025 with dedicated category sessions for international organisations, industry, startups, academia AND civil society, plus a Global South Showcase and a research symposium. UN ODET ran side events.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: The stakeholder consultation form at impact.indiaai.gov.in/stakeholder-consultation (now closed — the sessions it served ran in June 2025). Civil society was a named, separately-slotted category, so engagement was formally possible. Physical attendance required accreditation/registration. Side events were the more open route.
committees_and_bodies.format_rules: No signature threshold. Accreditation and invitation controlled participation in the main programme.
committees_and_bodies.language: English.
committees_and_bodies.realistic: Civil society engagement was real but curated. The stakeholder consultation genuinely had a civil-society slot, which is better than the Paris or Bletchley precedent. However, the window was in June 2025 — eight months before the event — so anyone who discovered the Summit in 2026 had already missed the substantive input point. The realistic lesson for future summits: the consultation opens roughly 6-9 months before, on the summit's own domain, not on the ministry's. Watch impact.indiaai.gov.in, not meity.gov.in.
committees_and_bodies.note: Summit dates, venue and the existence of a civil-society consultation track VERIFIED from impact.indiaai.gov.in. The consultation sessions are dated June 2025 on that page; the page does not state whether the form remains open, and it appears to be historical.

committees_and_bodies.body: MyGov (Citizen Engagement Platform)
committees_and_bodies.local_name: माईगव
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: Cross-government citizen consultation platform under MeitY/Digital India Corporation. Used inconsistently for MeitY drafts; hosts discussions, polls, and 'Share your ideas' consultations, including on AI and digital policy.

chair.name: UNVERIFIED
chair.role: CEO, MyGov — I did not verify the current officeholder and am not naming one.

committees_and_bodies.business: Runs alongside, not instead of, MeitY's email-based consultations. Not every MeitY AI consultation is mirrored here — the 2026 IT Rules AI-labelling consultation ran by email only.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: Register a free account (mobile number or email), then comment on an open 'Discuss' or 'Consultation' task. Comments are public and visible to other users, which is the opposite of MeitY's confidential email route.
committees_and_bodies.format_rules: None. Free registration. Requires an Indian mobile number for some functions.
committees_and_bodies.language: English and Hindi interface; some content in other Indian languages. No foreign-language support.
committees_and_bodies.realistic: Usable and low-friction if a relevant consultation is live, and it is the only Indian route where your submission is publicly visible. But it is not the authoritative channel — for AI policy specifically, the email consultation is where MeitY actually reads submissions. Treat MyGov as supplementary. Do not rely on it as the only place you check for open windows.
committees_and_bodies.note: Platform existence and function VERIFIED; I deliberately did not verify current MyGov leadership and have marked it UNVERIFIED rather than guess. MyGov's role relative to MeitY email consultations is inferred from the observed pattern that the April 2026 IT Rules consultation used email only.

committees_and_bodies.body: House of Representatives Committee on Cabinet
committees_and_bodies.local_name: 衆議院 内閣委員会
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: The lead Diet committee for AI. Handles legislation under the Cabinet Office, which owns the AI Act (人工知能関連技術の研究開発及び活用の推進に関する法律), the AI Strategy Headquarters, science and technology policy, digital policy and personal information protection. Japan's AI Act was scrutinised here.

chair.name: UNVERIFIED — see note
chair.role: 委員長 (Chair). The official roster dated 24 April 2026 lists YAMASHITA Takashi (山下貴司, LDP), but Yamashita became Minister of Justice in the cabinet inaugurated 17 September 2026 and cannot simultaneously chair the committee.

committees_and_bodies.business: Implementation oversight of the AI Act (in force since 2025) and the AI Basic Plan Phase II adopted by Cabinet decision on 14 July 2026. The AI Act is a promotion statute with no penalties, so committee scrutiny is about plan implementation and budget rather than enforcement.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: There is effectively no direct public-submission route to a Japanese Diet committee. Committees hear 参考人 (sankōnin, expert witnesses) and hold 公聴会 (kōchōkai, public hearings) on major bills, but witnesses are selected by the committee's 理事会 (board of directors) on party nomination. The Diet petition system (請願) requires a sitting Diet member to formally introduce your petition — you cannot file one yourself.
committees_and_bodies.format_rules: No signature threshold, but the Diet petition route has a hard procedural gate: a Diet member must sponsor and introduce the petition (紹介議員). Without a sponsoring member it does not exist.
committees_and_bodies.language: Japanese only. Proceedings, rosters and all submission procedures are Japanese-language. No English service.
committees_and_bodies.realistic: Not realistically usable by an outsider, and not usable at all by a non-Japanese speaker acting alone. Be blunt about this: the Japanese Diet has no equivalent of a select-committee call for written evidence. The practical route into Japanese AI policy is the executive branch's public comment system (e-Gov), not the legislature. If you must reach the committee, the realistic path is through a member's office or an affiliated industry/academic association.
committees_and_bodies.note: The committee's existence, jurisdiction and membership URL are VERIFIED. The CHAIR IS NOT VERIFIED as of today: the live Shugiin roster page was still showing an as-of date of 24 April 2026 with Yamashita Takashi as chair, which is stale given the 17 September 2026 cabinet. Re-check the roster page directly — it carries a 現在 (as-of) date in the top-right which is the field to read. Do not cite Yamashita as current chair.

committees_and_bodies.body: House of Councillors Committee on Cabinet
committees_and_bodies.local_name: 参議院 内閣委員会
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: Upper-house counterpart. Same jurisdiction: Cabinet Office bills including AI, science and technology policy, digital, personal information protection. Reviews AI legislation after Lower House passage.

chair.name: KITAMURA Tsuneo (北村経夫)
chair.role: 委員長 (Chair), Liberal Democratic Party

committees_and_bodies.business: AI Act implementation oversight and the AI Basic Plan Phase II. Committee composition: chair plus 4 理事 (directors) and 18 members, spanning LDP, CDP, DPP, Komeito, Ishin, Sanseitō, JCP and others.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: Same as the Lower House: 参考人 (expert witness) appearance by committee invitation only, or a 請願 (petition) which requires a sitting Councillor to introduce it. No open written-evidence process.
committees_and_bodies.format_rules: Petition requires a sponsoring member (紹介議員). No numeric threshold.
committees_and_bodies.language: Japanese only. The Sangiin site has a thin English section but committee rosters and petition procedure are Japanese-only.
committees_and_bodies.realistic: Not realistically usable by an outsider. Same assessment as the Lower House committee. Its one practical advantage is that the Sangiin roster page is better maintained — it carried an as-of date of 21 September 2026, one day before this research, which is why this chair is verified and the Lower House one is not.
committees_and_bodies.note: Chair VERIFIED from the official Sangiin roster page, as-of date 21 September 2026. Session context: the 221st Diet (special session) shown as running 18 February to 25 July 2026.

committees_and_bodies.body: House of Representatives Committee on Economy, Trade and Industry
committees_and_bodies.local_name: 衆議院 経済産業委員会
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: Scrutinises METI, which owns AI industrial policy, the AI Guidelines for Business (jointly with MIC), semiconductor and compute policy, and — new in 2026 — a dedicated AI Industry Strategy Division (AI産業戦略課). This is the committee for the industrial/economic side of AI rather than the governance framework side.

chair.name: KUDŌ Shōzō (工藤彰三)
chair.role: 委員長 (Chair)

committees_and_bodies.business: METI oversight including the AI Industry Strategy Division established in 2026 and METI's role in delivering the AI Basic Plan Phase II. METI minister: AKAZAWA Ryosei.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: 参考人 by invitation; 請願 requires a sponsoring member. No open call for written evidence. The productive route to METI policy is METI's own public comment channel, which feeds into e-Gov.
committees_and_bodies.format_rules: Petition requires a sponsoring Diet member.
committees_and_bodies.language: Japanese only.
committees_and_bodies.realistic: Not usable directly. Go to METI's consultation page instead — that is where an outsider's written input can actually land. Note that meti.go.jp/feedback renders poorly for automated fetching; the reliable aggregator is the e-Gov public comment portal.
committees_and_bodies.note: Chair and as-of date (令和8年9月17日 = 17 September 2026) VERIFIED from the official Shugiin roster page. Note the Shugiin URL pattern: iin_j0090.htm is Economy/Trade/Industry and iin_j0110.htm is Environment — the numbering does not follow the display order, so do not guess URLs.

committees_and_bodies.body: House of Councillors Committee on Economy, Trade and Industry
committees_and_bodies.local_name: 参議院 経済産業委員会
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: Upper-house METI oversight: AI industrial policy, compute and semiconductor strategy, AI Guidelines for Business.

chair.name: HAMAGUCHI Makoto (浜口誠)
chair.role: 委員長 (Chair)

committees_and_bodies.business: METI oversight under AKAZAWA Ryosei; AI Basic Plan Phase II industrial delivery.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: 参考人 by invitation; 請願 requires a sponsoring Councillor.
committees_and_bodies.format_rules: Petition requires a sponsoring member.
committees_and_bodies.language: Japanese only.
committees_and_bodies.realistic: Not usable directly by an outsider. Use e-Gov public comment for METI rule-making instead.
committees_and_bodies.note: Chair VERIFIED from the official Sangiin roster page, as-of 令和8年9月11日 = 11 September 2026. Caution: automated readers frequently mis-convert Reiwa 8 to 2024 — Reiwa 8 is 2026.

committees_and_bodies.body: Artificial Intelligence Strategy Headquarters
committees_and_bodies.local_name: 人工知能戦略本部
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: The statutory apex AI body, established under the AI Act (人工知能関連技術の研究開発及び活用の推進に関する法律). Drafts and administers the AI Basic Plan (人工知能基本計画), coordinates all ministries on AI, and is the control tower for Japanese AI policy. Because it is statutory rather than advisory, it displaced the earlier non-statutory AI Strategy Council.

chair.name: TAKAICHI Sanae (高市早苗)
chair.role: 本部長 (Director-General) — ex officio as Prime Minister. Deputy Directors: KIHARA Minoru (Chief Cabinet Secretary) and the Minister of State for AI Strategy. Members: all other Ministers of State.

committees_and_bodies.business: Adopted the first AI Basic Plan (人工知能基本計画, 'Trustworthy AI / Japan's Revival') by Cabinet decision on 23 December 2025. Adopted the AI Basic Plan Phase II (第Ⅱ期, 'Japan AX — stronger, richer') by Cabinet decision on 14 July 2026. A public comment on the Phase II draft (素案) opened 19 June 2026. Secretariat sits in the Cabinet Office.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: The Headquarters itself does not take direct submissions. It exposes itself to the public exclusively through the e-Gov public comment system when it puts a draft Basic Plan or implementing order out — that is the single, real handle. Meeting agendas, distributed materials and summary minutes (議事要旨) are published on the Cabinet Office page after each meeting, which makes it unusually transparent to read even though it is closed to input.
committees_and_bodies.format_rules: None. Comment periods are, as a matter of the Administrative Procedure Act, in principle 30 days or more from the notice date.
committees_and_bodies.language: Japanese only for the Headquarters pages and for e-Gov submissions.
committees_and_bodies.realistic: Read-only for most people, but genuinely open at the plan-drafting moments. The 19 June 2026 Phase II draft consultation is the pattern to watch: when a Basic Plan is revised, a real 30-day window opens on e-Gov and anyone may submit. Outside those windows there is nothing to engage with. Note the Cabinet Office explicitly states it weighs comments on substance, not volume, so organised mass-identical submissions are discounted by design.
committees_and_bodies.note: Structure, leadership formula, statutory basis and both Basic Plan cabinet decision dates VERIFIED from the Cabinet Office pages www8.cao.go.jp/cstp/ai/ai_hq/ai_hq.html and www8.cao.go.jp/cstp/ai/index.html. The Minister of State for AI Strategy as at the 17 September 2026 reshuffle is FURUKAWA Toshiharu (see separate entry); the Cabinet Office HQ page was still naming the previous holder, ONODA Kimi, indicating the page lags the reshuffle.

committees_and_bodies.body: Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence Strategy / Minister for Digital Transformation
committees_and_bodies.local_name: AI戦略担当大臣 / デジタル大臣
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: The named political owner of the AI brief. Concurrently Minister for Digital Transformation and Minister of State for Science and Technology Policy, plus cybersecurity, intellectual property, space and ocean policy. Deputy Director of the AI Strategy Headquarters.

chair.name: FURUKAWA Toshiharu
chair.role: Minister for Digital Transformation / Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence Strategy / Minister of State for Science and Technology Policy (plus further portfolios). Appointed in the Takaichi reshuffled cabinet inaugurated 17 September 2026. Predecessor in the AI Strategy brief: ONODA Kimi, who moved to Economic Security.

committees_and_bodies.business: Delivering the AI Basic Plan Phase II (Cabinet decision 14 July 2026). Note the significant 2026 consolidation: AI Strategy, Digital Transformation and Science & Technology Policy are now held by one person, where in the first Takaichi cabinet (Oct 2025) AI Strategy sat with Science & Technology under Onoda and Digital sat separately.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: No direct route to the minister. Digital Agency and Cabinet Office rule-making under this portfolio goes out for public comment via e-Gov.
committees_and_bodies.format_rules: None.
committees_and_bodies.language: The Kantei site has a full English mirror at japan.kantei.go.jp, which is genuinely useful and one of the few English-language Japanese government resources that is kept current. Consultation itself is Japanese-only.
committees_and_bodies.realistic: The minister is not directly reachable, but japan.kantei.go.jp is the correct authoritative English source for who holds the AI brief, and it is updated promptly — it already reflected the 17 September 2026 reshuffle. Use it rather than Wikipedia, which was still showing the October 2025 line-up.
committees_and_bodies.note: VERIFIED from the official Kantei English cabinet list at japan.kantei.go.jp/105/meibo/daijin/index.html, which explicitly attributes 'Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence Strategy' to FURUKAWA Toshiharu and dates the cabinet to 17 September 2026. Other ministers verified on the same page: AKAZAWA Ryosei (METI), FUJII Hisayuki (MIC), KIHARA Minoru (Chief Cabinet Secretary). Cross-check note: English Wikipedia's 'First Takaichi cabinet' article gave the superseded October 2025 line-up (Onoda for AI, Hayashi for MIC) — a concrete example of why prior knowledge fails here.

committees_and_bodies.body: AI Strategy Council
committees_and_bodies.local_name: AI戦略会議
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: The non-statutory expert advisory council established in 2023 that produced Japan's interim AI policy positions and laid the groundwork for the AI Act. Now largely superseded.

chair.name: UNVERIFIED
chair.role: Chair — I did not verify the current or final chair and will not name one.

committees_and_bodies.business: Largely dormant. The most recent meeting recorded on the Cabinet Office page is the 14th session on 2 June 2025, with the previous one on 4 February 2025. Its function has been absorbed by the statutory AI Strategy Headquarters and its expert panel (専門調査会). Included here specifically so it is not mistaken for the live body — a lot of secondary commentary still points at it.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: None. Advisory body, closed membership. Agendas, distributed materials and summary minutes are published as PDFs after each meeting.
committees_and_bodies.format_rules: None.
committees_and_bodies.language: Japanese only.
committees_and_bodies.realistic: Not usable and, more importantly, no longer the right target. If someone directs you to the AI戦略会議 as Japan's AI control tower, that advice is out of date — go to the 人工知能戦略本部 instead.
committees_and_bodies.note: Meeting history (last recorded session 2 June 2025) VERIFIED from the Cabinet Office page. The chair is deliberately left UNVERIFIED. The supersession by the statutory Headquarters is an inference from the meeting record plus the AI Act's creation of the Headquarters — stated here as an inference, not a fact.

committees_and_bodies.body: e-Gov Public Comment (Administrative Procedure Act public comment procedure)
committees_and_bodies.local_name: e-Gov パブリックコメント（意見公募手続）
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: The single mandatory consultation channel for all Japanese ministries when making 命令等 (cabinet orders, ministerial ordinances, notices/告示, administrative guidance). Every AI-related ordinance, notice and Basic Plan draft from the Cabinet Office, METI, MIC and the Digital Agency passes through here. Statutory basis: Administrative Procedure Act (行政手続法), Chapter 6. Policy oversight sits with MIC's Administrative Management Bureau.

chair.name: Not applicable
chair.role: System, not a body. Administered across government; procedure overseen by the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications (総務省行政管理局).

committees_and_bodies.business: Continuously open. Live cases are listed on the portal's 意見募集中案件一覧. AI-relevant recent case: the AI Basic Plan Phase II draft (人工知能基本計画（素案）), comment call announced 19 June 2026.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: Find the case on the portal, open it, read the 意見募集要項 (the case-specific comment call sheet — this is the load-bearing document), then use the 意見提出 (submit opinion) form. Required fields vary BY CASE and are controlled by that sheet: if a name/address/phone/email field is not displayed on the form, that information is not required. The only universally mandatory field is the opinion text itself, which has a character limit that will hard-error if exceeded. No account registration is required.
committees_and_bodies.format_rules: No signature or supporter threshold. Statutory minimum comment period: in principle 30 days or more from the notice date. The agency must publish a summary of comments received and its response when it finalises the rule.
committees_and_bodies.language: Japanese only. There is no English interface, no English guidance, and comments are expected in Japanese. Nothing formally bars a non-Japanese speaker or a foreign national from submitting — there is no nationality check — but in practice a submission that officials cannot read will not be processed meaningfully.
committees_and_bodies.realistic: This is the single most usable formal route in Japan and the one to actually recommend — no account, no fee, no nationality bar, a statutory 30-day floor, and a legal duty on the agency to publish its response to comments. Two honest limits. First, language: it is Japanese-only end to end, so a non-speaker needs a translated submission and cannot navigate the portal unaided; machine translation of the interface works but machine-translating your own submission into Japanese produces text officials visibly discount. Second, the system explicitly weights substance over volume and says identical repeated opinions do not get proportional weight — a coordinated campaign of identical comments is designed not to work here. One well-argued Japanese-language submission beats a thousand copies.
committees_and_bodies.note: System description, the 30-day statutory floor, the no-account/conditional-fields submission mechanics and the substance-over-volume rule are all VERIFIED from the official e-Gov pages public-comment.e-gov.go.jp/contents/about-public-comment and /contents/help/guide/submission.html. The absence of English support is a verified negative — the official pages carry no language options and no guidance for foreign submitters. The e-Gov top page is JavaScript-rendered and will not load for simple fetchers; the /contents/ subpages do.

committees_and_bodies.body: National Assembly Science, ICT, Broadcasting and Communications Committee
committees_and_bodies.local_name: 국회 과학기술정보방송통신위원회 (과방위)
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: The lead standing committee for AI. Oversees the Ministry of Science and ICT (과학기술정보통신부), the Korea Communications Commission (방송통신위원회) and the Nuclear Safety and Security Commission (원자력안전위원회). It produced and passed the AI Framework Act (consolidating 19 separate bills) and handles all amendments to it, plus semiconductors, R&D budget and broadcasting.

chair.name: SONG Gi-heon (송기헌)
chair.role: 위원장 (Chair), Democratic Party of Korea, three-term member. Elected for the second half of the 22nd National Assembly.

committees_and_bodies.business: Song took the chair on 30 June 2026, naming AI, semiconductors and broadcasting fairness as his stated priorities. Oversight of AI Framework Act implementation since its 22 January 2026 entry into force, and of MSIT's enforcement decree and notices. Note the political context: the People Power Party members reportedly submitted en-bloc resignation letters around the handover, so committee composition may be unstable.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: Two routes. (1) 입법예고 (legislative pre-announcement) on National Assembly bills — bills referred to committee are posted for public comment on the Assembly's bill information system, typically 10 days, and anyone may submit written opinions online. (2) 공청회 (public hearings) with invited witnesses, by committee selection. The separate 국민동의청원 petition route (below) also lands bills in this committee.
committees_and_bodies.format_rules: No threshold for a written 입법예고 opinion. Requires the standard Korean identity verification for the Assembly's online systems.
committees_and_bodies.language: Korean only. The committee site (science.na.go.kr) and the bill pre-announcement system are Korean-language. The National Assembly has an English site but it does not carry participation functions.
committees_and_bodies.realistic: The 입법예고 route is formally open and genuinely used, but it has two practical gates that exclude most outsiders: everything is in Korean, and the Assembly's online systems generally require Korean identity verification (본인인증) which in practice needs a Korean mobile number or a joint certificate — foreign residents with an ARC can often do this, foreign non-residents usually cannot. The 10-day window is also short. For a non-Korean-speaker this is effectively closed without a Korean intermediary.
committees_and_bodies.note: Chair and date VERIFIED via Korean press reporting of the 30 June 2026 Democratic Party decision and vote (Song selected over Lee Eon-ju). Jurisdiction over MSIT/KCC/NSSC VERIFIED from Korean Wikipedia. The official committee site science.na.go.kr blocks automated access via robots.txt, so the member list was not directly retrieved — individual member names are UNVERIFIED. The site is served on port 444 in some links (science.na.go.kr:444); the standard URL above should resolve for a human browser.

committees_and_bodies.body: Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT)
committees_and_bodies.local_name: 과학기술정보통신부 (과기정통부)
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: The competent authority under the AI Framework Act. Powers include: investigating suspected violations and conducting on-site inspections (Art. 40), issuing corrective orders and service suspension orders, confirming on request whether a system is 'high-impact AI', and drafting the Presidential Decree and notices. Also owns national AI R&D, compute and the AI Safety Institute.

chair.name: BAE Kyung-hoon (배경훈)
chair.role: Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Science and ICT (부총리 겸 과학기술정보통신부 장관)

committees_and_bodies.business: Implementing the AI Framework Act, in force 22 January 2026. Released the draft regulatory package for public comment on 8 September 2025: Enforcement Decree, Safety Assurance Notice (using a 10^26 FLOP training-compute threshold plus risk criteria), Business Responsibilities Notice for high-impact AI operators, AI Safety Guidelines, and the High-Impact AI Determination Guideline. MSIT has indicated a one-year grace period before administrative fines are imposed — i.e. to roughly January 2027. The minister's elevation to Deputy Prime Minister rank is itself significant: AI policy now sits at DPM level.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: Ministry rule-making goes through 입법예고 / 행정예고 (legislative and administrative pre-announcement) posted on the Government Legislation Centre's citizen participation portal, 국민참여입법센터. Anyone may submit an opinion online against a specific posted draft. MSIT also runs 공청회 (public hearings) and 간담회 (roundtables) on major AI notices, generally invitation-based.
committees_and_bodies.format_rules: No threshold. Statutory pre-announcement periods: normally 40 days for 입법예고 of decrees, 20 days for 행정예고 of notices — shorter in urgent cases, which MSIT has used.
committees_and_bodies.language: Korean only. 국민참여입법센터 has no English interface and drafts are published only in Korean.
committees_and_bodies.realistic: Formally open to anyone including foreign companies and individuals — Korea does not restrict pre-announcement comments by nationality, and international law firms routinely file on behalf of clients. But it is Korean-language end to end and the portal's submission function generally expects Korean identity verification. The honest assessment: usable by a Korean speaker or through Korean counsel; not usable unaided by a non-speaker. The 10^26 FLOP threshold and the high-impact criteria were both meaningfully shaped by comments in the 2025 window, so this route does have demonstrated influence.
committees_and_bodies.note: Minister VERIFIED same-day (22 September 2026) from Korean press coverage of him speaking as 부총리 겸 과학기술정보통신부 장관. Act effective date (22 Jan 2026), the September 2025 regulatory package contents, the 10^26 FLOP threshold and the one-year fine grace period VERIFIED from Baker Botts and Cooley analyses. I could not verify whether the enforcement decree has since been finalised in its consulted form — treat the final text as UNVERIFIED.

committees_and_bodies.body: National AI Committee
committees_and_bodies.local_name: 국가인공지능위원회 (National AI Strategy Committee / 국가인공지능전략위원회 — naming UNVERIFIED, see note)
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: Presidentially-chaired apex AI body referenced in the AI Framework Act. Article 34 empowers it to impose additional safety and reliability requirements on high-impact AI deployers beyond the Act's baseline — a genuinely substantive power, not merely advisory. Functions as the national AI control tower above MSIT.

chair.name: UNVERIFIED
chair.role: Chaired ex officio by the President of the Republic of Korea (currently Lee Jae-myung). The vice-chair and the private-sector membership were not verified and are not named here.

committees_and_bodies.business: Operative under the AI Framework Act since 22 January 2026. Its Article 34 power to add requirements on high-impact AI is the provision to watch, because it lets Korea tighten obligations without amending the statute.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: No direct public submission route. Indirect only: comment on MSIT drafts via 국민참여입법센터, or reach the committee's agenda through the National Assembly's 과방위.
committees_and_bodies.format_rules: None applicable.
committees_and_bodies.language: Korean only.
committees_and_bodies.realistic: Not usable directly. A presidentially-chaired committee with closed membership. Its importance to an outside observer is analytical rather than participatory: because Article 34 lets it add binding requirements administratively, watching its output matters more than trying to address it.
committees_and_bodies.note: MARKED UNVERIFIED ON NAME AND MEMBERSHIP. The Act's creation of a presidentially-chaired national AI committee and its Article 34 power are VERIFIED from FPF and Cooley analyses of the Act, which use the English rendering 'National AI Committee'. Separately, Korean-language sources use 국가인공지능전략위원회 ('National AI Strategy Committee') for a body launched under the Lee administration. I could not establish within this research whether these are the same body, a renaming, or two distinct structures. Resolve this before citing — do not treat the Korean and English names above as confirmed equivalents, and do not name a vice-chair.

committees_and_bodies.body: AI Safety Institute (Korea AISI)
committees_and_bodies.local_name: AI안전연구소
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: Statutory body established under the AI Framework Act to evaluate AI risk and develop safety standards. Korea's node in the International Network of AI Safety Institutes. Co-produced the bilingual Korea AI Basic Act resource with the Future of Life Institute.

chair.name: KIM Myuhngjoo
chair.role: Director, AI Safety Institute

committees_and_bodies.business: Operates under MSIT with the Electronics and Telecommunications Research Institute (ETRI) as host/supporting organisation — note this dual line: it is statutorily grounded but institutionally embedded in a government research institute rather than standing alone. Work programme covers AI safety policy, evaluation methodology and international AISI collaboration.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: No formal comment mechanism. Practical routes: research collaboration enquiries and general contact via aisi.re.kr; international engagement through the AI Safety Institute network; policy input indirectly via MSIT pre-announcement.
committees_and_bodies.format_rules: None; no formal participation process exists to have a threshold.
committees_and_bodies.language: Korean and English. Korea AISI maintains a genuine English site — a notable exception in this jurisdiction and the most accessible Korean AI body for a non-Korean speaker.
committees_and_bodies.realistic: Not a participation route in any formal sense, but it is the most approachable Korean AI institution for an outsider because it has a working English presence and an internationally-facing research remit. Researchers and technical contributors can realistically make contact. Ordinary citizens have no route here and should use the petition or the MSIT pre-announcement instead.
committees_and_bodies.note: Director and the MSIT/ETRI institutional relationship VERIFIED from the institute's own English site aisi.re.kr/eng/contents/23 and its site footer. The statutory basis under the AI Framework Act is VERIFIED indirectly via Cooley's analysis, which refers to an 'AI Safety Research Institute' established by the law; the exact article number is UNVERIFIED.

committees_and_bodies.body: National Assembly National Petition System (electronic petition with public assent)
committees_and_bodies.local_name: 국민동의청원 (국회전자청원)
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: Not AI-specific, but AI petitions are routed to the 과학기술정보방송통신위원회. This is the one route in this entire research with a genuine, automatic legislative trigger, which is why it deserves precise treatment.

chair.name: Not applicable
chair.role: System operated by the National Assembly Secretariat.

committees_and_bodies.business: Continuously open. Any petition reaching threshold is referred to the subject-matter standing committee.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: Precise mechanism, in three stages. (1) REGISTRATION: an identity-verified citizen drafts a petition. (2) PUBLICITY GATE: the petition must gather 100 supporters within a set window; the Assembly then conducts a compliance/legality review within 7 days, and if it passes, the petition becomes publicly listed. (3) ASSENT: 50,000 signatures within 30 days of public listing. On reaching 50,000 the petition is 성립 (established) and is AUTOMATICALLY REFERRED to the relevant standing committee, which is then obliged to take it up as a formal agenda item under its petition-review procedure. The threshold was lowered from 100,000 to 50,000 in December 2021. Both petitioning and signing require real-name authentication (본인인증), which eliminates duplicate-account inflation — a deliberate design difference from the former Blue House petition system.
committees_and_bodies.format_rules: 100 supporters to pass the publicity gate; then 50,000 verified signatures within 30 days to be formally established and referred to committee. Real-name authentication required to create or to sign.
committees_and_bodies.language: Korean only. No English interface. Identity verification is built on Korean domestic authentication infrastructure.
committees_and_bodies.realistic: The trigger is real and this is the most powerful citizen route in any of the four jurisdictions covered — 50,000 verified signatures compel committee referral, which no other system here does. But be honest about two things. First, referral is not action: Korean press and civic groups have documented petitions that cleared 50,000 and were then left without a single 청원심사소위 review session, sometimes indefinitely, with the criticism '5만명 동의 받으면 뭐하나' ('what good is 50,000 signatures'). The trigger compels referral, not consideration, and certainly not legislation. Second, the real-name authentication gate means it is a Korean-citizens-and-residents system in practice; a non-Korean-speaker cannot use it and a non-resident generally cannot authenticate. Within those limits, an ordinary Korean citizen genuinely can use it, and 50,000 in 30 days is achievable for a motivated constituency.
committees_and_bodies.note: The two-stage threshold (100 then 50,000/30 days), the December 2021 reduction from 100,000, the automatic committee referral and the real-name authentication requirement are VERIFIED from Korean-language sources including the National Assembly's own guidance page (assembly.go.kr menuNo=600249, which blocks automated fetching via robots.txt but is publicly readable). The portal URL is VERIFIED as the National Assembly e-petition site (국회전자청원). The post-referral inaction problem is VERIFIED from Korean press criticism (Newstomato, Danbi News).

committees_and_bodies.body: Special Committee on Artificial Intelligence (on PL 2338/2023)
committees_and_bodies.local_name: Comissão Especial sobre Inteligência Artificial (PL 2338/23) — Câmara dos Deputados
committees_and_bodies.ai_jurisdiction: The decisive seat for Brazilian AI regulation right now. A temporary special committee of the Chamber of Deputies, 57th Legislature, created to analyse PL 2338/2023 (the Marco Legal da IA) after the Senate passed it. Under Brazil's rapporteur system, the relator's substitutive text is what the Chamber votes on — the relator, not the committee president, is the controlling seat.

chair.name: Luisa Canziani (President) and Aguinaldo Ribeiro (Relator)
chair.role: Presidente: Dep. Luisa Canziani (PSD-PR). Relator: Dep. Aguinaldo Ribeiro (PP-PB), designated 20 May 2025. Committee installed 20 May 2025. Secretary-Executive: Ana Karina de Macedo Tito, +55 61 3216-6235.

committees_and_bodies.business: Status as of September 2026: 'Aguardando Parecer do(a) Relator(a) na Comissão Especial' — still awaiting the rapporteur's opinion, sixteen months after his designation. 31 meetings held, 180 guests heard, 163 proposals voted. 37 bills now appended (apensados) to PL 2338/2023, with further appendings approved by the Mesa Diretora on 17 June, 1 September and 2 September 2026. The bill is under regime de prioridade (Art. 151, II, RICD) and will go to Plenary. The government's own AI governance bill creating the Sistema Nacional de Governança para a IA (SIA), proposed December 2025, was articulated with the relator and folded into this process. Separately PL 762/2026 (Rubens Pereira Júnior, PT-MA, 25 Feb 2026, high-consequence-sector AI framework amending the LGPD, Marco Civil and Consumer Code) was appended to PL 7132/2025 and received by this committee on 6 April 2026.
committees_and_bodies.public_route: Three real routes. (1) AUDIÊNCIAS PÚBLICAS — the committee has held 31 meetings and heard 180 guests; hearing requests are made by deputies, but civil society organisations are routinely invited and Data Privacy Brasil, IDEC and others have appeared. The route for an outsider is to ask a committee member to request your inclusion. (2) Written contributions sent directly to the committee secretariat or to the relator's office (gabinete) — Brazilian practice accepts and often publishes these as 'contribuições'. (3) e-Democracia, the Chamber's citizen participation portal, which runs Wikilegis text-commenting and enquetes on bills.
